questions.text: The area above the zygomatic arch is called:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (D) because the temporal fossa is the shallow depression on the side of the skull lying above the zygomatic arch, occupied mainly by the temporalis muscle. The infratemporal fossa (e) is the space below the zygomatic arch, so it is the mirror-image answer. The scalp (a) covers the vault of the skull, while the face (b) and preauricular region (c) lie anterior and inferior to this area.
questions.keyConcept: The temporal fossa lies above the zygomatic arch; the infratemporal fossa lies below it.

questions.text: The muscle that divides the neck into anterior & posterior triangles is:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (C) because the sternomastoid (sternocleidomastoid) runs obliquely across the neck from the manubrium and clavicle to the mastoid process, dividing each side of the neck into an anterior and a posterior triangle. Sternohyoid and sternothyroid (a, b) are infrahyoid strap muscles that lie within the muscular triangle. Omohyoid (d) and digastric (e) subdivide those triangles further but do not create the primary anterior/posterior division.
questions.keyConcept: The sternomastoid is the landmark muscle that separates the anterior from the posterior triangle of the neck.

questions.text: All the following arteries share in the blood supply of the head & neck EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (E) because the axillary artery is the continuation of the subclavian artery beyond the outer border of the first rib and supplies the upper limb, not the head and neck. The common carotid (a) and its internal (b) and external (c) divisions are the principal suppliers of the head and neck. The subclavian artery (d) contributes through its vertebral, thyrocervical and costocervical branches.
questions.keyConcept: The head and neck are supplied by the carotid and subclavian systems; the axillary artery supplies the upper limb.

questions.text: Right common carotid artery:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (C) because the right common carotid artery ends at the upper border of the thyroid cartilage, which lies opposite the disc between C3 and C4. Option (a) is wrong because the right common carotid is a branch of the brachiocephalic artery, not the arch of the aorta. Option (b) is wrong as it ends at the upper border of thyroid cartilage, (d) is wrong because the carotid sinus and body lie at its termination, and (e) is wrong because it divides into external and internal carotid arteries.
questions.keyConcept: The common carotid artery ends at the upper border of the thyroid cartilage (C3/C4 disc) by dividing into internal and external carotid arteries.
options: Is a branch of arch of aorta.
Ends at the level of the lower border of the cricoid cartilage.
Ends opposite the disc between C3 & C4.
Shows carotid sinus & body at its beginning.
Divides into external carotid & subclavian artery.

questions.text: The artery that ends inside the parotid gland is the:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (B) because the external carotid artery enters the substance of the parotid gland and ends within it at the level of the neck of the mandible by dividing into the superficial temporal and maxillary arteries. The internal carotid (c) does not enter the parotid; it ascends in the carotid sheath and enters the skull. The common carotid (a) ends in the neck, while the subclavian (d) and brachiocephalic (e) arteries never reach the parotid region.
questions.keyConcept: The external carotid artery is the deepest structure in the parotid gland and terminates inside it at the neck of the mandible.

questions.text: Match each artery in the left column with its appropriate description in the right column:
questions.explanation: The common carotid ends at the upper border of the thyroid cartilage by dividing into internal and external carotids. The external carotid terminates within the parotid gland at the neck of the mandible, whereas the internal carotid gives no branch in the neck and ends by supplying the brain. The vertebral artery is the first branch of the subclavian artery, and the left common carotid arises directly from the arch of the aorta.
questions.keyConcept: Each major head and neck artery has a characteristic termination: common carotid at the thyroid cartilage, external carotid in the parotid, internal carotid at the brain.

pairs.target: Ends at upper border of thyroid cartilage.
Ends at level of neck of mandible.

questions.text: The external carotid artery gives all the following branches EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (B) because the vertebral artery is the first branch of the subclavian artery, not of the external carotid. The facial (a) and occipital (c) arteries are true branches of the external carotid, and the superficial temporal (d) and maxillary (e) arteries are its two terminal branches within the parotid gland.
questions.keyConcept: The vertebral artery arises from the subclavian artery, never from the external carotid.

questions.text: Costocervical trunk is a branch of:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (D) because the costocervical trunk arises from the second part of the subclavian artery and divides into the superior intercostal and deep cervical arteries. The common carotid arteries (b, c) give no branches in the neck before their terminal division, and the internal carotid (e) similarly gives no cervical branches. The brachiocephalic artery (a) simply divides into the right common carotid and right subclavian arteries.
questions.keyConcept: The costocervical trunk is a branch of the second part of the subclavian artery.

questions.text: The vein that ends in subclavian vein is the:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (A) because the external jugular vein descends superficially across the sternomastoid and pierces the investing layer of deep fascia to drain into the subclavian vein. The internal jugular vein (b) joins the subclavian vein to form the brachiocephalic vein rather than ending in it. The brachiocephalic veins (d, e) unite to form the superior vena cava (c), which drains into the right atrium.
questions.keyConcept: The external jugular vein drains into the subclavian vein.

questions.text: Superior vena cava is formed by the union of:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (E) because the superior vena cava is formed behind the first right costal cartilage by the union of the right and left brachiocephalic veins. Option (c) describes the formation of a brachiocephalic vein, not the superior vena cava. The external jugular vein (a, b) drains into the subclavian vein and takes no direct part in forming the superior vena cava.
questions.keyConcept: The superior vena cava is formed by the union of the right and left brachiocephalic veins.

questions.text: As regards the parotid gland, choose the CORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (A) because the parotid gland occupies the space below and in front of the external auditory meatus, between the ramus of the mandible and the mastoid process. Option (b) is wrong because the duct pierces the buccinator rather than crossing over it, and (c) is wrong because the duct crosses over the masseter instead of piercing it. Option (d) is wrong because the gland contains the external carotid artery, and (e) is wrong because the parotid duct opens into the vestibule of the mouth opposite the second upper molar.
questions.keyConcept: The parotid gland lies below the external auditory meatus; its duct crosses masseter and pierces buccinator to open into the vestibule of the mouth.
options: It lies below external auditory meatus.
Its duct opens in floor of mouth.

questions.text: As regards the submandibular gland, choose the CORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (B) because the submandibular gland is J-shaped and folded around the posterior border of the mylohyoid, giving it a large superficial part and a smaller deep part. Option (a) is wrong because the parotid is the largest salivary gland, and (c) is wrong because its duct opens in the floor of the mouth beside the frenulum of the tongue. Option (d) describes the sublingual gland, and (e) is wrong because the facial nerve lies within the parotid gland.
questions.keyConcept: The submandibular gland wraps around the posterior border of mylohyoid, giving it superficial and deep parts.
options: It is the largest salivary gland.
It is formed of a superficial part & a deep part.
Its duct opens in the vestibule of the mouth.
It lies beneath the mucous membrane of the floor of the mouth.
It contains the facial nerve inside it.

questions.text: Match each structure in the neck in the left column with its related statement in the right column:
questions.explanation: The superficial fascia of the neck encloses the platysma, a muscle of facial expression supplied by the facial nerve. The investing layer of deep cervical fascia completely encircles the neck like a collar, splitting to enclose sternomastoid and trapezius. The pretracheal fascia forms a sheath for the thyroid gland, the prevertebral fascia covers the prevertebral muscles in front of the vertebral column, and the carotid sheath encloses the carotid arteries, the internal jugular vein and the vagus nerve.
questions.keyConcept: Each cervical fascial layer has a signature content: platysma in superficial fascia, thyroid in pretracheal fascia, and internal jugular vein in the carotid sheath.

questions.text: As regards the anterior triangle in the neck, choose the CORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (E) because the anterior triangle is subdivided by the digastric and omohyoid muscles into four smaller triangles: the digastric (submandibular), carotid, muscular and submental triangles. Option (a) is wrong because the anterior triangle lies in front of sternomastoid, and (b) and (c) are wrong because it is bounded posteriorly by sternomastoid and anteriorly by the midline of the neck. Option (d) is wrong because the base of the mandible forms its superior, not inferior, boundary.
questions.keyConcept: The anterior triangle of the neck is subdivided into four triangles: digastric, carotid, muscular and submental.
options: It lies behind the sternomastoid muscle.
It is bounded anteriorly by sternomastoid.
It is bounded posteriorly by midline of neck.
It is bounded inferiorly by base of mandible.

questions.text: Match each structure in the left column with its enclosing triangle in the right column:
questions.explanation: The muscular triangle contains the infrahyoid strap muscles together with the thyroid gland, larynx and trachea. The digastric (submandibular) triangle is occupied mainly by the submandibular salivary gland. The carotid triangle contains the carotid system and its related structures, including the common carotid artery, the facial vein as it descends to join the internal jugular vein, and the hypoglossal nerve as it crosses the carotid arteries.
questions.keyConcept: The carotid triangle houses the carotid vessels, hypoglossal nerve and facial vein; the muscular triangle holds the strap muscles; the digastric triangle holds the submandibular gland.

questions.text: All the following are contents of orbit EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (E) because the maxillary nerve leaves the middle cranial fossa through the foramen rotundum to enter the pterygopalatine fossa, not the orbit proper. The oculomotor nerve (a) and ophthalmic nerve (b) enter through the superior orbital fissure, and the ophthalmic artery (d) enters via the optic canal. The lacrimal gland (c) occupies the lacrimal fossa in the upper lateral part of the orbit.
questions.keyConcept: The maxillary nerve passes into the pterygopalatine fossa; only its infraorbital continuation runs in the orbital floor.

questions.text: As regards the bony orbit, choose the INCORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (B) because this statement is incorrect: the apex of the orbit is directed posteriorly, while the opening on the face is the orbital base. The orbit is indeed pyramidal (a), with the optic canal at its posteriorly directed apex (c). It has superior and inferior orbital fissures (d) and contains the lacrimal gland, sac and duct (e).
questions.keyConcept: The orbit is a pyramid whose base opens on the face and whose apex points posteriorly at the optic canal.
options: Its apex is the opening on face.
It shows optic canal at its apex.

questions.text: Match each muscle in the left column with its nerve supply in the right column:
questions.explanation: The oculomotor nerve supplies all the extraocular muscles except two, so levator palpebrae superioris, superior rectus and medial rectus are all oculomotor. The two exceptions follow the classic rule LR6 SO4: lateral rectus is supplied by the abducent (6th) nerve and superior oblique by the trochlear (4th) nerve. The ophthalmic and optic nerves are purely sensory and supply no eye muscles.
questions.keyConcept: LR6 SO4: lateral rectus is abducent, superior oblique is trochlear, and the oculomotor nerve supplies all the rest.

questions.text: Sensory supply of lacrimal gland is:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (D) because the lacrimal nerve, a branch of the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve, carries the sensory supply to the lacrimal gland. The oculomotor (a), trochlear (b) and abducent (c) nerves are purely motor to the extraocular muscles. The optic nerve (e) is a special sensory nerve concerned only with vision.
questions.keyConcept: The lacrimal gland receives its sensory supply from the lacrimal branch of the ophthalmic nerve.

questions.text: All the following are contents of cranial cavity EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (D) because the external carotid artery remains entirely outside the skull, ending within the parotid gland. The middle meningeal vessels (a) run in the extradural space of the cranial cavity, and the vertebral (b) and internal carotid (e) arteries both enter the cranial cavity to supply the brain. The pituitary gland (c) sits in the sella turcica within the middle cranial fossa.
questions.keyConcept: The external carotid artery never enters the cranial cavity; the internal carotid and vertebral arteries do.

questions.text: Match each artery in the left column with its artery of origin in the right column:
questions.explanation: The anterior spinal artery arises from the intracranial part of the vertebral artery, and the two vertebral arteries then unite to form the basilar artery, which ends by dividing into the two posterior cerebral arteries. The internal carotid artery gives the ophthalmic artery within the cranial cavity and ends by dividing into the anterior and middle cerebral arteries. The middle meningeal artery is a branch of the first part of the maxillary artery and enters the skull through the foramen spinosum.
questions.keyConcept: The anterior circulation of the brain comes from the internal carotid, while the posterior cerebral arteries are the terminal branches of the basilar artery.

questions.text: Choose the CORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The second scalp layer is dense connective tissue containing the main vessels and nerves. Occipitofrontalis and its epicranial aponeurosis form the third, musculoaponeurotic layer.
questions.keyConcept: Orbicularis oculi closes the eye, orbicularis oris surrounds the lips, and buccinator forms the cheek and is pierced by the parotid duct.
options: Scalp extends from hair margin to lower border of mandible.
The aponeurosis of scalp contains blood vessels & muscles of scalp.
Orbicularis oculi muscle closes the eye.
Orbicularis oris muscle is the muscle of the cheecks.
Buccinator is pierced by submandibular duct.

questions.text: Match each structure in the left column with its nerve supply in the right column:
questions.explanation: The general rule is that the trigeminal nerve is sensory to the skin of the face and to the scalp in front of the auricle, while the facial nerve is motor to all muscles of facial expression, including orbicularis oris and occipitofrontalis. The important exception is the skin over the angle of the mandible, which is supplied by the great auricular nerve from the cervical plexus (C2, C3) rather than by the trigeminal nerve. This exception is clinically useful in distinguishing trigeminal from cervical sensory loss.
questions.keyConcept: Trigeminal is sensory to the face and facial nerve is motor to facial muscles, but skin over the angle of the mandible is supplied by cervical nerves.

pairs.premise: Skin of scalp infront of auricle.

questions.text: Blood supply of face comes from:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (D) because the face receives blood from both carotid systems: the external carotid supplies most of it through the facial, superficial temporal and maxillary arteries, while the internal carotid contributes through the ophthalmic artery, whose supratrochlear, supraorbital and dorsal nasal branches supply the upper face. Options (a) and (b) are each only half the answer, and (e) is only one branch of the internal carotid contribution. The common carotid (c) supplies the face only indirectly through its terminal divisions.
questions.keyConcept: The face is supplied by both the external carotid artery and the ophthalmic branch of the internal carotid artery.

questions.text: Lateral pterygoid muscle is surrounded by:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (E) because the pterygoid venous plexus surrounds the lateral pterygoid muscle, lying around and between its two heads within the infratemporal fossa. The ramus of the mandible (a) and masseter (b) lie lateral to the muscle rather than surrounding it. Branches of the mandibular nerve (c) and maxillary artery (d) are related to the muscle but do not envelop it in the way the venous plexus does.
questions.keyConcept: The pterygoid venous plexus surrounds the lateral pterygoid muscle in the infratemporal fossa.

questions.text: Suprahyoid muscles include all the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (C) because sternomastoid is a large muscle running from the sternum and clavicle to the mastoid process and is not attached to the hyoid bone at all. The suprahyoid group consists of the digastric (a), stylohyoid (b), mylohyoid (d) and geniohyoid (e), all of which lie above the hyoid bone and elevate it during swallowing.
questions.keyConcept: The four suprahyoid muscles are digastric, stylohyoid, mylohyoid and geniohyoid.

questions.text: Which one of the following muscles has 2 bellies?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (A) because the digastric muscle, as its name indicates, has an anterior and a posterior belly joined by an intermediate tendon that is held to the hyoid bone by a fibrous sling. The two bellies also have different nerve supplies, the anterior from the mandibular nerve and the posterior from the facial nerve. Stylohyoid (b), mylohyoid (d) and geniohyoid (e) are single-bellied, and sternomastoid (c) has two heads of origin but not two bellies.
questions.keyConcept: The digastric muscle has anterior and posterior bellies united by an intermediate tendon slung from the hyoid bone.

questions.text: Choose the CORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (E) because the sublingual gland drains by numerous small ducts that open directly onto the floor of the mouth along the sublingual fold. Option (a) is wrong because the parotid is the largest salivary gland, and (c) is wrong because it is the sublingual gland that lies beneath the mucosa of the floor of the mouth. Option (d) is wrong because the submandibular duct opens in the floor of the mouth beside the frenulum, and it is the parotid duct that opens into the vestibule.
questions.keyConcept: Sublingual gland ducts open directly onto the floor of the mouth; the parotid duct alone opens into the vestibule.
options: Submandibular salivary gland is the largest salivary gland.
Submandibular gland lies below mucosa of floor of mouth.
Submandibular duct opens in vestibule of mouth.
Sublingual salivary gland ducts open in floor of mouth.

questions.text: Match each part of the nose in the left column with its related statement in the right column:
questions.explanation: The roof of the nasal cavity is narrow and formed largely by the cribriform plate of the ethmoid, lying above the cavity and separating it from the anterior cranial fossa. The floor is formed by the hard palate, which also serves as the roof of the mouth. The medial wall is the nasal septum shared by the two cavities, while the lateral wall is characterised by the superior, middle and inferior conchae, beneath which the paranasal sinuses drain.
questions.keyConcept: The lateral wall of the nose carries the three conchae and receives the paranasal sinus openings; the hard palate forms its floor.

questions.text: Which of the following lies between orbit & nose?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (A) because the ethmoidal air cells occupy the ethmoidal labyrinth, which forms the thin medial wall of the orbit and the upper lateral wall of the nose, placing them directly between the two cavities. The frontal sinus (b) lies above the orbit and the maxillary sinus (d) below it. The sphenoidal sinus (c) lies behind the nasal cavity, and the cavernous sinus (e) is a dural venous sinus inside the cranial cavity.
questions.keyConcept: The ethmoidal air sinuses separate the orbit from the nasal cavity.

questions.text: Choose the INCORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (D) because this statement is incorrect: the oral cavity proper is roofed by the hard and soft palates, while the tongue occupies its floor. The vestibule is correctly described as the slit outside the teeth (a) that receives the parotid duct opposite the second upper molar (e). The oral cavity proper does end posteriorly at the palatoglossal arch (b), and the mylohyoid forms the muscular floor (c).
questions.keyConcept: The palate roofs the oral cavity proper; the tongue and mylohyoid form its floor.
options: Vestibule of mouth lies outside the teeth.
Oral cavity proper ends by palatoglossal arch.
Mylohyoid muscle forms floor of oral cavity proper.
Oral cavity proper is roofed by tongue.
Vestibule of mouth receives opening of parotid duct.

questions.text: As regards the pharynx, choose the CORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (A) because the pharynx is a fibromuscular tube that begins at the base of the skull and descends to become continuous with the oesophagus. Option (b) is wrong because it ends at the level of the 6th cervical vertebra, and (c) is wrong because the pharynx has a complete posterior wall but an incomplete anterior wall where it opens into the nose, mouth and larynx. Option (d) is wrong because the palatine tonsil lies in the oropharynx, and (e) is wrong because the pharyngeal tonsil lies in the nasopharynx.
questions.keyConcept: The pharynx extends from the base of the skull to the level of C6, where it becomes the oesophagus.
options: It begins at base of skull.
Ends at level of 4th cervical vertebra.

questions.text: As regards the larynx, choose the INCORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (B) because this statement is incorrect: the thyroid cartilage is a single unpaired cartilage, as are the cricoid and epiglottis, while the arytenoid, corniculate and cuneiform cartilages are the paired ones. The remaining statements are true: the larynx ends at C6 where it continues as the trachea (a), it contains two vestibular folds above and two vocal folds below (c), the vestibule lies between the inlet and the vestibular folds (d), and the laryngeal sinus lies between the vestibular and vocal folds (e).
questions.keyConcept: Thyroid, cricoid and epiglottis are unpaired laryngeal cartilages; arytenoid, corniculate and cuneiform are paired.
options: It ends at level of C6.
It has 2 upper vestibular folds & 2 lower vocal cords.
Its vestibule lies between its inlet & vestibular folds.
Its sinus lies between its vestibular & vocal folds.

questions.text: As regards the ear, choose the INCORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (C) because this statement is incorrect: the stapes is the third and smallest auditory ossicle, a bone rather than a muscle. The two muscles of the middle ear are the stapedius and the tensor tympani (e). The remaining statements are true, as the middle ear cavity lies within the petrous temporal bone (a), the auricle is part of the external ear (b), and the malleus is the first auditory ossicle (d).
questions.keyConcept: The middle ear contains three ossicles (malleus, incus, stapes) and two muscles (tensor tympani, stapedius).
options: Middle ear lies within the temporal bone.
Stapes is one of the muscles that lie within the middle ear.
Tensor tympani is a middle ear muscle.

questions.text: All of the following are branches of external carotid artery except:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (C) because the supraorbital artery is a branch of the ophthalmic artery, which arises from the internal carotid, and so belongs to the internal carotid system. The lingual, posterior auricular and superior thyroid arteries are all named branches of the external carotid artery.
questions.keyConcept: The supraorbital artery comes from the ophthalmic artery (internal carotid system), not from the external carotid.

questions.text: All of the following are branches of subclavian artery except:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (B) because the occipital artery is a posterior branch of the external carotid artery, not of the subclavian. The internal thoracic artery, the vertebral artery and the thyrocervical trunk all arise from the first part of the subclavian artery.
questions.keyConcept: First part of subclavian: vertebral, internal thoracic and thyrocervical trunk. The occipital artery belongs to the external carotid.

questions.text: Scalenus anterior divides which of the following arteries?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (D) because scalenus anterior crosses in front of the subclavian artery and divides it into three parts: the first medial to the muscle, the second behind it and the third lateral to it. The carotid and vertebral arteries are not divided in this way.
questions.keyConcept: Scalenus anterior divides the subclavian artery into its three parts.

questions.text: All of the following are branches of vertebral artery except:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (D) because the posterior cerebral artery is a terminal branch of the basilar artery, not of the vertebral artery. The anterior and posterior spinal arteries and the posterior inferior cerebellar artery all arise from the vertebral artery in the cranial cavity.
questions.keyConcept: The posterior cerebral artery arises from the basilar artery; the vertebral gives the spinal arteries and PICA.

questions.text: The occipitofrontalis muscle occupies which layer of the scalp:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (B) because occipitofrontalis lies in the third layer of the scalp, the musculo-aponeurotic layer formed by the muscle and the intervening epicranial aponeurosis. The first layer is skin, the second the dense superficial fascia carrying the vessels and nerves, and the fourth the loose areolar layer.
questions.keyConcept: Scalp layers: skin, superficial fascia, musculo-aponeurotic layer (occipitofrontalis), loose areolar tissue, pericranium.

questions.text: Skin covering angle of mandible is supplied by:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (C) because the skin over the angle of the mandible is supplied by the great auricular nerve, a branch of the cervical plexus, and not by the trigeminal nerve like the rest of the face. This is why sensation there is spared in trigeminal neuralgia, and the facial nerve (b, d) is motor rather than cutaneous here.
questions.keyConcept: The skin over the angle of the mandible is supplied by the great auricular nerve (C2, C3), not by the trigeminal.

questions.text: Ext jugular vein ends in which of the following?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (C) because the external jugular vein descends over sternomastoid, pierces the deep fascia above the clavicle and drains into the subclavian vein. It is formed in part by the posterior division of the retromandibular vein, so the retromandibular vein is its source rather than its termination.
questions.keyConcept: The external jugular vein ends in the subclavian vein.

questions.text: All of the following muscles supplied by occulo motor nerve except:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (D) because the superior oblique is supplied by the trochlear nerve, the fourth cranial nerve. The oculomotor nerve supplies the superior, inferior and medial recti, the inferior oblique and levator palpebrae superioris, while lateral rectus is supplied by the abducent nerve.
questions.keyConcept: LR6 SO4, all the rest 3: superior oblique is trochlear and lateral rectus is abducent.

questions.text: Which of the following muscles don't belong to infra hyoid muscles?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (B) because the posterior belly of digastric is a suprahyoid muscle, lying above the hyoid bone and supplied by the facial nerve. The four infrahyoid or strap muscles are sternohyoid, sternothyroid, thyrohyoid and omohyoid.
questions.keyConcept: Infrahyoid muscles: sternohyoid, sternothyroid, thyrohyoid, omohyoid. Digastric is suprahyoid.

questions.text: Nerves and vessels of scalp located in which layer?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (A) because the vessels and nerves of the scalp run in the second layer, the dense superficial fascia, where the fibrous septa hold cut vessels open and cause profuse bleeding from scalp wounds. The fourth layer, the loose areolar tissue, is instead the dangerous area for the spread of infection.
questions.keyConcept: Scalp vessels and nerves run in the dense superficial fascia (2nd layer), which is why scalp wounds bleed profusely.

questions.text: Para nasal sinus drain in the which part of the nose?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (B) because all the paranasal sinuses open onto the lateral wall of the nasal cavity, on or around the three conchae and in the hiatus semilunaris. The roof carries the olfactory mucosa, the medial wall is the septum and the floor is formed by the palate.
questions.keyConcept: All paranasal sinuses drain onto the lateral wall of the nose.

questions.text: Auditory tube opens into:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (D) because the pharyngeal opening of the auditory (Eustachian) tube lies on the lateral wall of the nasopharynx, behind the inferior concha and above the level of the soft palate. This is why nasopharyngeal infection readily spreads to the middle ear, especially in children.
questions.keyConcept: The auditory tube opens on the lateral wall of the nasopharynx.

questions.text: Pretrachial fascia enclose which of the following?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (D) because the pretracheal fascia splits to enclose the thyroid gland, forming its false capsule and binding it to the larynx and trachea so that it moves on swallowing. Sternomastoid is enclosed by the investing layer and the carotid vessels by the carotid sheath.
questions.keyConcept: The pretracheal fascia forms the false capsule of the thyroid gland and makes it move on swallowing.

questions.text: Which of the following doesn't carry taste?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (C) because the hypoglossal nerve is purely motor to the muscles of the tongue and carries no taste fibers. Taste is carried by the facial nerve from the anterior two thirds of the tongue, by the glossopharyngeal from the posterior third, and by the vagus from the epiglottic region.
questions.keyConcept: Taste travels in VII, IX and X; the hypoglossal nerve is purely motor.

questions.text: Which nerve supplies all intrinsic tongue muscles and most extrinsic tongue muscles, with palatoglossus as the exception?
questions.explanation: The hypoglossal nerve supplies all intrinsic tongue muscles and most extrinsic muscles. Palatoglossus is supplied by the vagus nerve through the pharyngeal plexus.
questions.keyConcept: The hypoglossal nerve supplies all tongue muscles except palatoglossus.

questions.text: Which of the following nerves supplies the muscles of facial expression?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (D) because the muscles of facial expression are supplied by the facial nerve, the seventh cranial nerve, which is not among the options offered. The trigeminal nerve (V) is sensory to the face and motor only to the muscles of mastication, while III moves the eye and VIII serves hearing and balance.
questions.keyConcept: The muscles of facial expression are supplied by the facial nerve (VII).

questions.text: All of the following nerves carry parasympathetic except:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (B) because the hypoglossal nerve carries no parasympathetic fibers, being purely motor to the tongue muscles. The four cranial nerves carrying parasympathetic fibers are the oculomotor, facial, glossopharyngeal and vagus.
questions.keyConcept: Cranial parasympathetic outflow travels in III, VII, IX and X only.

questions.text: All of the following nerves are pure sensory except:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (C) because the trochlear nerve is purely motor, supplying the superior oblique muscle. The three purely sensory cranial nerves are the olfactory, the optic and the vestibulocochlear.
questions.keyConcept: Purely sensory cranial nerves: I, II and VIII. The trochlear (IV) is purely motor.

questions.text: All of the following at the level of C6 except:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (C) because the trachea ends much lower, at the level of the sternal angle opposite the T4/T5 disc, where it bifurcates. The sixth cervical vertebra marks the end of the larynx and pharynx and the beginning of the trachea and oesophagus.
questions.keyConcept: C6: larynx and pharynx end, trachea and oesophagus begin. The trachea ends at T4/T5.

questions.text: All the following cartilages are paired except:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (A) because the epiglottis is a single, unpaired cartilage, like the thyroid and cricoid cartilages. The arytenoid, corniculate and cuneiform cartilages all occur in pairs.
questions.keyConcept: Unpaired laryngeal cartilages: thyroid, cricoid, epiglottis. Paired: arytenoid, corniculate, cuneiform.

questions.text: Posterior boundary of post. Triangle of the neck is:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (B) because the anterior border of trapezius forms the posterior boundary of the posterior triangle of the neck. Sternomastoid forms its anterior boundary and the middle third of the clavicle its base.
questions.keyConcept: Posterior triangle: sternomastoid in front, trapezius behind, clavicle below.

questions.text: Ant cerebral artery is branch from:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (B) because the anterior cerebral artery is one of the two terminal branches of the internal carotid artery, the other being the middle cerebral artery. The external carotid supplies structures outside the cranial cavity, and the vertebral artery contributes to the posterior part of the circle of Willis.
questions.keyConcept: The internal carotid artery ends by dividing into the anterior and middle cerebral arteries.

questions.text: Which of the following muscles is responsible for pushing the food from vestibule of mouth?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (D) because buccinator forms the muscular wall of the cheek and, on contracting, presses the cheek against the teeth to push food from the vestibule back onto the occlusal surfaces. Masseter elevates the mandible, orbicularis oris closes the lips and mylohyoid forms the floor of the mouth.
questions.keyConcept: Buccinator empties the vestibule of the mouth by pressing the cheek against the teeth.

questions.text: Arterio-venous anastomosis is frequently present in:
questions.explanation: Arteriovenous anastomoses are abundant in nasal skin and aid thermoregulation.
questions.keyConcept: Arteriovenous Anastomoses: Arteriovenous anastomoses are abundant in nasal skin and aid thermoregulation

questions.text: What is the joint that contains a cartilaginous disc?
questions.explanation: The temporomandibular joint contains an articular disc.
questions.keyConcept: Temporomandibular Joint: The temporomandibular joint contains an articular disc

questions.text: Which of the following is a uniaxial joint?
questions.explanation: The median atlanto-axial joint is a uniaxial pivot joint.
questions.keyConcept: Atlanto-axial Joint: The median atlanto-axial joint is a uniaxial pivot joint

questions.text: What is the type of joint that connects the bones of the skull?
questions.explanation: Most skull bones are connected by fibrous sutures.
questions.keyConcept: Skull Sutures: Most skull bones are connected by fibrous sutures

questions.text: Which one of the following muscles has spiralized fibers?
questions.explanation: The source identifies trapezius as an example of spiralized fiber arrangement.
questions.keyConcept: Muscle Fiber Arrangement: The source identifies trapezius as an example of spiralized fiber arrangement

questions.text: An example of the pivot joints is:
questions.explanation: The atlanto-axial joint is a pivot joint.
questions.keyConcept: The atlanto-axial joint is a pivot joint

questions.text: The joint that connects the root of a tooth with its socket?
questions.explanation: A gomphosis is the fibrous peg-and-socket joint between a tooth root and its alveolus.
questions.keyConcept: Teeth: A gomphosis is the fibrous peg-and-socket joint between a tooth root and its alveolus

questions.text: Regarding the mouth cavity proper all the following boundaries are true, except:
questions.explanation: The oral cavity proper communicates posteriorly with the oropharynx, not directly with the larynx.
questions.keyConcept: The oral cavity proper opens into the oropharynx posteriorly.
options: In front and sides it is bounded by gums and teeth
Posteriorly, it communicates with the larynx.

questions.text: Regarding the tongue, all the following statements are true except:
questions.explanation: Taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue is mainly carried by chorda tympani, not the vagus nerve.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior two-thirds taste is carried mainly by chorda tympani.
options: Its tip is the anterior free end.
General sensation of the Anterior 2/3 is supplied by lingual nerve.
General sensation of the posterior 1/3 is supplied by glossopharyngeal nerve.
Taste sensation of the posterior 1/3 is supplied by glossopharyngeal nerve.
Taste sensation of the Anterior 2/3 is supplied by vagus nerve.

questions.text: Regarding the pharynx, all the following statements are true except:
questions.explanation: The auditory tube openings are in the lateral walls of the nasopharynx, not its posterior wall.
questions.keyConcept: The auditory tube opens into the lateral wall of the nasopharynx.
options: The nasopharynx lies behind the nasal cavity.
The nasopharynx contains on its posterior wall the two opening of the auditory tubes.
The oropharynx lies behind the oral cavity.
The laryngopharynx lies behind the larynx.
The oropharynx contains in its lateral walls the Palatine tonsils.

questions.text: Regarding the salivary glands one of the following statements is true;
questions.explanation: The submandibular duct opens at the sublingual papilla in the floor of the mouth.
questions.keyConcept: The submandibular duct opens at the sublingual papilla.
options: The parotid glands lie below the angle of the mandible.
The submandibular glands have numerous small ducts.
The parotid glands duct opens in the vestibule of the mouth opposite the upper canine tooth.
The submandibular glands duct opens in the floor of the mouth below the tongue at sublingual papillae.
The Sublingual glands lie under the mucous membrane of the pharynx.

questions.text: In the oral cavity proper, ___ forms the roof.
questions.explanation: The palate forms the roof of the oral cavity proper.
questions.keyConcept: The palate forms the roof of the oral cavity.

questions.text: Palate is the partition between the ___ and ___ cavities.
questions.explanation: The palate separates the oral cavity from the nasal cavity.
questions.keyConcept: The palate separates the oral and nasal cavities.

questions.text: The main arterial supply of the tongue is ___.
questions.explanation: The lingual artery is the main arterial supply of the tongue.
questions.keyConcept: The tongue is supplied mainly by the lingual artery.

questions.text: The ___ nerve provides motor supply to all intrinsic and most extrinsic tongue muscles, except palatoglossus.
questions.explanation: The hypoglossal nerve provides motor supply to most tongue muscles.
questions.keyConcept: The hypoglossal nerve supplies tongue motor function.

questions.text: The ___ nerve supplies general sensation to the anterior part of the tongue.
questions.explanation: The lingual nerve supplies general sensation to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue.
questions.keyConcept: The lingual nerve supplies sensation to the anterior tongue.

questions.text: Each individual has two sets of teeth ___ and ___.
questions.explanation: Humans develop temporary teeth first, followed by permanent teeth.
questions.keyConcept: Human dentition includes temporary and permanent teeth.

questions.text: Palatine tonsils are present in the lateral wall of ___.
questions.explanation: The palatine tonsils lie in the lateral walls of the oropharynx.
questions.keyConcept: Palatine tonsils lie in the oropharynx.

questions.text: Adenoids are present in the posterior wall of ___.
questions.explanation: Adenoids or the pharyngeal tonsil lie in the nasopharynx.
questions.keyConcept: Adenoids are located in the nasopharynx.

questions.text: As regards Trigeminal nerve, choose the CORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (C) because the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve is motor to the four muscles of mastication as well as to mylohyoid, anterior belly of digastric, tensor tympani and tensor palati. Option (a) is wrong because it is the 5th cranial nerve, and (b) is wrong because it is a mixed nerve, being mainly sensory to the face. Option (d) is wrong because equilibrium is served by the 8th cranial nerve, and (e) is wrong because the trigeminal itself carries no secretomotor fibers to salivary glands.
questions.keyConcept: The trigeminal nerve is the 5th cranial nerve, mainly sensory to the face but motor to the muscles of mastication.
options: It is a purely motor nerve.

questions.text: As regards Facial nerve, choose the CORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (A) because the facial nerve is a mixed nerve, carrying motor fibers to the muscles of facial expression, special sensory taste fibers from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, and secretomotor fibers to the submandibular, sublingual and lacrimal glands. Option (b) is wrong because it is the 7th cranial nerve, and (c) is wrong because the vagus is motor to the pharyngeal muscles. Option (d) is wrong because the glossopharyngeal nerve is secretory to the parotid, and (e) is wrong because the trigeminal is sensory to the face.
questions.keyConcept: The facial nerve is the 7th cranial nerve and is mixed: motor, secretomotor and special sensory for taste.
options: It is motor to muscles of pharynx.
It is secretory to parotid gland.

questions.text: As regards glossopharyngeal nerve, choose the CORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (C) because the glossopharyngeal nerve supplies only one muscle, the stylopharyngeus. Option (a) is wrong because it is the 9th cranial nerve, and (b) is wrong because it is a mixed nerve. Option (d) is wrong because it is secretory to the parotid gland only, and (e) is wrong because the remaining pharyngeal muscles are supplied by the vagus through the pharyngeal plexus.
questions.keyConcept: The glossopharyngeal nerve is the 9th cranial nerve and supplies only stylopharyngeus, plus secretomotor fibers to the parotid.
options: It is a purely motor nerve.
It supplies one muscle of pharynx.
It is secretory to 2 salivary glands.
It is motor to muscles of pharynx.

questions.text: Match each nerve in the left column with its appropriate description in the right column:
questions.explanation: The first two cranial nerves are purely special sensory, the olfactory carrying smell and the optic carrying vision. The oculomotor nerve is motor to most of the extraocular muscles, and the trigeminal nerve, through its mandibular division, supplies the muscles of mastication. The facial nerve carries taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue through its chorda tympani branch.
questions.keyConcept: Olfactory carries smell, optic carries vision, oculomotor moves the eye, facial carries taste, and trigeminal supplies the muscles of mastication.

questions.text: Match each nerve in the left column with its appropriate description in the right column:
questions.explanation: The facial nerve is secretomotor to the submandibular and sublingual salivary glands through the chorda tympani and submandibular ganglion. The glossopharyngeal nerve supplies only stylopharyngeus, while the vagus carries parasympathetic fibers to the heart as well as to the rest of the thoracic and abdominal viscera. The spinal part of the accessory nerve supplies sternomastoid and trapezius in the neck, and the hypoglossal nerve is motor to the muscles of the tongue.
questions.keyConcept: Facial supplies two salivary glands, glossopharyngeal one pharyngeal muscle, vagus the heart, accessory the neck muscles, and hypoglossal the tongue.

questions.text: Which of the following cranial nerves is purely motor?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (D) because the trochlear nerve is purely motor, supplying only the superior oblique muscle. The olfactory and vestibulocochlear nerves are purely sensory and the trigeminal nerve is mixed, carrying sensation from the face and motor fibers to the muscles of mastication.
questions.keyConcept: The trochlear nerve is purely motor to the superior oblique.

subjects.name: Anatomy
subjects.lectures: Dural Folds, Dural Venous Sinuses, Cavernous Sinus, Cerebral Arterial Supply, Grey and White Matter, Neuroanatomical Terminology, Brain Stem, Cerebral Hemispheres, Cerebral Lobes and Their Functions, Internal Structure of the Cerebrum, Diencephalon, Cranial Nerve Attachments, Cerebellum, Meninges, Ventricular System, CSF Circulation, Functional Areas of the Cerebrum, White Matter of the Cerebrum, Arterial Supply of the Brain, Medulla Oblongata, Lymphatic System, Brainstem

questions.text: Match each structure in the left column with its appropriate description in the right column:
questions.explanation: The falx cerebri is a sickle-shaped vertical fold of dura that descends between the two cerebral hemispheres, which is the origin of its name. The tentorium cerebelli is a horizontal tent-like fold separating the occipital lobes of the cerebrum above from the cerebellum below. The falx cerebelli is a small vertical fold between the two cerebellar hemispheres, while the diaphragma sellae roofs the hypophyseal fossa and covers the pituitary gland.
questions.keyConcept: The four dural folds are falx cerebri, tentorium cerebelli, falx cerebelli and diaphragma sellae, each named for the structures it separates or covers.

questions.text: All the following are paired venous sinuses EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (A) because the straight sinus is a single midline sinus lying at the junction of the falx cerebri with the tentorium cerebelli, draining into the confluence of sinuses. The sigmoid (b), transverse (c), cavernous (d) and superior petrosal (e) sinuses all exist as right and left pairs.
questions.keyConcept: The straight sinus is unpaired and midline, unlike the transverse, sigmoid, cavernous and petrosal sinuses.

questions.text: Which of the following sinuses lies on either side of pituitary gland?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (D) because the cavernous sinuses lie one on each side of the body of the sphenoid, flanking the pituitary gland in the sella turcica. This close relationship explains why pituitary tumours can compress structures in the cavernous sinus. The straight sinus (a) is midline and posterior, while the transverse (c) and sigmoid (b) sinuses lie in the posterior cranial fossa and the superior petrosal sinus (e) runs along the upper border of the petrous temporal bone.
questions.keyConcept: The cavernous sinus lies on either side of the pituitary gland and transmits the internal carotid artery and several cranial nerves.

questions.text: Choose the INCORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (D) because this statement is incorrect: the two vertebral arteries unite at the lower border of the pons to form the basilar artery, not the posterior cerebral artery. The posterior cerebral arteries are instead the terminal branches of the basilar artery. The other statements are true: the middle meningeal artery runs extradurally (a), the anterior cerebral artery is a terminal branch of the internal carotid (b), the posterior inferior cerebellar artery branches from the vertebral artery (c), and the basilar artery gives pontine branches (e).
questions.keyConcept: The two vertebral arteries unite to form the basilar artery, which then divides into the two posterior cerebral arteries.
options: Middle meningeal artery runs an extradural course.
Anterior cerebral artery is a branch of internal carotid artery.
Posterior inferior cerebellar artery is a branch of vertebral artery.
The 2 vertebral arteries unite to form posterior cerebral artery.

questions.text: Which of the following dural folds covering pituitary gland?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (B) because the diaphragma sellae is the small circular fold of dura that roofs the hypophyseal fossa over the pituitary gland, pierced centrally by the infundibulum. The falx cerebri lies between the cerebral hemispheres, the falx cerebelli between the cerebellar hemispheres, and the tentorium cerebelli between the cerebrum and cerebellum.
questions.keyConcept: The diaphragma sellae roofs the pituitary fossa and is pierced by the pituitary stalk.

questions.text: Superior sagittal sinus related to which fold?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (A) because the superior sagittal sinus runs in the attached upper (convex) margin of the falx cerebri, while the inferior sagittal sinus runs in its free lower margin. The diaphragma sellae carries no sagittal sinus, and the tentorium cerebelli is related to the transverse and superior petrosal sinuses.
questions.keyConcept: The superior sagittal sinus lies in the upper attached border of the falx cerebri.

questions.text: Choose the INCORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (C) because this statement is reversed: in the spinal cord the white matter lies peripherally and surrounds the centrally placed H-shaped grey matter. The arrangement is the opposite of that in the cerebrum and cerebellum, where grey matter forms an outer cortex. The other statements are true, as grey matter consists of cell bodies (a), white matter of fibers (b), brain stem grey matter is broken up into nuclei (d), and the cerebellum has an outer cerebellar cortex (e).
questions.keyConcept: In the spinal cord white matter surrounds grey matter; in the cerebrum and cerebellum grey matter forms the outer cortex.
options: Grey matter is formed of nerve cell bodies.
White matter is formed of nerve fibers.
In spinal cord, the grey matter surrounds the white matter.
In brain stem, the grey matter collects into nuclei.
Cerebellum is covered from outside by cerebellar cortex.

questions.text: Match each structure in the left column with its appropriate description in the right column:
questions.explanation: These four terms follow a simple two-by-two rule based on cell bodies versus fibers and inside versus outside the central nervous system. Collections of cell bodies are called nuclei inside the CNS and ganglia outside it. Bundles of nerve fibers are called tracts inside the CNS and nerves outside it.
questions.keyConcept: Cell bodies: nucleus inside CNS, ganglion outside. Fiber bundles: tract inside CNS, nerve outside.

pairs.target: A collection of cell bodies within CNS.
A collection of cell bodies outside CNS.
A bundle of nerve fibers within CNS.
A bundle of nerve fibers outside CNS.

questions.text: Match each structure in the left column with its appropriate description in the right column:
questions.explanation: A decussation is the crossing of nerve fibers across the midline and may involve either ascending or descending pathways. The other pairs describe their listed nervous-system structures.
questions.keyConcept: Commissures are white-matter connections between the two sides of the CNS.

pairs.target: A band of white matter connecting right & left sides of CNS.
Crossing of tract fibers across the midline.
A chain of successive tracts having same function.
A collection of ascending fibers in brain stem.

questions.text: Brain stem is formed of:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (E) because the brain stem consists of three parts from above downwards: the midbrain, the pons and the medulla oblongata. The cerebellum (a, d) lies behind the brain stem and is connected to it by peduncles but is not part of it. The diencephalon (b, c), containing the thalamus and hypothalamus, belongs to the forebrain rather than the brain stem.
questions.keyConcept: The brain stem is composed of the midbrain, pons and medulla oblongata.

questions.text: As regards cerebral hemispheres, choose the CORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (C) because the insula is a buried area of cerebral cortex lying deep within the lateral sulcus, hidden by the overlying opercula. Option (a) is wrong because the inferior surface is formed of orbital and tentorial parts, and (b) is wrong because the three poles are frontal, temporal and occipital. Option (d) is wrong because the most important sulci are the central and lateral sulci, and (e) is wrong because the parietal lobe is mainly sensory in function.
questions.keyConcept: The insula is cerebral cortex buried in the floor of the lateral sulcus.
options: Its inferior surface is formed of orbital & medial parts.
It has 3 poles; frontal, parietal & occipital.
Insula is a part of cerebral cortex deep into lateral sulcus.
The most important sulci are the central & medial sulci.
Its parietal lobe is mainly motor in its function.

questions.text: Match each lobe in the left column with its appropriate function in the right column:
questions.explanation: The frontal lobe contains the primary motor cortex in its precentral gyrus, while the parietal lobe contains the primary sensory cortex in its postcentral gyrus, the two being separated by the central sulcus. The temporal lobe houses the auditory cortex and the occipital lobe the visual cortex around the calcarine sulcus. The limbic lobe, on the medial surface, is concerned with emotion and memory through structures such as the cingulate gyrus and hippocampus.
questions.keyConcept: Frontal is motor, parietal is sensory, temporal is hearing, occipital is vision, and limbic is emotion and memory.

questions.text: Choose the CORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (D) because the caudate nucleus is one of the basal nuclei, together with the putamen, globus pallidus, amygdala and claustrum. Option (a) is wrong because the corpus callosum is formed of white matter, and (b) is wrong because it is the corpus callosum, not the internal capsule, that connects the two hemispheres. Option (c) is wrong because the anterior limb, genu and posterior limb belong to the internal capsule, and (e) is wrong because the lateral ventricle is the cavity of the cerebral hemisphere.
questions.keyConcept: The caudate nucleus is a basal nucleus; the internal capsule has an anterior limb, genu and posterior limb.
options: Corpus callosum is formed of grey matter.
Corpus callosum has anterior limb, genu & posterior limb.
Caudate nucleus is one of the basal nuclei.
The lateral ventricle is the cavity of the diencephalon.

questions.text: As regards the brain stem, choose the INCORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (A) because this statement is incorrect: the pyramid and the olive are surface elevations of the medulla oblongata, not of the midbrain. The midbrain instead shows the two cerebral peduncles anteriorly (b) and the four colliculi of the tectum posteriorly (d). The pons gives attachment to the middle four cranial nerves, the 5th to 8th (c), and the trochlear nerve emerges from the dorsal aspect of the midbrain (e).
questions.keyConcept: The pyramid and olive are features of the medulla oblongata; the midbrain shows cerebral peduncles and four colliculi.
options: Midbrain shows 2 anterior elevations which are pyramid & olive.
Pons gives attachment to middle 4 cranial nerves.
Fourth cranial nerve is attached to midbrain.

questions.text: What are the cranial nerves attached to the midbrain?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (C) because only the oculomotor (3rd) and trochlear (4th) nerves are attached to the midbrain, the oculomotor emerging from the interpeduncular fossa anteriorly and the trochlear from the dorsal surface below the inferior colliculus. The 1st and 2nd cranial nerves (a, b) are not attached to the brain stem at all, arising from the cerebrum. The middle four cranial nerves (e) are attached to the pons.
questions.keyConcept: The midbrain gives attachment to the 3rd and 4th cranial nerves only.

questions.text: As regards the cerebellum, choose the INCORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (B) because this statement is incorrect: the cerebellar cortex covering the surface is formed of grey matter, not white matter, with the white matter lying deep to it. The remaining statements are true, as the cerebellum consists of two hemispheres joined by the midline vermis (a), the archicerebellum (flocculonodular lobe) maintains equilibrium (c), the middle cerebellar peduncles connect it to the pons (d), and the paleocerebellum controls posture and muscle tone (e).
questions.keyConcept: The cerebellar cortex is grey matter covering an inner core of white matter.
options: It is formed of 2 hemispheres joined by a vermis.
Its surface is covered by a layer of white matter called cerebellar cortex.
Its middle peduncles connect it with pons.

questions.text: As regards the cerebellum, choose the INCORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (E) because this statement is incorrect: the cerebellum forms the roof of the fourth ventricle, while the floor is formed by the posterior surface of the pons and medulla, the rhomboid fossa. The remaining statements are true, since the neocerebellum plans and coordinates movement (a), there are three pairs of peduncles making six in total (b), the cerebellar nuclei lie embedded in the white matter (c), and functionally it is divided into archi-, paleo- and neocerebellum (d).
questions.keyConcept: The cerebellum forms the roof of the fourth ventricle; the pons and medulla form its floor.
options: Neocerebellum helps in planning of movements.
Has cerebellar nuclei embedded in white matter.

questions.text: Which one of the following is the closest to brain tissue?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (D) because the pia mater is the innermost meningeal layer and adheres intimately to the surface of the brain, dipping into its sulci. From outside inwards the order is epidural space, dura mater, arachnoid mater, subarachnoid space and finally pia mater. The subarachnoid space (e) lies just superficial to the pia and contains cerebrospinal fluid.
questions.keyConcept: The pia mater is the innermost meninx and is closely applied to the brain surface.

questions.text: Subarachnoid space lies:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (B) because the subarachnoid space lies deep to the arachnoid mater and superficial to the pia mater, and it is filled with cerebrospinal fluid. The space between the dura and arachnoid (a) is the potential subdural space, and nothing lies deep to the pia (d) since it is adherent to brain tissue. Option (e) is too broad because it would include the arachnoid membrane itself.
questions.keyConcept: The subarachnoid space lies between the arachnoid and pia mater and contains cerebrospinal fluid.

questions.text: As regards the 3rd ventricle, choose the INCORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (D) because this statement is incorrect: it is the fourth ventricle, not the third, that has three foramina opening into the subarachnoid space, namely the median foramen of Magendie and the two lateral foramina of Luschka. The remaining statements are true, since the third ventricle is the midline cleft between the two thalami (a), communicates with each lateral ventricle through the foramen of Monro (b), belongs to the ventricular system (c), and drains to the fourth ventricle through the cerebral aqueduct (e).
questions.keyConcept: The three foramina opening into the subarachnoid space belong to the fourth ventricle, not the third.
options: It is connected with the lateral ventricle through interventricular foramen of Monro.
It is a part of the ventricular system.
It has 3 foramina that open in subarachnoid space.
It is connected to 4th ventricle through cerebral acquiduct of Sylvius.

questions.text: Match each structure in the left column with its appropriate statement in the right column:
questions.explanation: Each part of the ventricular system is the cavity of the region of the neural tube from which it develops. The lateral ventricles are the cavities of the cerebral hemispheres and the third ventricle is the midline cavity of the diencephalon between the two thalami. The cerebral aqueduct is the narrow canal of the midbrain, the fourth ventricle is the tent-shaped cavity between the brain stem in front and the cerebellum behind, and the central canal is the cavity of the spinal cord.
questions.keyConcept: The ventricular system follows the neural tube: lateral ventricles in the hemispheres, third between the thalami, aqueduct in the midbrain, fourth behind the brain stem, central canal in the cord.

questions.text: The only cranial nerve that emerges from back of brain stem is:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (B) because the trochlear nerve is the only cranial nerve to emerge from the dorsal aspect of the brain stem, appearing below the inferior colliculi before winding round the midbrain. The abducent and oculomotor nerves emerge ventrally, and the cranial root of the accessory nerve emerges from the side of the medulla.
questions.keyConcept: The trochlear nerve is the only cranial nerve emerging from the back of the brain stem.

questions.text: Cavity of Diencephalon is:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (B) because the third ventricle is the midline cavity of the diencephalon, bounded laterally by the thalamus and hypothalamus. The lateral ventricles belong to the cerebral hemispheres, the aqueduct to the midbrain and the fourth ventricle to the pons and medulla with the cerebellum.
questions.keyConcept: The third ventricle is the cavity of the diencephalon.

questions.text: CSF is drained to:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (D) because cerebrospinal fluid is absorbed into the venous blood through the arachnoid villi that project into the superior sagittal sinus and its lateral lacunae. The other sinuses listed receive cerebral venous blood but are not the site of CSF absorption.
questions.keyConcept: CSF is absorbed through arachnoid villi into the superior sagittal sinus.

questions.text: Motor cortex is in which lobe of cerebrum?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (A) because the primary motor cortex occupies the precentral gyrus of the frontal lobe. The occipital lobe carries the visual cortex, the temporal lobe the auditory cortex and the parietal lobe the general sensory cortex in the postcentral gyrus.
questions.keyConcept: The primary motor cortex is the precentral gyrus of the frontal lobe.

questions.text: Auditory cortex is in which lobe of cerebrum?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (C) because the auditory cortex lies in the superior temporal gyrus of the temporal lobe, in and around the transverse temporal gyri. The frontal lobe carries the motor cortex, the parietal lobe the sensory cortex and the occipital lobe the visual cortex.
questions.keyConcept: The auditory cortex lies in the superior temporal gyrus of the temporal lobe.

questions.text: All are true about Diencephalon except:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (D) because olfaction is the one special sensation that reaches the cortex without relaying in the thalamus, so not all special sensations relay there. The remaining statements are true, since the epithalamus with its pineal gland restrains the onset of puberty, the hypothalamus governs the autonomic system and influences the spleen, and the cavity of the diencephalon is the third ventricle.
questions.keyConcept: Smell is the only special sensation that does not relay in the thalamus.
options: Epithalamus is responsible for delay of puberty.
Hypothalamus can control spleen and autonomic system.
All special sensations must relay in thalamus.

questions.text: All are true about cerebellum except:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (C) because the outer grey matter of the cerebellum is its cortex, while the cerebellar nuclei are islands of grey matter buried deep within the white matter. The remaining statements are true, since the vermis joins the two hemispheres, the paleocerebellum is concerned with posture and muscle tone and the neocerebellum with the planning and coordination of voluntary movement.
questions.keyConcept: Cerebellar nuclei lie deep in the white matter; the outer grey matter is the cortex.
options: The 2 cerebellar hemispheres are connected by vermis.
The outer gray matter contains nuclei.
The Neo cerebellum is for motor planes.

questions.text: Which of the following brain fibers is considered as best example of commissural fibers?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (B) because the corpus callosum is the largest commissure of the brain, connecting corresponding areas of the two cerebral hemispheres. Descending tracts and the internal capsule are projection fibers, carrying impulses between the cortex and lower centres.
questions.keyConcept: The corpus callosum is the largest commissural bundle of the brain.

questions.text: The artery that runs in front of pons is:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (C) because the basilar artery, formed by the union of the two vertebral arteries at the lower border of the pons, ascends in the midline on the ventral surface of the pons. The vertebral arteries lie on the medulla and the posterior cerebral arteries are its terminal branches around the midbrain.
questions.keyConcept: The basilar artery lies on the front of the pons and ends as the two posterior cerebral arteries.

questions.text: The nerve that emerges between olive and ICP of medulla oblongata is:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (C) because the glossopharyngeal nerve emerges from the postolivary sulcus, the groove between the olive and the inferior cerebellar peduncle, along with the vagus and the cranial root of the accessory nerve. The hypoglossal nerve emerges in front of the olive, and the facial and trigeminal nerves emerge at the pons.
questions.keyConcept: IX, X and cranial XI emerge between the olive and the inferior cerebellar peduncle; XII emerges in front of the olive.

questions.text: Which of the following tissues lacks conventional lymphatic vessels within its parenchyma?
questions.explanation: Brain parenchyma lacks conventional lymphatic vessels. This does not mean that the entire cranial compartment lacks lymphatic drainage: meningeal lymphatic vessels are present.
questions.keyConcept: Lymphatic System: The classical teaching is that brain parenchyma lacks conventional lymphatic vessels

questions.text: Thalamus is a part of:
questions.explanation: The thalamus is a major component of the diencephalon.
questions.keyConcept: Diencephalon: The thalamus is a major component of the diencephalon

questions.text: The following meningeal space contains CSF:
questions.explanation: Cerebrospinal fluid is found in the subarachnoid space.
questions.keyConcept: Subarachnoid space

questions.text: Regarding the brain stem, it consists of:
questions.explanation: The brainstem is made up of the midbrain, pons and medulla oblongata.
questions.keyConcept: Components of the brainstem
options: Midbrain, pons, medulla oblongata and cerebellum.
Midbrain, pons, medulla oblongata and spinal cord.

questions.text: Regarding the ventricles of the brain, one is correct:
questions.explanation: The cerebral aqueduct connects the third ventricle to the fourth ventricle.
questions.keyConcept: The third and fourth ventricles communicate through the cerebral aqueduct.
options: The lateral ventricles lie in thalamus.
The third ventricle lies in cerebral hemisphere.
The third ventricle is connected to the fourth ventricle by aqueduct.
The fourth ventricle lies posterior to midbrain.
The fourth ventricle is connected to the third ventricle by interventricular foramen.

questions.text: Regarding the meninges the middle layer is:
questions.explanation: The arachnoid mater lies between the dura mater and pia mater.
questions.keyConcept: Arachnoid mater is the middle meningeal layer.
