questions.text: The bones sharing in the formation of the hip bone meet at:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (D) because the three bones that fuse to form the hip bone, namely the ilium, ischium and pubis, all meet at the acetabulum. Options (a), (b) and (c) simply name the three constituent bones rather than their meeting point. The iliac fossa (e) is a smooth concavity on the inner surface of the ilium alone.
questions.keyConcept: The ilium, ischium and pubis fuse at the acetabulum to form the hip bone.

questions.text: As regards the hip bone, choose the CORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The ischial spine separates the greater and lesser sciatic notches. The iliac crest is the upper border of the ilium, and the pubis has two rami. The obturator foramen is bounded by both pubis and ischium, rather than by either bone alone.
questions.keyConcept: The ischial spine separates the greater and lesser sciatic notches.
options: Lower border of ilium is called iliac crest.
Pubis is formed of a body & one ramus.
Ischial spine separates greater & lesser sciatic notches.
Pubic arch is formed of ischial tuberosity & inferior pubic ramus.
Obturator foramen is enclosed by the ischial rami.

questions.text: As regards the sacrum, choose the CORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (C) because the body of the first sacral vertebra lies in the midline between the two expanded alae. Option (a) is wrong because the sacrum is formed of 5 fused vertebrae, and (b) is wrong because it shows 4 anterior sacral foramina on each side. Option (d) is wrong because it is the apex that articulates with the coccyx, and (e) is wrong because the apex is the lower end and the base is the upper end.
questions.keyConcept: The sacrum is 5 fused vertebrae with 4 pairs of sacral foramina; its base is above and its apex articulates with the coccyx.
options: It is formed of 4 fused vertebrae.
Its body lies between the alae.
Its promontory articulates with the coccyx.
Its upper end forms the apex.

questions.text: As regards the female pelvis, choose the INCORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (B) because this statement is incorrect: the female pelvis is short as well as wide, an adaptation for childbirth. The remaining statements are true, since the female pelvis is broad (a), has a relatively narrow acetabulum (c), a wide subpubic angle (d), and like every pelvis is formed by the two hip bones together with the sacrum and coccyx (e).
questions.keyConcept: The female pelvis is wide and short with a wide subpubic angle; the male pelvis is narrow and long.
options: It is formed of 2 hip bones & sacrum.

questions.text: Sacrum shares in the formation of all the following joints EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (C) because the symphysis pubis is the midline joint between the right and left hip bones and does not involve the sacrum at all. The sacrum does take part in the two sacroiliac joints (a, b), in the sacrococcygeal joint below (d) and in the lumbosacral joint above (e). Recognising which bones form each pelvic joint is the key to this question.
questions.keyConcept: The symphysis pubis unites the two hip bones and does not involve the sacrum.

questions.text: Which listed articulation includes an intervertebral-body symphysis, a secondary cartilaginous joint?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (D) because the lumbosacral joint is an intervertebral disc joint, and all intervertebral discs are secondary cartilaginous joints (symphyses). Every option that includes the sacroiliac joint is wrong, because the sacroiliac joint is a plane synovial joint, which excludes options (a), (b), (c) and (e).
questions.keyConcept: The lumbosacral disc is a secondary cartilaginous joint; the sacroiliac joint is a plane synovial joint.

questions.text: Which of the following shares in the formation of the pelvic inlet?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (C) because the arcuate line of the ilium forms part of the pelvic brim, which is the boundary of the pelvic inlet, together with the sacral promontory, the ala of the sacrum and the pubic crest. The tip of the coccyx (a), the ischial tuberosity (b) and the inferior pubic ramus (d) are all boundaries of the pelvic outlet instead. The obturator foramen (e) lies in the lateral wall of the pelvis.
questions.keyConcept: The pelvic inlet is bounded by the pelvic brim, which includes the arcuate line.

questions.text: As regards the obturator internus, choose the INCORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (C) because this statement is incorrect: obturator internus leaves the pelvis through the lesser sciatic notch, not the greater sciatic foramen, and it is piriformis that uses the greater sciatic foramen. The remaining statements are true, since obturator internus lines the lateral pelvic wall (a), arises from the hip bone around the obturator foramen (b), is covered by obturator fascia (d), and that fascia gives origin to levator ani along its thickened tendinous arch (e).
questions.keyConcept: Obturator internus leaves the pelvis through the lesser sciatic notch; piriformis uses the greater sciatic foramen.
options: It lies in the lateral wall of the pelvic cavity.
It arises from the hip bone.
It leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen.
It is covered by a fascia.
Its fascia gives origin to levator ani muscle.

questions.text: As regards the pelvic muscles, choose the CORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (A) because piriformis passes out of the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen, which it almost fills, to reach the greater trochanter. Option (b) is wrong because piriformis takes origin from the front of the sacrum, and (c) is wrong because the pelvic floor is formed by levator ani and coccygeus. Option (d) is wrong because the retropubic space lies anteriorly, and (e) reverses the parts of levator ani, since pubococcygeus is anterior and iliococcygeus posterior.
questions.keyConcept: Piriformis arises from the sacrum and leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen; the pelvic floor is levator ani plus coccygeus.
options: Piriformis muscle leaves pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen.
Piriformis muscle takes origin from hip bone.
The pelvic floor is formed by the levator ani & piriformis.
The levator ani is formed of iliococcygeus anteriorly & pubococcygeus posteriorly.

questions.text: Which one of the following is a parietal branch?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (D) because the internal pudendal artery supplies the perineum and the pelvic walls rather than a pelvic viscus, and is therefore classed as a parietal branch of the internal iliac artery. The vaginal, inferior vesical, middle rectal and uterine arteries all supply pelvic organs and are visceral branches. Sorting the branches into parietal and visceral groups is the simplest way to handle these questions.
questions.keyConcept: The internal pudendal artery is a parietal branch of the internal iliac artery.

questions.text: Which one of the following is a branch of posterior division of internal iliac artery?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (B) because the iliolumbar artery is one of the three branches of the posterior division of the internal iliac artery, together with the lateral sacral and superior gluteal arteries. All the other arteries listed arise from the anterior division. The posterior division gives only parietal branches, which is a useful check when answering.
questions.keyConcept: The posterior division of the internal iliac artery gives the iliolumbar, lateral sacral and superior gluteal arteries.

questions.text: Which one of the following is a visceral branch?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (C) because the middle rectal artery supplies the rectum, a pelvic viscus, and is therefore a visceral branch of the internal iliac artery. The superior gluteal, lateral sacral, internal pudendal and obturator arteries are all parietal branches supplying the pelvic walls, gluteal region and perineum. Visceral branches are named after the organs they supply.
questions.keyConcept: The middle rectal artery is a visceral branch of the internal iliac artery.

questions.text: Which one of the following is a branch of the lumbar plexus & runs on ala of sacrum?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (E) because the lumbosacral trunk is the descending contribution of the lumbar plexus to the sacral plexus, and it crosses the ala of the sacrum to enter the pelvis. Option (a) is wrong because the obturator nerve runs on the side wall of the pelvis, and (b) is wrong because the sympathetic trunk is not a branch of the lumbar plexus. The sciatic and pudendal nerves (c, d) are branches of the sacral plexus.
questions.keyConcept: The lumbosacral trunk carries L4 and L5 fibers across the ala of the sacrum to join the sacral plexus.

questions.text: Which one of the following carries ganglia?
questions.explanation: The sympathetic trunk is a chain of autonomic paravertebral ganglia. The other listed nerves have no ganglia along the specified pelvic course. Ganglia are collections of neuronal cell bodies in the peripheral nervous system and may be sensory or autonomic.
questions.keyConcept: The sympathetic trunk is a ganglionated chain; somatic pelvic nerves carry no ganglia.

questions.text: Which one of the following pairs pass through greater sciatic foramen?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (C) because both the sciatic nerve and the pudendal nerve leave the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen below piriformis, the pudendal nerve then re-entering the perineum through the lesser sciatic foramen. The obturator nerve leaves through the obturator canal, and the lumbosacral trunk and sympathetic trunk remain within the pelvis or descend over its wall. Only option (c) pairs two structures that both use this foramen.
questions.keyConcept: The sciatic and pudendal nerves both leave the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen.

questions.text: As regards the sacral plexus, choose the CORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (D) because the sacral plexus is formed by the ventral rami of the upper four sacral nerves together with the lumbosacral trunk descending from the lumbar plexus. Option (a) is wrong because the plexus lies in front of piriformis, and (b) is wrong because the obturator nerve is a branch of the lumbar plexus. Option (c) is wrong because it is the sympathetic trunk that lies medial to the anterior sacral foramina, and (e) is wrong because it is the sympathetic trunks that unite in front of the coccyx.
questions.keyConcept: The sacral plexus is formed by S1–S4 ventral rami plus the lumbosacral trunk, lying in front of piriformis.
options: It is formed infront of levator ani.
It is formed medial to anterior sacral foramina.
It is formed by ventral rami of S1,2,3,4 & lumbosacral trunk.
The plexus of both sides unite infront of coccyx.

questions.text: Which of the following organs runs along the concavity of the sacrum?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (B) because the rectum follows the anterior concavity of the sacrum and coccyx, which gives it its characteristic sacral flexure. The sigmoid colon (a) lies above it in the left iliac fossa and pelvis, and the anal canal (d) passes downwards and backwards below the pelvic floor. The bladder (c) and prostate (e) lie anteriorly, behind the pubis.
questions.keyConcept: The rectum curves along the concavity of the sacrum and coccyx.

questions.text: Choose the CORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (C) because the rectum ends and the anal canal begins about one inch beyond the tip of the coccyx, where the gut turns sharply backwards to pierce the pelvic floor. Option (a) is wrong because the sigmoid colon ends at S3, and (b) is wrong because it is the sigmoid colon and not the rectum that has a mesocolon. Option (d) is wrong because the anal canal runs downwards and backwards, and (e) is wrong because it is the anal canal that ends at the anal orifice.
questions.keyConcept: The sigmoid colon ends at S3; the anal canal begins 1 inch beyond the tip of the coccyx and runs downwards and backwards.
options: Anal canal begins 1 inch beyond tip of coccyx.

questions.text: Choose the INCORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (C) because this statement is incorrect: the trigone is the smooth triangular area of the base, or posterior surface, of the bladder, bounded by the two ureteric orifices and the internal urethral orifice. The remaining statements are true, since the empty bladder is pyramidal (a), its apex is continuous with the median umbilical ligament (b), the ureters open at the superolateral angles of the base (d), and the prostatic urethra begins at the bladder neck (e).
questions.keyConcept: The trigone is part of the base of the bladder, not of its neck.
options: Urinary bladder is pyramidal in shape.
Urinary bladder apex gives attachment to median umbilical ligament.
Trigone of urinary bladder is a part of its neck.
Ureters open in superolateral angles of urinary bladder.
Prostatic urethra emerges from neck of urinary bladder.

questions.text: Match each structure in the left column with its appropriate description in the right column:
questions.explanation: The prostate is below the bladder neck and is traversed by prostatic urethra. Membranous urethra traverses the deep perineal region. The bulbar spongy urethra is in the superficial pouch, while its penile portion continues into the free penis. Seminal vesicles lie behind the bladder base.
questions.keyConcept: Prostatic urethra begins at the bladder neck, membranous urethra lies in the deep perineal pouch, and penile urethra in the superficial pouch.

pairs.target: Lies below neck of urinary bladder.
Emerges at neck of urinary bladder.

pairs.premise: Bulbar part of the spongy urethra.
pairs.target: Traverses the bulb of the penis in the superficial perineal pouch.
Lies behind base of urinary bladder.

questions.text: Choose the CORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (B) because the ampulla is the dilated terminal part of the vas deferens, lying behind the base of the bladder. Option (a) is wrong because the seminal vesicles lie lateral to these ampullae, and (c) is wrong because the ejaculatory duct is formed by the union of the duct of the seminal vesicle with the vas deferens of the same side. Option (d) is wrong because the ejaculatory ducts pierce the base of the prostate, and (e) is wrong because they open on the back of the prostatic urethra.
questions.keyConcept: Each ejaculatory duct is formed by the union of the vas deferens with the duct of the seminal vesicle and opens on the back of the prostatic urethra.
options: Seminal vesicles lie medial to ampullae of vasa deferentia.
Ampullae of vasa deferentia are thin dilated parts.
The necks of the 2 seminal vesicles unite to form the ejaculatory duct.
Ejaculatory ducts pierce apex of prostate.
Ejaculatory ducts open on the front of the prostatic urethra.

questions.text: Match each structure in the left column with its appropriate description in the right column:
questions.explanation: The pelvic peritoneum sweeps over the pelvic organs and leaves characteristic fossae and pouches. The sigmoid colon retains a mesocolon, while the rectum progressively loses its peritoneal covering, being clothed in front and at the sides in its upper third and in front only in its middle third. The peritoneum then reflects forwards onto the bladder to form the rectovesical pouch, and paravesical fossae lie on either side of the bladder.
questions.keyConcept: Rectal peritoneal covering decreases from above downwards, and the rectovesical pouch marks where the peritoneum leaves the rectum.

pairs.target: Lie on each side of urinary bladder.
Formed at junction between middle 1/3 & lower 1/3 of rectum.

questions.text: In male pelvis, peritoneum covers all the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (B) because the lower third of the rectum lies below the level of the rectovesical pouch and has no peritoneal covering at all. The middle third is covered anteriorly (a), and the peritoneum of the rectovesical pouch also covers the uppermost part of the base of the bladder and the upper parts of the seminal vesicles (c, d), as well as the superior surface of the bladder (e).
questions.keyConcept: The lower third of the rectum has no peritoneal covering.
options: Uppermost part of base of urinary bladder.

questions.text: Choose the CORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (A) because each uterine tube is attached to the lateral angle, or cornu, of the uterus and runs laterally in the upper border of the broad ligament. Option (b) is wrong because it is the lateral end that opens into the peritoneal cavity, and (c) is wrong because the fimbriae surround that lateral end. Option (d) is wrong because the fundus is the uppermost part of the uterus, and (e) is wrong because the hymen covers the lower end of the vagina.
questions.keyConcept: The uterine tubes arise from the lateral angles of the uterus and open laterally into the peritoneal cavity.
options: Uterine tubes are attached to the lateral angles of the uterus.
Medial end of uterine tube opens in peritoneal cavity.
Fimbria surround medial end of uterine tube.
The cervix is the uppermost part of the uterus.
Cervix of uterus is closed by hymen.

questions.text: Match each structure in the left column with its appropriate description in the right column:
questions.explanation: The lateral end of the uterine tube is the infundibulum, whose margin bears the fimbriae. The cervix projects into the upper anterior wall of the vagina, and the angle between the axis of the cervix and that of the vagina is the angle of anteversion. The ovaries lie against the lateral pelvic wall, and the cavity of the body of the uterus is triangular in shape.
questions.keyConcept: Anteversion is the angle between the cervix and the vagina.

pairs.target: Projects into the anterior wall of vagina.
Forms the angle of anteversion with the cervix of the uterus.
Lie on side wall of pelvis.

pairs.premise: Cavity of the body of the uterus.

questions.text: In female pelvis, peritoneum covers all the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (E) because the anterior surface of the cervix is not covered by peritoneum, the peritoneum leaving the uterus at this level to reflect onto the bladder and form the uterovesical pouch. The posterior surface of the cervix and the upper part of the posterior vaginal wall are covered as part of the rectouterine pouch (a), as are the superior surface and fundus of the uterus (b, c) and the upper surface of the bladder (d).
questions.keyConcept: The front of the cervix is bare of peritoneum, which reflects onto the bladder to form the uterovesical pouch.
options: Upper part of posterior wall of vagina.

questions.text: Uterine tubes lie in:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (D) because each uterine tube runs laterally in the free upper border of the broad ligament, the double fold of peritoneum passing from the uterus to the lateral pelvic wall. The uterovesical and rectovaginal pouches (a, b) are peritoneal recesses in front of and behind the uterus, and the paravesical and pararectal fossae (c, e) flank the bladder and rectum. The broad ligament also contains the ovarian ligament, vessels and the round ligament.
questions.keyConcept: The uterine tube lies in the free upper border of the broad ligament.

questions.text: Choose the INCORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (C) because this statement is incorrect: the perineum is divided by a line between the two ischial tuberosities into the urogenital triangle anteriorly and the anal triangle posteriorly, which is the reverse of what is stated. The remaining statements are true, since the perineum lies below the pelvic diaphragm (a) and is bounded by the pubic arch in front (b), the tip of the coccyx behind (d) and the sacrotuberous ligaments posterolaterally (e).
questions.keyConcept: The perineum has the urogenital triangle anteriorly and the anal triangle posteriorly.
options: Perineum is bounded anteriorly by pubic arch.
Perineum is divided into anal triangle anteriorly & urogenital triangle posteriorly.
Tip of coccyx forms the posterior boundary of the perineum.
Posterolateral boundary of perineum is formed by sacrotuberous lig.

questions.text: Choose the CORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (B) because the perineal membrane divides the urogenital triangle into a superficial and a deep perineal pouch. Option (a) is wrong because the urogenital triangle lies below the pelvic floor, between it and the membranous superficial fascia. Option (c) is wrong because the sphincter urethrae lies in the deep pouch and (d) is wrong because the root of the external genitalia lies in the superficial pouch, and (e) is wrong because the anal triangle contains two ischiorectal fossae.
questions.keyConcept: The perineal membrane divides the urogenital triangle into deep and superficial perineal pouches.
options: Urogenital triangle lies above pelvic floor.
Urogenital triangle is divided by perineal membrane into 2 pouches.
Superficial perineal pouch contains sphincter urethrae.
Deep perineal pouch contains root of external genitalia.
Anal triangle contains anal canal & one ischiorectal fossa.

questions.text: Female external genitalia include all the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (E) because the glans penis is part of the male external genitalia. The female external genitalia, collectively the vulva, comprise the labia majora and minora, the vestibule of the vagina and the clitoris. The clitoris is the female homologue of the penis, but the glans penis itself is a male structure.
questions.keyConcept: The vulva comprises the labia majora and minora, the vestibule and the clitoris.

questions.text: In male, perineal pouches contain all the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (A) because the bulb of the vestibule is a female structure lying in the superficial perineal pouch of the female, and it has no place in the male perineum. The male superficial pouch contains the crura and bulb of the penis (b, c), while the deep pouch contains the bulbourethral glands and the sphincter urethrae (d, e). The bulb of the vestibule is the female homologue of the bulb of the penis.
questions.keyConcept: The bulb of the vestibule is the female homologue of the bulb of the penis and lies in the female superficial perineal pouch.

questions.text: Lat wall of pelvis is formed by:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (B) because the lateral wall of the pelvis is formed by the hip bone below the pelvic brim, covered by obturator internus and its fascia. Piriformis and coccygeus clothe the posterior wall, while iliococcygeus is a part of levator ani forming the pelvic floor.
questions.keyConcept: Obturator internus forms the lateral wall of the pelvis; piriformis and coccygeus the posterior wall.

questions.text: Sigmoid colon end at level of:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (D) because the sigmoid colon begins at the pelvic brim opposite the left sacroiliac joint and ends in front of the third piece of the sacrum, where it becomes the rectum. The rectum then runs from S3 to the tip of the coccyx, where it pierces the pelvic diaphragm as the anal canal.
questions.keyConcept: The sigmoid colon ends and the rectum begins at the level of S3.

questions.text: The Ejaculatory duct opens in:
questions.explanation: Each ejaculatory duct opens on the seminal colliculus in the posterior wall of the prostatic urethra, beside the prostatic utricle. Prostatic gland ducts, rather than ejaculatory ducts, open into the prostatic sinuses.
questions.keyConcept: The ejaculatory ducts open on the posterior wall of the prostatic urethra beside the prostatic utricle.

questions.text: All are true about Anal triangle of perineum except:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (D) because the perineal membrane belongs to the urogenital triangle, where it separates the superficial from the deep perineal pouch; the anal triangle has no perineal membrane. The remaining statements are true, since the anal triangle is bounded laterally by the sacrotuberous ligament and the ischial tuberosities, is traversed by the anal canal and contains an ischioanal fossa on either side of it.
questions.keyConcept: The perineal membrane belongs to the urogenital triangle, not the anal triangle.
options: Bounded laterally by sacro tuberous ligament.
Contains ischiorectal (ischio anal) fossa on sides of anal canal.

questions.text: Which is not true about urinary bladder?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (D) because the median umbilical ligament, the remnant of the urachus, is attached to the apex of the bladder and ascends to the umbilicus, not to the neck. The remaining statements are true, since the ureters open at the posterosuperior angles, the base is related to the seminal vesicles and vasa in the male, and the superior surface is covered by peritoneum forming the uterovesical pouch in the female.
questions.keyConcept: The median umbilical ligament (urachal remnant) attaches to the apex of the bladder.
options: The ureter opens in the post sup angle.
The base is related to seminal vesicle in male.
Sup surface related to utero vesical pouch in female.
The median umbilical ligament attached to the Neck.

questions.text: All are true about female pelvis except:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (C) because the female pelvic cavity is shallower than the male, so its vertical axis is shorter, not longer. The remaining statements are true, since the female peritoneum forms both a uterovesical and a rectouterine pouch, and the subpubic angle and the transverse dimensions are all wider than in the male to favour childbirth.
questions.keyConcept: The female pelvis is wider and shallower than the male, with a wider subpubic angle.
options: The sub pubic angle is wider than males.
The vertical axis is longer than males.
The horizontal axis is wider than males.

questions.text: The anterior articular portion of the sacroiliac joint is classified as:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is Plane synovial. The remaining options do not fit the same anatomical relationship or classification.
questions.keyConcept: Plane synovial

questions.text: The pelvic inlet is bounded by all the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is Ischial tuberosity. The remaining options describe the normal anatomy correctly.
questions.keyConcept: Ischial tuberosity

questions.text: The major part of the pelvic floor is formed by:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is Levator ani. The remaining options do not fit the same anatomical relationship or classification.
questions.keyConcept: The correct answer is Levator ani. The remaining options do not fit the same anatomical relationship or classification

questions.text: The uterine artery is a branch from which artery?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is Anterior division of internal iliac. The remaining options do not fit the same anatomical relationship or classification.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior division of internal iliac

questions.text: The sacral plexus is formed in front of which muscle?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is Piriformis. The remaining options do not fit the same anatomical relationship or classification.
questions.keyConcept: The correct answer is Piriformis. The remaining options do not fit the same anatomical relationship or classification

questions.text: The rectum starts at the level of which vertebra?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is S3. The remaining options do not fit the same anatomical relationship or classification.
questions.keyConcept: The correct answer is S3. The remaining options do not fit the same anatomical relationship or classification

questions.text: The trigone lines the ______ of the urinary bladder.
questions.explanation: The correct answer is Base. The remaining options do not fit the same anatomical relationship or classification.
questions.keyConcept: The correct answer is Base. The remaining options do not fit the same anatomical relationship or classification

questions.text: The ejaculatory duct opens in which part of the male urethra?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is Prostatic. The remaining options do not fit the same anatomical relationship or classification.
questions.keyConcept: The correct answer is Prostatic. The remaining options do not fit the same anatomical relationship or classification

questions.text: The superficial perineal pouch lies:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is Between perineal membrane and superficial fascia of the perineum. The remaining options do not fit the same anatomical relationship or classification.
questions.keyConcept: Between perineal membrane and superficial fascia of the perineum
options: Between levator ani and perineal membrane
Between perineal membrane and superficial fascia of the perineum

questions.text: The sphincter urethrae is present in:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is Deep perineal pouch. The remaining options do not fit the same anatomical relationship or classification.
questions.keyConcept: Deep perineal pouch

questions.text: An example of a girdle bone is:
questions.explanation: The hip bone is part of the pelvic girdle.
questions.keyConcept: The hip bone is part of the pelvic girdle

questions.text: The..........is cartilaginous joint:
questions.explanation: The pubic symphysis is a secondary cartilaginous joint.
questions.keyConcept: Cartilaginous joint

questions.text: The spermatic cord contains all the following structures, except:
questions.explanation: The epididymis lies on the testis and is not a content of the spermatic cord.
questions.keyConcept: The epididymis is not a content of the spermatic cord.

questions.text: All the followings are parts of the uterus, except:
questions.explanation: The fallopian tubes are related adnexal structures, not parts of the uterus itself.
questions.keyConcept: The uterus includes fundus, body, and cervix; not the fallopian tubes.

questions.text: Regarding the pelvic cavity, one is incorrect:
questions.explanation: In the female pelvis, the uterus and vagina occupy the middle compartment; the posterior compartment contains the rectum.
questions.keyConcept: Female pelvic organs occupy anterior, middle, and posterior compartments.
options: The male and female pelvis contains Urinary bladder and urethra anteriorly.
The male and female pelvis contains Ureters and large blood vessels laterally.
The female pelvis contains Uterus, Uterine tubes and vagina posteriorly.
The male pelvis contains Seminal vesicles and vas deferens in the middle.

questions.text: Regarding the male urethra, one is correct:
questions.explanation: The penile or spongy urethra is about 15 cm long.
questions.keyConcept: The penile urethra is the longest part of the male urethra.
options: The Prostatic urethra passes through the deep perineal pouch.
Penile Urethra is 15 cm in length.
The Prostatic urethra is 8 cm in length.
Membranous urethra passes through the prostate.

questions.text: Internal anal sphincter is ___ while the external anal sphincter is ___.
questions.explanation: The internal sphincter is smooth muscle and involuntary, while the external sphincter is skeletal muscle and voluntary.
questions.keyConcept: Internal anal sphincter is involuntary; external is voluntary.

questions.text: Which one of the following shares in formation of shoulder girdle?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (A) because the shoulder girdle is formed of the clavicle and the scapula, which together attach the free upper limb to the axial skeleton. The humerus (d) is the bone of the arm, the radius and ulna (b, c) are forearm bones and the scaphoid (e) is a carpal bone, so none of them belongs to the girdle.
questions.keyConcept: The shoulder girdle is formed by the clavicle and the scapula.

questions.text: Which of the following is a bone of distal row of carpal bone?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (C) because the capitate belongs to the distal carpal row, together with the trapezium, trapezoid and hamate. The scaphoid, lunate, triquetral and pisiform all belong to the proximal row, the pisiform lying in front of the triquetral as a sesamoid in the tendon of flexor carpi ulnaris.
questions.keyConcept: Distal carpal row: trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, hamate.

questions.text: Match each joint in left column with its type in right column:
questions.explanation: Synovial joints are classified by the shape of their articular surfaces and the movements they allow. The acromioclavicular and intercarpal joints are plane joints permitting only gliding, the elbow is a uniaxial hinge, the superior radioulnar joint is a pivot allowing rotation of the radial head, and the shoulder is a multiaxial ball and socket joint, the most mobile joint in the body.
questions.keyConcept: Shoulder = ball & socket, elbow = hinge, superior radioulnar = pivot, acromioclavicular and intercarpal = plane.

questions.text: Match each joint in left column with its type in right column:
questions.explanation: The wrist (radiocarpal) joint is ellipsoid, allowing flexion, extension and side to side movement. The carpometacarpal joint of the thumb is the classic saddle joint, which is what permits opposition, while the carpometacarpal joint of the index is a plane joint with almost no movement. The metacarpophalangeal joints are condylar and the interphalangeal joints are simple hinges.
questions.keyConcept: Wrist = ellipsoid, CMC of thumb = saddle, MCP = condylar, IP = hinge.

questions.text: Choose the CORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (D) because the distal end of the radius carries the articular surface for the scaphoid and lunate at the wrist joint. Option (a) is wrong because the humerus articulates with both radius and ulna at the elbow, and (b) is wrong because the inferior radioulnar joint is a pivot. Option (c) is wrong because interphalangeal joints are hinge joints, and (e) is wrong because the lower end of the ulna does not articulate with the capitate.
questions.keyConcept: The lower end of the radius articulates with the scaphoid and lunate; the ulna is excluded from the wrist joint proper.
options: In elbow joint, humerus articulates with radius only.
Lower end of radius articulates with scaphoid & lunate.
Lower end of ulna articulates with capitate.

questions.text: Match each structure in left column with its appropriate description in right column:
questions.explanation: The upper limb is described region by region. The axilla is the pyramidal space between the upper arm and the chest wall, the pectoral region contains the muscles running from the thoracic wall to the limb, and the shoulder region contains the scapulohumeral muscles including the rotator cuff. The back carries the muscles linking the limb to the vertebral column, and the cubital fossa is the triangular hollow in front of the elbow.
questions.keyConcept: Axilla = space between arm and chest; cubital fossa = triangular hollow in front of the elbow.

pairs.target: Muscles connecting upper limb to thoracic wall.
Muscles connecting upper limb to vertebral column.

questions.text: Which of the following is inserted in the humerus?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (B) because latissimus dorsi passes from the trunk to the floor of the bicipital groove of the humerus, which is why it can extend, adduct and medially rotate the arm. Trapezius is inserted into the clavicle and scapula, and levator scapulae and both rhomboids are inserted into the scapula only.
questions.keyConcept: Latissimus dorsi is the only superficial back muscle inserted into the humerus.

questions.text: Which of the following is the most superficial?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (E) because pectoralis major is the most superficial structure of the pectoral region, lying immediately deep to the superficial fascia and breast. Deep to it lie the clavipectoral fascia and, enclosed by that fascia, subclavius and pectoralis minor, with the ribs deepest of all.
questions.keyConcept: Pectoralis major is the most superficial muscle of the pectoral region.

questions.text: Which of the following shares in the formation of the medial wall of the axilla?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (C) because the medial wall of the axilla is formed by the upper ribs with their intercostal muscles covered by serratus anterior. Subscapularis and latissimus dorsi (a, b) form the posterior wall, pectoralis major (d) the anterior wall, and the axillary fascia (e) forms the base.
questions.keyConcept: The medial wall of the axilla is the upper ribs and intercostals covered by serratus anterior.

questions.text: Which of the following shares in formation of lateral wall of axilla?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (A) because the lateral wall of the axilla is very narrow, being formed by the bicipital groove of the humerus with the muscles attached there, that is the coracobrachialis and the two heads of biceps. Serratus anterior (c) forms the medial wall, the pectoral muscles (b, d) the anterior wall and teres major (e) the posterior wall.
questions.keyConcept: The lateral wall of the axilla is the bicipital groove with coracobrachialis and biceps.

questions.text: Axillary fascia shares in the formation of:
questions.explanation: The narrow lateral wall of the axilla is formed by the intertubercular sulcus of the humerus, with coracobrachialis and biceps related to it. Serratus anterior forms the medial wall; the pectoral muscles form the anterior wall; teres major contributes to the posterior wall.
questions.keyConcept: The axillary fascia forms the base of the axilla.

questions.text: As regards the axillary artery, choose the CORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (D) because the axillary artery ends at the lower border of teres major, where it becomes the brachial artery. Option (a) is wrong because it is the continuation of the subclavian artery, and (b) is wrong because it begins at the outer border of the first rib. Option (c) reverses the sequence, and (e) is wrong because it is pectoralis minor that divides the artery into three parts.
questions.keyConcept: The axillary artery runs from the outer border of the first rib to the lower border of teres major and is divided into three parts by pectoralis minor.
options: It is the continuation of the brachial artery.
It begins at inner border of 1st rib.
It ends by forming subclavian artery.
It ends at lower border of teres major.
It is divided into 3 parts by pectoralis major.

questions.text: As regards the axillary vein, choose the INCORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (E) because this statement is incorrect: the axillary vein lies medial to the axillary artery throughout its course. The other statements are true, since the vein is the upward continuation of the basilic vein beginning at the lower border of teres major (a, d) and ends at the outer border of the first rib by becoming the subclavian vein (b, c).
questions.keyConcept: The axillary vein lies medial to the axillary artery.
options: It is the continuation of the basilic vein.
It ends at outer border of 1st rib.
It ends by forming subclavian vein.
It begins at lower border of teres major.
It lies lateral to axillary artery.

questions.text: Brachial plexus gives all the following branches EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (C) because the accessory nerve is the eleventh cranial nerve, which supplies trapezius and has nothing to do with the brachial plexus. The radial, median and musculocutaneous nerves and the ulnar nerve are all terminal branches of the plexus, arising from its cords.
questions.keyConcept: The accessory nerve is a cranial nerve, not a branch of the brachial plexus.

questions.text: Axilla contains all the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (C) because trapezius is a muscle of the back that does not enter the axilla at all. The axilla contains the axillary vessels, the cords and branches of the brachial plexus including the radial and median nerves, axillary lymph nodes and the axillary tail of the breast.
questions.keyConcept: The axilla contains the axillary vessels, brachial plexus cords, lymph nodes and the axillary tail of the breast.

questions.text: Which one of the following can be seen from front of scapula?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (E) because subscapularis arises from the costal, that is anterior, surface of the scapula and is therefore the only one of these muscles seen from the front. Supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor and teres major all arise from the dorsal surface of the scapula.
questions.keyConcept: Subscapularis is the only muscle on the anterior (costal) surface of the scapula.

questions.text: All the following share in the formation of the rotator cuff EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (A) because teres major is not part of the rotator cuff; it is inserted into the humerus below the cuff and is a medial rotator and adductor. The cuff is formed by supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor and subscapularis, whose tendons blend with the capsule of the shoulder joint and hold the head of the humerus in the glenoid.
questions.keyConcept: The rotator cuff is supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor and subscapularis.

questions.text: Dislocation of shoulder joint is common to occur in:
questions.explanation: Most shoulder dislocations are anterior, usually anteroinferior. The inferior capsule is the weakest part of the joint, which helps explain the path of escape, but the usual clinical direction is anterior rather than simply inferior.
questions.keyConcept: The common clinical shoulder dislocation is anterior, typically anteroinferior.

questions.text: Anterior compartment of arm contains all the following muscles EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (E) because brachioradialis, despite its name, belongs to the extensor compartment of the forearm and is supplied by the radial nerve. The anterior compartment of the arm contains the two heads of biceps brachii, coracobrachialis and brachialis, all supplied by the musculocutaneous nerve.
questions.keyConcept: The anterior compartment of the arm contains biceps, coracobrachialis and brachialis; brachioradialis is a forearm extensor.

questions.text: As regards the muscles of the anterior compartment of the arm, choose the INCORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (A) because this statement is incorrect: brachialis is the deeper muscle and biceps lies superficial to it. The remaining statements are true, since biceps has two heads (b), the long or lateral head passes through the shoulder joint inside the capsule (c), and coracobrachialis is the shortest muscle of the compartment and lies medial to the short head of biceps (d, e).
questions.keyConcept: Brachialis lies deep to biceps in the anterior compartment of the arm.
options: Biceps lies deep to brachialis muscle.
Lateral head of biceps passes through shoulder joint.
Coracobrachialis is the shortest muscle of anterior compartment of arm.
Coracobrachialis lies medial to short head of biceps.

questions.text: As regards the vessels in front of arm, choose the INCORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (B) because this statement is incorrect: the brachial artery is the continuation of the axillary artery and ends by dividing into the radial and ulnar arteries, not by being formed from them. The other statements are true, since the artery ends at the level of the neck of the radius (a), the basilic vein begins from the medial end of the dorsal venous arch (c), and the cephalic vein ascends in the superficial fascia to end in the axillary vein (d, e).
questions.keyConcept: The brachial artery continues the axillary artery and divides into radial and ulnar arteries at the neck of the radius.
options: Brachial artery ends at level of neck of radius.
Brachial artery is formed by union of radial & ulnar arteries.
Basilic vein begins from dorsal venous arch.
Cephalic vein ends in axillary vein.
Cephalic vein ascends in superficial fascia.

questions.text: As regards nerves in front of arm, choose the CORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (C) because the ulnar nerve passes behind the medial epicondyle of the humerus to enter the forearm, where it can be rolled against the bone. Options (a) and (d) are wrong because biceps and brachialis are supplied by the musculocutaneous nerve, and (b) is wrong because it is the ulnar nerve that pierces the medial intermuscular septum. Option (e) is wrong because the median nerve stays in front of the arm and gives no branches there.
questions.keyConcept: The ulnar nerve passes behind the medial epicondyle; the musculocutaneous nerve supplies the anterior arm muscles.
options: Musculocutaneous nerve pierces medial intermuscular septum.
Ulnar nerve passes behind medial epicondyle.
Median nerve passes to back of arm.

questions.text: As regards back of arm, choose the INCORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (E) because this statement is incorrect: triceps brachii has long, medial and lateral heads, there being no short head. The other statements are true, since the radial nerve pierces the lateral intermuscular septum and then passes in front of the lateral epicondyle (a, d), the axillary nerve winds round the surgical neck of the humerus (b), and the profunda brachii accompanies the radial nerve in the spiral groove (c).
questions.keyConcept: Triceps brachii has long, lateral and medial heads.
options: Radial nerve pierces lateral intermuscular septum.
Axillary nerve lies close to surgical neck of humerus.
Profunda brachii artery runs in spiral groove.
Radial nerve passes infront of lateral epicondyle.
Triceps brachii muscle has long, short & lateral heads.

questions.text: Lateral boundary of cubital fossa is formed by:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (B) because brachioradialis forms the lateral boundary of the triangular cubital fossa. Pronator teres (a) forms the medial boundary, brachialis (d) with supinator (c) forms the floor, and the bicipital aponeurosis (e) reinforces the roof.
questions.keyConcept: Cubital fossa: brachioradialis laterally, pronator teres medially, base between the epicondyles.

questions.text: Match each structure in the left column with its relation to cubital fossa in the right column:
questions.explanation: The cubital fossa is a triangular hollow in front of the elbow. Its base is an imaginary line joining the two humeral epicondyles, its lateral and medial boundaries are brachioradialis and pronator teres, its floor is brachialis with supinator, and its roof is the deep fascia strengthened by the bicipital aponeurosis, with the median cubital vein lying in the superficial fascia above.
questions.keyConcept: Cubital fossa boundaries: base between epicondyles, brachioradialis laterally, pronator teres medially, brachialis floor, bicipital aponeurosis in the roof.

questions.text: As regards contents of cubital fossa, choose the CORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (C) because the brachial artery divides into the radial and ulnar arteries at the level of the neck of the radius, within the fossa. Option (a) is wrong because the biceps tendon lies lateral to the artery, and (b) and (d) are wrong because the radial nerve is the most lateral structure while the artery lies in the middle of the fossa. Option (e) is wrong because the median nerve lies medial to the brachial artery.
questions.keyConcept: From lateral to medial in the cubital fossa: radial nerve, biceps tendon, brachial artery, median nerve.
options: Brachial artery lies lateral to tendon of biceps.
Radial nerve is the most medial structure in the fossa.
Brachial artery bifurcates at level of neck of radius.
Brachial artery is the most lateral structure in the fossa.
Median nerve lies lateral to brachial artery.

questions.text: The artery used in measurement of blood pressure is the:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (A) because the brachial artery in the cubital fossa is compressed by the cuff and auscultated to measure arterial blood pressure, as it is large, superficial and lies against the humerus. The radial artery (b) is used for feeling the pulse rather than for cuff measurement, and the ulnar, axillary and subclavian arteries are less accessible for routine measurement.
questions.keyConcept: Blood pressure is measured over the brachial artery in the cubital fossa.

questions.text: Which superficial vein at the elbow is commonly used for venepuncture?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (D) because the median cubital vein lies superficially in the roof of the cubital fossa, is relatively fixed and is separated from the brachial artery by the bicipital aponeurosis, which makes it the standard site for venepuncture. The cephalic and basilic veins (a, b) are more mobile, while the axillary and subclavian veins (c, e) are deep.
questions.keyConcept: The median cubital vein is the usual site for venepuncture, protected from the brachial artery by the bicipital aponeurosis.

questions.text: In the front of the forearm, which one of the following is the most lateral & superficial muscle?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (D) because pronator teres is the most lateral muscle of the superficial flexor group, passing obliquely from the medial epicondyle to the lateral surface of the radius. Flexor carpi ulnaris (a) is the most medial, flexor digitorum superficialis (e) lies deep to the other superficial muscles, and pronator quadratus (c) is the deepest muscle at the wrist.
questions.keyConcept: Pronator teres is the most lateral of the superficial flexors of the forearm.

questions.text: In the front of the forearm, which one of the following is the most Medial & deep muscle?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (A) because flexor digitorum profundus is a deep muscle occupying the medial side of the front of the forearm, arising from the ulna and interosseous membrane. Flexor pollicis longus (c) is the deep muscle on the lateral side, while flexor carpi radialis, palmaris longus and flexor digitorum superficialis belong to the superficial group.
questions.keyConcept: Deep flexors of the forearm: flexor digitorum profundus medially, flexor pollicis longus laterally, pronator quadratus distally.

questions.text: In the front of the forearm, which one of the following muscles lies over the lower ends of radius & ulna?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (C) because pronator quadratus is a flat quadrilateral muscle stretching across the lower quarter of the anterior surfaces of the ulna and radius, deep to all the flexor tendons. Pronator teres (d) lies at the upper end of the forearm, and the other muscles listed run longitudinally as flexors of the wrist and fingers.
questions.keyConcept: Pronator quadratus crosses the lower ends of the radius and ulna and is the deepest muscle there.

questions.text: Which of the following lies medially in front of forearm?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (B) because the ulnar nerve descends on the medial side of the front of the forearm, under cover of flexor carpi ulnaris and with the ulnar artery on its lateral side. The median nerve (c) runs in the middle of the forearm, the radial nerve (d) is on the lateral side, and the anterior interosseous nerve and vessels (a, e) lie deeply on the interosseous membrane.
questions.keyConcept: The ulnar nerve runs medially in the front of the forearm beneath flexor carpi ulnaris.

questions.text: Most muscles in front of forearm are supplied by:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (C) because the median nerve, directly and through its anterior interosseous branch, supplies all the flexor muscles of the front of the forearm except flexor carpi ulnaris and the medial half of flexor digitorum profundus, which are supplied by the ulnar nerve. The radial nerve supplies the extensor compartment, and the musculocutaneous nerve ends in the arm.
questions.keyConcept: The median nerve supplies most flexors of the forearm; the ulnar nerve supplies only FCU and the medial half of FDP.

questions.text: All the following pass deep to flexor retinaculum EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (B) because the ulnar nerve passes superficial to the flexor retinaculum, lateral to the pisiform, and so escapes compression in the carpal tunnel. The median nerve and the tendons of flexor pollicis longus, flexor digitorum superficialis and flexor digitorum profundus all pass deep to the retinaculum within the tunnel.
questions.keyConcept: The ulnar nerve passes superficial to the flexor retinaculum; the median nerve and long flexor tendons pass deep to it.

questions.text: Choose the INCORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (A) because this statement is incorrect: carpal tunnel syndrome is caused by compression of the median nerve, not the ulnar nerve, which passes superficial to the retinaculum. The other statements are true, since median nerve compression causes thenar wasting and pain in the lateral three and a half digits (b, c), and the palmar aponeurosis receives palmaris longus at its apex and improves grip (d, e).
questions.keyConcept: Carpal tunnel syndrome is compression of the median nerve, causing thenar wasting and pain in the lateral 3½ digits.
options: Carpal tunnel syndrome is due to compression of ulnar nerve.
In carpal tunnel syndrome, there is wasting of muscles of thenar eminence.
In carpal tunnel syndrome, there is pain in lateral 3½ fingers.
Apex of palmar aponeurosis gives attachment to palmaris longus.
Palmar aponeurosis improves gripping of objects.

questions.text: Match each structure in the left column with its appropriate description in the right column:
questions.explanation: The short muscles of the hand are grouped by the digit they move. The thenar muscles form the ball of the thumb and act on it, the hypothenar muscles act on the little finger, and the four lumbricals arise from the tendons of flexor digitorum profundus and are inserted into the extensor expansions. Palmaris brevis is exceptional in lying within the superficial fascia over the hypothenar eminence.
questions.keyConcept: Thenar muscles act on the thumb, hypothenar on the little finger, lumbricals arise from the profundus tendons.

questions.text: In the back of the forearm, which one of the following is superficial & lateral?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (D) because brachioradialis is the most lateral and superficial muscle of the extensor compartment, forming the lateral border of the forearm as it passes to the styloid process of the radius. Extensor carpi ulnaris and extensor digiti minimi lie medially and posteriorly, extensor digitorum lies in the middle, and anconeus is a small muscle at the back of the elbow.
questions.keyConcept: Brachioradialis is the most superficial and lateral muscle of the back of the forearm.

questions.text: In the back of the forearm, which one of the following is superficial & posterior?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (C) because extensor carpi ulnaris lies superficially on the posterior aspect of the forearm along its ulnar side. The two extensores carpi radiales and brachioradialis lie laterally (a, b, d), while abductor pollicis longus (e) belongs to the deep group emerging distally between the superficial muscles.
questions.keyConcept: Extensor carpi ulnaris is the superficial posterior extensor on the ulnar side of the forearm.

questions.text: In the back of the forearm, which one of the following is deep?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (E) because extensor indicis belongs to the deep group of extensors, along with supinator, abductor pollicis longus and the extensores pollicis brevis and longus. Extensor digiti minimi, extensor carpi ulnaris, brachioradialis and anconeus all belong to the superficial group of the extensor compartment.
questions.keyConcept: The deep extensors of the forearm include supinator, abductor pollicis longus, extensor pollicis brevis and longus, and extensor indicis.

questions.text: Choose the INCORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The radial artery crosses the floor of the anatomical snuffbox. The cephalic vein and superficial radial nerve cross its roof, so it is misleading to call the artery its only content. Extensor pollicis longus forms the medial boundary.
questions.keyConcept: The radial artery is the only content of the anatomical snuff box.
options: Dorsal venous arch lies in superficial fascia.
The only content in anatomical snuff box is ulnar artery.
Snuff box is bounded medially by tendon of extensor pollicis longus.
Cephalic vein begins from lateral end of dorsal venous arch.
Extensor retinaculum lies on back of wrist.

questions.text: The shoulder joint liable to dislocate in which direction:
questions.explanation: The shoulder joint most commonly dislocates anteriorly, usually in an anteroinferior direction. Inferior capsular weakness explains why the humeral head escapes in that direction, but the standard clinical description is anterior dislocation.
questions.keyConcept: Shoulder dislocation is most commonly anterior.

questions.text: Flexors (ant group) of fore arm is mainly supplied by:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (B) because the median nerve supplies all the muscles of the anterior (flexor) compartment of the forearm except flexor carpi ulnaris and the medial half of flexor digitorum profundus, which are ulnar. The radial nerve supplies the extensor compartment, and the musculocutaneous nerve ends in the arm as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm.
questions.keyConcept: The median nerve supplies the forearm flexors except flexor carpi ulnaris and the medial half of flexor digitorum profundus.

questions.text: Upper limb is connected to vertebral column by which of the following muscles:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (C) because trapezius and latissimus dorsi both arise from the vertebral spines and insert into the pectoral girdle or humerus, so they link the upper limb to the vertebral column. Pectoralis major and minor connect the limb to the anterior chest wall, while the teres and spinati muscles run from the scapula to the humerus only.
questions.keyConcept: Trapezius and latissimus dorsi connect the upper limb to the vertebral column.

questions.text: All are the following pass through cubital fossa except:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (D) because the ulnar nerve passes behind the medial epicondyle of the humerus and so lies outside the cubital fossa altogether. The contents of the fossa from medial to lateral are the median nerve, the brachial artery and the tendon of biceps, with the radial nerve under cover of brachioradialis at its lateral angle.
questions.keyConcept: The ulnar nerve passes behind the medial epicondyle and is not a content of the cubital fossa.

questions.text: The brachial artery ends at which level:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (C) because the brachial artery ends in the cubital fossa at the level of the neck of the radius by dividing into the radial and ulnar arteries. The lower border of teres major marks where the axillary artery becomes the brachial, and the outer border of the first rib marks the beginning of the axillary artery.
questions.keyConcept: The brachial artery ends at the level of the neck of the radius by dividing into radial and ulnar arteries.

questions.text: Which of the following content of carpal tunnel:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (C) because the median nerve passes through the carpal tunnel deep to the flexor retinaculum, together with the tendons of the long flexors of the fingers and thumb. The ulnar nerve and artery pass superficial to the retinaculum in the ulnar canal, and the radial and musculocutaneous nerves do not reach the tunnel.
questions.keyConcept: The carpal tunnel transmits the median nerve and the long flexor tendons.

questions.text: Wound in the most lateral part of cubital fossa could affect all the following except:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (C) because the ulnar nerve lies far medially, behind the medial epicondyle, and cannot be injured by a wound in the lateral part of the fossa. The biceps tendon, the supinator forming part of the floor, and the radial nerve dividing under brachioradialis all lie in or near the lateral angle of the fossa.
questions.keyConcept: The lateral part of the cubital fossa contains the biceps tendon, supinator and radial nerve; the ulnar nerve is medial.

questions.text: Pulsation of which artery could be felt at the snuff box:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (B) because the radial artery crosses the floor of the anatomical snuff box on the scaphoid and trapezium, where its pulsation can be felt. The ulnar and anterior interosseous arteries remain on the flexor side of the wrist, and the brachial artery ends in the cubital fossa.
questions.keyConcept: The radial artery crosses the floor of the snuff box and its pulse can be felt there.

questions.text: Carpal tunnel syndrome is due to compression on which of the following nerves:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (D) because carpal tunnel syndrome results from compression of the median nerve beneath the flexor retinaculum, producing tingling and sensory loss in the lateral three and a half digits and wasting of the thenar muscles. The ulnar nerve escapes because it passes superficial to the retinaculum.
questions.keyConcept: Carpal tunnel syndrome is compression of the median nerve under the flexor retinaculum.

questions.text: Nerves of the post compartment of the arm:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (B) because the radial nerve is the nerve of the posterior compartment of the arm, running in the spiral groove and supplying the three heads of triceps. The median and ulnar nerves simply traverse the arm without supplying any muscle in it, and the axillary nerve supplies deltoid and teres minor around the shoulder.
questions.keyConcept: The radial nerve is the nerve of the posterior compartment of the arm and supplies triceps.

questions.text: Nerve that pierce coracobrachialis muscle:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (C) because the musculocutaneous nerve leaves the axilla by piercing coracobrachialis, then runs between biceps and brachialis supplying all three flexors of the arm. The median and ulnar nerves descend without piercing any muscle in the arm, and the radial nerve passes into the spiral groove.
questions.keyConcept: The musculocutaneous nerve pierces coracobrachialis and supplies the anterior compartment of the arm.

questions.text: Nerve that pierce the lateral inter muscular septum of the arm:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (B) because the radial nerve leaves the spiral groove by piercing the lateral intermuscular septum to enter the anterior compartment above the elbow. It is the ulnar nerve that pierces the medial intermuscular septum to reach the back of the arm.
questions.keyConcept: The radial nerve pierces the lateral intermuscular septum; the ulnar nerve pierces the medial one.

questions.text: Artery related to spiral groove of humerus:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (C) because the profunda brachii artery accompanies the radial nerve in the spiral groove on the back of the humerus. The brachial artery runs on the front of the arm, and the radial and ulnar arteries begin only in the cubital fossa.
questions.keyConcept: The spiral groove transmits the radial nerve with the profunda brachii artery.

questions.text: Muscles of hand is mainly supplied by:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (C) because the ulnar nerve supplies all the intrinsic muscles of the hand except the three thenar muscles and the lateral two lumbricals, which are median. This is why an ulnar lesion produces the characteristic claw hand with wasting of the interossei.
questions.keyConcept: The ulnar nerve supplies most intrinsic hand muscles, sparing the thenar muscles and lateral two lumbricals.

questions.text: The Axillary artery is divided by which muscle:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (D) because pectoralis minor crosses the axillary artery and divides it into three parts, the first above the muscle, the second behind it and the third below it. Scalenus anterior performs the same role for the subclavian artery, not the axillary.
questions.keyConcept: Pectoralis minor divides the axillary artery into three parts.

questions.text: The axillary vein is continuation of which:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (B) because the basilic vein pierces the deep fascia in the arm, joins the brachial veins and continues as the axillary vein at the lower border of teres major. The cephalic vein instead ends by joining the axillary vein near the clavicle, and the axillary vein itself continues as the subclavian vein at the first rib.
questions.keyConcept: The basilic vein continues as the axillary vein at the lower border of teres major.

questions.text: The muscle that form the lateral boundary of cubital fossa is:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (C) because brachioradialis forms the lateral boundary of the triangular cubital fossa, while pronator teres forms its medial boundary. Supinator and brachialis form part of the floor, and the biceps tendon is a content of the fossa rather than a boundary.
questions.keyConcept: Cubital fossa: brachioradialis laterally, pronator teres medially, and a line between the epicondyles as its base.

questions.text: Which of the following muscles enclosed within clavipectoral fascia:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (C) because the clavipectoral fascia extends from the clavicle to the axillary fascia and splits to enclose pectoralis minor and subclavius. Pectoralis major lies superficial to this fascia, and deltoid and subscapularis lie well outside it.
questions.keyConcept: The clavipectoral fascia encloses subclavius and pectoralis minor.

questions.text: Which of the following muscle not related to rotator cuff:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (C) because teres major is inserted into the medial lip of the bicipital groove and takes no part in the rotator cuff. The cuff is formed by supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor and subscapularis, whose tendons blend with the capsule of the shoulder joint.
questions.keyConcept: Rotator cuff: supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor and subscapularis. Teres major is not part of it.

questions.text: Which tendon passes within the capsule of the shoulder joint?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (C) because the long head of biceps arises from the supraglenoid tubercle inside the joint and pierces the capsule to descend in the bicipital groove, making it an intracapsular but extrasynovial structure. The long head of triceps arises from the infraglenoid tubercle outside the capsule, and the short head of biceps arises from the coracoid process.
questions.keyConcept: The tendon of the long head of biceps runs inside the shoulder joint and pierces its capsule.

questions.text: Which is wrong statement about cephalic vein:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (B) because the cephalic vein does not end in the basilic vein; it pierces the clavipectoral fascia in the deltopectoral groove and ends in the axillary vein. It is only connected to the basilic vein by the median cubital vein in front of the elbow. The remaining statements are correct, since it begins from the lateral end of the dorsal venous arch and ascends along the lateral side of the limb.
questions.keyConcept: The cephalic vein ascends laterally and ends in the axillary vein, communicating with the basilic vein through the median cubital vein.
options: Begins at the lateral side of dorsal venous arch.
Runs along lat side of upper limb.

questions.text: Choose the incorrect statement about ulnar nerve:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (D) because the ulnar nerve gives no muscular branches in the arm at all; its first muscular branches are to flexor carpi ulnaris and the medial half of flexor digitorum profundus in the forearm. The other statements are true, since it crosses superficial to the flexor retinaculum, pierces the medial intermuscular septum to reach the back of the arm, is the principal motor nerve of the hand and passes behind the medial epicondyle.
questions.keyConcept: The ulnar nerve supplies no muscle in the arm, but is the main motor nerve of the hand.
options: Share in supplying muscle of arm.

questions.text: Regarding axilla all are true except:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (B) because serratus anterior forms the medial wall of the axilla over the upper ribs, whereas the posterior wall is formed by subscapularis, teres major and latissimus dorsi. The remaining statements are true, since the two pectoral muscles form the anterior wall, the apex is bounded by the clavicle, the first rib and the upper border of the scapula, and the lateral wall is the bicipital groove with coracobrachialis and biceps.
questions.keyConcept: Axilla: pectorals in front, subscapularis and teres major behind, serratus anterior medially, bicipital groove laterally.
options: Pectoralis major, minor forms the ant wall.
Serratus ant shares in post wall.

questions.text: All the following is related to the snuff box except:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (C) because abductor pollicis brevis is a thenar muscle in the palm and has no relation to the snuff box. The anterior boundary of the box is formed by the tendons of abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis, and its posterior boundary by the tendon of extensor pollicis longus.
questions.keyConcept: Snuff box boundaries: abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis in front, extensor pollicis longus behind.

questions.text: Which of the following pass deep to flexor Retinaculum:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (D) because the tendon of flexor pollicis longus passes deep to the flexor retinaculum through the carpal tunnel, in its own synovial sheath. The ulnar nerve and artery pass superficial to the retinaculum, and palmaris longus is inserted into its anterior surface and into the palmar aponeurosis.
questions.keyConcept: Deep to the flexor retinaculum: the long flexor tendons including flexor pollicis longus, plus the median nerve.

questions.text: Wrist joint formed by all the following bones except:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (C) because the ulna takes no part in the wrist joint, being separated from the carpus by the triangular articular disc of the inferior radioulnar joint. The joint is formed above by the lower end of the radius and that disc, and below by the scaphoid, lunate and triquetral bones.
questions.keyConcept: The wrist joint is formed by the radius and articular disc above and the scaphoid, lunate and triquetral below; the ulna is excluded.

questions.text: Which of the following pairs pass through spiral groove of the humerus:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (C) because the spiral (radial) groove on the back of the humerus transmits the radial nerve together with the profunda brachii artery and its accompanying veins. This close relationship explains why a mid-shaft fracture of the humerus may cause wrist drop from radial nerve injury.
questions.keyConcept: The spiral groove of the humerus transmits the radial nerve and the profunda brachii vessels.

questions.text: Which one of the following joints is ellipsoid?
questions.explanation: The radiocarpal joint is ellipsoid/condyloid.
questions.keyConcept: Wrist Joint: The radiocarpal joint is ellipsoid/condyloid

questions.text: Which type of bone is the pisiform?
questions.explanation: Pisiform is a sesamoid carpal bone within the flexor carpi ulnaris tendon.
questions.keyConcept: Carpal Bones: Pisiform is a sesamoid carpal bone within the flexor carpi ulnaris tendon

questions.text: The shoulder joint is:
questions.explanation: The glenohumeral joint is a multiaxial ball-and-socket joint.
questions.keyConcept: Shoulder Joint: The glenohumeral joint is a multiaxial ball-and-socket joint

questions.text: The elbow joint is:
questions.explanation: The humeroulnar component of the elbow is a hinge joint.
questions.keyConcept: Elbow Joint: The humeroulnar component of the elbow is a hinge joint

questions.text: An example of unipennate muscle:
questions.explanation: Flexor pollicis longus is classically described as unipennate.
questions.keyConcept: Muscle Architecture: Flexor pollicis longus is classically described as unipennate

questions.text: What is the type of the lunate (carpal) bone?
questions.explanation: The lunate is classified as a short carpal bone because it is one of the small cuboidal bones of the wrist.
questions.keyConcept: The lunate is one of the short carpal bones.

questions.text: Which of the following is a long bone?
questions.explanation: The clavicle is classified as a modified long bone.
questions.keyConcept: Bone Classification: The clavicle is classified as a modified long bone

questions.text: The retinacula:
questions.explanation: Retinacula are localized transverse thickenings of deep fascia that hold tendons in place at joints such as the wrist.
questions.keyConcept: Retinacula: Retinacula are localized transverse thickenings of deep fascia that hold tendons in place at joints such as the wrist
options: Surround the muscles of the upper and lower limbs.
Separate different groups of muscles which have different actions.
Are transverse thickened bands of deep fascia present at wrist joint.
Form tough sheaths around big blood vessels.

questions.text: The scapula is considered:
questions.explanation: The scapula is classified as a flat bone because it is thin, broad, and mainly provides a large surface for muscle attachment rather than a shaft like a long bone.
questions.keyConcept: The scapula is a flat bone specialized for broad muscle attachment.

questions.text: The following bone is part of the appendicular skeleton:
questions.explanation: The scapula belongs to the appendicular skeleton as part of the pectoral girdle.
questions.keyConcept: Appendicular skeleton

questions.text: The humerus is considered:
questions.explanation: The humerus is a long bone because it has a shaft with expanded ends and serves as the single long skeletal element of the arm.
questions.keyConcept: The humerus is the long bone of the arm.

questions.text: Regarding the saddle joint, one of the following is true:
questions.explanation: The first carpometacarpal joint of the thumb is the classic example of a saddle joint.
questions.keyConcept: Saddle joint
options: Allows supination and pronation movements only.
The carpometacarpal joint of the thumb is an example.

questions.text: The elbow joint is an example of:
questions.explanation: The elbow is a hinge-type synovial joint with movement mainly around one axis.
questions.keyConcept: Uniaxial hinge joint

questions.text: The superior radio-ulnar joint is an example of:
questions.explanation: The superior radioulnar joint is a pivot synovial joint and is functionally uniaxial.
questions.keyConcept: The superior radioulnar joint is a pivot synovial joint and is functionally uniaxial

questions.text: The wrist joint is an example of:
questions.explanation: The wrist joint is a condyloid synovial joint and allows biaxial movement.
questions.keyConcept: Biaxial synovial joint

questions.text: The intercarpal joint is an example of:
questions.explanation: Intercarpal joints are plane synovial joints that permit gliding.
questions.keyConcept: Plane synovial joint

questions.text: Shoulder girdle is formed of ___ and ___.
questions.explanation: The shoulder girdle consists of the scapula and clavicle.
questions.keyConcept: The shoulder girdle is formed by the scapula and clavicle.

questions.text: The skeleton of the arm is formed of ___.
questions.explanation: The arm contains a single bone, the humerus.
questions.keyConcept: The humerus is the bone of the arm.

questions.text: Forearm consists of two bones ___ medially and ___ laterally.
questions.explanation: In anatomical position, the ulna is medial and the radius is lateral.
questions.keyConcept: Ulna is medial and radius is lateral in the forearm.
