questions.text: As regards the hip bone, choose the INCORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (B) because this statement is incorrect: the inner surface of the ilium forms the iliac fossa, while the gluteal surface is its outer surface. The other statements are true, since the ischium forms the lower and posterior part of the hip bone and has a body and one ramus (a, d), the iliac crest is the upper border of the ilium (c), and the ischial spine separates the greater from the lesser sciatic notch (e).
questions.keyConcept: The inner surface of the ilium is the iliac fossa; the gluteal surface is its outer surface.
options: The ischium forms the lower & posterior part of the hip bone.
The inner surface of the ilium is the gluteal surface.
The upper border of the ilium forms the iliac crest.
Ischium has one body & one ramus.
Ischial spine lies between greater & lesser sciatic notches.

questions.text: As regards the femur, choose the CORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (C) because the intercondylar notch or fossa separates the medial and lateral condyles of the femur posteriorly. Option (a) is wrong because the lesser trochanter projects posteriorly, and (b) is wrong because the linea aspera lies on the posterior aspect of the shaft. Option (d) is wrong because the lower end of the femur articulates with the tibia and patella, not the fibula, and (e) is wrong because the head articulates with the acetabulum.
questions.keyConcept: The femoral condyles are separated posteriorly by the intercondylar notch; the linea aspera and lesser trochanter are posterior.
options: Anterior aspect of shaft shows linea aspera.
Intercondylar notch separates the 2 condyles posteriorly.
Its lower end articulates with tibia & fibula.
Head articulates with obturator foramen in hip joint.

questions.text: As regards the deep fascia of thigh, choose the CORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (A) because the deep fascia of the thigh is named the fascia lata. Option (b) is wrong because the fascia lata is thickened laterally to form the iliotibial tract, and (c) and (d) are wrong because the saphenous opening lies in the upper part of the thigh below the medial part of the inguinal ligament. Option (e) is wrong because it is the great saphenous vein that pierces the saphenous opening.
questions.keyConcept: The fascia lata is thickened laterally as the iliotibial tract, and its saphenous opening transmits the great saphenous vein.
options: It is thickened medially to form iliotibial tract.
Saphenous opening lies below lateral part of inguinal ligament.
Saphenous opening lies in lower part of thigh.
Saphenous opening is pierced by small saphenous vein.

questions.text: Choose the CORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (D) because the posterior compartment of the thigh contains the flexors of the knee, the hamstrings, and is supplied by the sciatic nerve. The anterior compartment is extensor and supplied by the femoral nerve, which makes (a) and (b) wrong, and the medial compartment is adductor and supplied by the obturator nerve, which makes (c) and (e) wrong.
questions.keyConcept: Thigh compartments: anterior extensor/femoral N., medial adductor/obturator N., posterior flexor/sciatic N.
options: Anterior compartment of thigh is extensor & supplied by obturator N.
Anterior compartment of thigh is adductor & is supplied by femoral N.
Medial compartment of thigh is adductor & is supplied by femoral N.
Posterior compartment of thigh is flexor & is supplied by sciatic N.
Posterior compartment of thigh is flexor & is supplied by femoral N.

questions.text: Which of the following IS NOT a hip flexor?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (D) because vastus medialis crosses only the knee joint and is therefore purely an extensor of the knee with no action on the hip. Sartorius, pectineus, iliacus and psoas major all cross the hip joint anteriorly and act as flexors of the hip.
questions.keyConcept: The vasti cross only the knee; rectus femoris is the single quadriceps component that also flexes the hip.

questions.text: Which one of the following DOES NOT extend knee?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (E) because psoas major is inserted into the lesser trochanter of the femur and acts only on the hip, flexing it. The three vasti and rectus femoris together form the quadriceps femoris, the great extensor of the knee.
questions.keyConcept: Quadriceps femoris = rectus femoris plus the three vasti; psoas major flexes the hip only.

questions.text: Femoral nerve supplies all the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (C) because psoas major is supplied directly by the ventral rami of the lumbar plexus and not by the femoral nerve. Sartorius, iliacus, vastus medialis and rectus femoris all belong to the anterior compartment territory of the femoral nerve.
questions.keyConcept: Psoas major is supplied directly by the lumbar plexus, while iliacus is supplied by the femoral nerve.

questions.text: Which one of the following is a bipennate muscle?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (C) because rectus femoris is bipennate, its fibers running obliquely into both sides of a central tendon. The vasti are unipennate or multipennate in arrangement and psoas major is a long fusiform muscle, so none of them answers the question.
questions.keyConcept: Rectus femoris is the bipennate member of the quadriceps.

questions.text: Medial boundary of femoral triangle is formed by:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (D) because the femoral triangle is bounded medially by the medial border of adductor longus. Its base above is the inguinal ligament (a) and its lateral boundary is the medial border of sartorius (b), while psoas major and iliacus (c, e) form part of its floor rather than its boundaries.
questions.keyConcept: Femoral triangle: inguinal ligament above, sartorius laterally, adductor longus medially.

questions.text: The most lateral muscle in the floor of the femoral triangle is:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (B) because the floor of the femoral triangle is formed, from lateral to medial, by iliacus, psoas major, pectineus and adductor longus, so iliacus is the most lateral. Rectus femoris (e) does not contribute to the floor of the triangle.
questions.keyConcept: Floor of the femoral triangle from lateral to medial: iliacus, psoas major, pectineus, adductor longus.

questions.text: The most medial content in femoral triangle is:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (A) because the contents of the femoral triangle are arranged from lateral to medial as femoral nerve, femoral artery, femoral vein and then the femoral canal, so the canal is the most medial. This is the reason a femoral hernia descends through the most medial compartment of the femoral sheath.
questions.keyConcept: From lateral to medial: femoral nerve, artery, vein, canal (NAVY, with the canal most medial).

questions.text: Intermediate compartment of femoral sheath contains:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (E) because the femoral sheath has three compartments: the lateral one contains the femoral artery, the intermediate one the femoral vein, and the medial one is the femoral canal. The femoral nerve lies outside the sheath altogether.
questions.keyConcept: Femoral sheath: artery laterally, vein intermediately, femoral canal medially.

questions.text: Femoral sheath contains all the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (B) because the femoral nerve lies outside and lateral to the femoral sheath, on iliacus. The sheath encloses the femoral artery and vein, the femoral branch of the genitofemoral nerve and, in its medial compartment, a deep inguinal lymph node with loose areolar tissue.
questions.keyConcept: The femoral nerve is the one structure of the femoral triangle that lies outside the femoral sheath.

questions.text: As regards the femoral nerve, choose the INCORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (A) because this statement is incorrect: the saphenous nerve is the long cutaneous branch of the femoral nerve, not a motor branch. The remaining statements are true, since the femoral nerve arises from the lumbar plexus, descends in the groove between iliacus and psoas major, lies outside the femoral sheath and supplies the anterior compartment of the thigh.
questions.keyConcept: The saphenous nerve is the cutaneous branch of the femoral nerve.
options: It gives a motor branch called saphenous nerve.
It is a branch of lumbar plexus.
It descends between iliacus & psoas major.
It supplies muscles of anterior compartment of thigh.

questions.text: As regards the femoral artery, choose the INCORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (D) because this statement is incorrect: the femoral artery lies inside the lateral compartment of the femoral sheath. The remaining statements are true, since the femoral artery begins at the midinguinal point as the continuation of the external iliac artery, traverses the adductor canal and becomes the popliteal artery at the opening in adductor magnus.
questions.keyConcept: The femoral artery begins at the midinguinal point within the femoral sheath and becomes the popliteal artery at the adductor magnus opening.
options: It is the continuation of external iliac artery.
It is a content of the adductor canal.
It ends by forming popliteal artery.

questions.text: As regards the femoral vein, choose the CORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (B) because the femoral vein begins at the opening in adductor magnus as the continuation of the popliteal vein. Options (a) and (e) are wrong because it is the continuation of the popliteal vein and ends by becoming the external iliac vein, and (c) is wrong because it ascends first in the adductor canal and then in the femoral triangle. Option (d) is wrong because in the femoral triangle it lies medial to the femoral artery.
questions.keyConcept: The femoral vein continues the popliteal vein from the adductor magnus opening and becomes the external iliac vein.
options: Femoral vein is the continuation of external iliac vein.
Femoral vein begins at opening in adductor magnus.
It ascends at first in femoral triangle followed by adductor canal.
It lies lateral to femoral artery.
It ends by forming internal iliac vein.

questions.text: The muscle which is formed of 2 parts belonging to 2 different compartments of thigh is:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (D) because adductor magnus is formed of an adductor part, which belongs to the medial compartment and is supplied by the obturator nerve, and an ischial or hamstring part, which belongs to the posterior compartment and is supplied by the sciatic nerve. The other muscles listed lie wholly within one compartment.
questions.keyConcept: Adductor magnus has an adductor part (obturator N.) and an ischial part (sciatic N.).

questions.text: Adductor canal contains all the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (C) because the femoral nerve itself ends in the femoral triangle by dividing into its branches and does not enter the adductor canal. The canal transmits the femoral artery and vein, the saphenous nerve and the nerve to vastus medialis.
questions.keyConcept: Adductor canal contents: femoral artery and vein, saphenous nerve, nerve to vastus medialis.

questions.text: As regards subsartorial canal, choose the INCORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (E) because this statement is incorrect: the subsartorial or adductor canal lies deep to sartorius, which is why it carries that name. The remaining statements are true, since it is an intermuscular tunnel in the middle third of the medial side of the thigh, begins at the apex of the femoral triangle and communicates below with the popliteal fossa through the opening in adductor magnus.
questions.keyConcept: The adductor (subsartorial) canal lies deep to sartorius and opens into the popliteal fossa.
options: It lies in middle 1/3 of medial side of thigh.
It begins at apex of femoral triangle.

questions.text: Match each muscle in the left column with its nerve supply in the right column:
questions.explanation: The short lateral rotators take their nerve supply from the nerves that lie alongside them. Piriformis is supplied directly by branches of the sacral plexus, the superior gemellus travels with and is supplied by the nerve to obturator internus, and the inferior gemellus is supplied by the nerve to quadratus femoris. Obturator externus, being a muscle of the obturator group on the outer aspect of the membrane, is supplied by the obturator nerve.
questions.keyConcept: Gemellus superior is supplied by the nerve to obturator internus and gemellus inferior by the nerve to quadratus femoris.

questions.text: Short lateral rotators of the hip include all the following muscles EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (E) because gluteus medius is an abductor and medial rotator of the hip, not one of the short lateral rotators. The short lateral rotators are piriformis, obturator internus and externus, the two gemelli and quadratus femoris.
questions.keyConcept: Short lateral rotators: piriformis, obturator internus and externus, gemelli, quadratus femoris.

questions.text: The structure that passes through greater sciatic foramen above piriformis is:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (C) because the superior gluteal nerve, with the superior gluteal vessels, is the only structure that leaves the pelvis above piriformis. The sciatic nerve, the posterior cutaneous nerve of the thigh, the inferior gluteal nerve and the pudendal nerve all emerge below piriformis.
questions.keyConcept: Only the superior gluteal nerve and vessels pass above piriformis; everything else passes below it.

questions.text: The nerve that passes from greater to lesser sciatic foramen is:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (E) because the nerve to obturator internus leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen and immediately re-enters the perineum through the lesser sciatic foramen to reach the muscle, exactly as the pudendal nerve does. The other nerves listed continue into the gluteal region and thigh and do not re-enter through the lesser foramen.
questions.keyConcept: The nerve to obturator internus and the pudendal nerve leave through the greater and re-enter through the lesser sciatic foramen.

questions.text: All the following pass through lesser sciatic foramen EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (A) because obturator externus lies on the outer surface of the obturator membrane and passes behind the neck of the femur without any relation to the lesser sciatic foramen. The tendon of obturator internus, the nerve to obturator internus, the internal pudendal vessels and the pudendal nerve all traverse that foramen.
questions.keyConcept: Lesser sciatic foramen: tendon and nerve of obturator internus, pudendal nerve, internal pudendal vessels.

questions.text: As regards sciatic nerve, choose the INCORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (D) because this statement is incorrect: the upper outer quadrant of the buttock is chosen precisely because it is safe, the sciatic nerve lying in the lower medial part of the gluteal region. The remaining statements are true, since the sciatic nerve is the thickest nerve in the body and the largest branch of the sacral plexus, descends in the midline of the back of the thigh and divides into the tibial and common peroneal nerves.
questions.keyConcept: Intramuscular injection in the upper outer quadrant of the buttock avoids the sciatic nerve.
options: It descends in middle of back of thigh.
It is the largest branch of sacral plexus.
It is the thickest nerve in the body.
It is commonly injured during intramuscular injection in upper outer quadrant of buttock.
It ends by dividing into tibial & common peroneal nerves.

questions.text: As regards back of thigh, choose the CORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (C) because the hamstrings receive their blood supply from the perforating branches of the profunda femoris artery. Options (a) and (b) are wrong because the hamstrings extend the hip and flex the knee, and (d) is wrong because biceps femoris lies laterally. Option (e) is wrong because semitendinosus is superficial and semimembranosus deep.
questions.keyConcept: The hamstrings extend the hip, flex the knee and are supplied by the profunda femoris artery.
options: It contains the hamstring muscles which flex the hip.
Hamstring muscles are supplied by profunda artery.

questions.text: Match each muscle in the left column with its position in popliteal fossa in the right column:
questions.explanation: The popliteal fossa is a diamond bounded above by the hamstrings and below by the heads of gastrocnemius. Biceps femoris forms the superolateral boundary and semitendinosus, with semimembranosus, the superomedial boundary. Below, the medial head of gastrocnemius is inferomedial while plantaris, arising with the lateral head from the lateral supracondylar line, is inferolateral.
questions.keyConcept: Popliteal fossa boundaries: biceps femoris superolateral, semitendinosus superomedial, plantaris/lateral head inferolateral, medial head of gastrocnemius inferomedial.

questions.text: Which of the following forms superomedial boundary of popliteal fossa?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (C) because semimembranosus, together with semitendinosus, forms the superomedial boundary of the popliteal fossa. Biceps femoris (a) is superolateral, while the popliteal fascia (d) is the roof and the popliteal surface of the femur (e) part of the floor. Adductor longus (b) does not reach the fossa.
questions.keyConcept: Semimembranosus and semitendinosus form the superomedial boundary of the popliteal fossa.

questions.text: Which of the following shares in the formation of the roof of the popliteal fossa?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (E) because the roof of the popliteal fossa is formed by the popliteal fascia, the thickened deep fascia bridging the fossa, covered by superficial fascia and skin. The fascia covering popliteus, the back of the capsule of the knee joint and the popliteal surface of the femur (a, b, d) all belong to the floor, and sartorius (c) lies on the medial side of the thigh.
questions.keyConcept: The roof of the popliteal fossa is the popliteal fascia; its floor includes the femur, knee capsule and popliteus fascia.
options: Back of capsule of knee joint.

questions.text: Which of the following is the uppermost structure in the floor of popliteal fossa?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (D) because the floor of the popliteal fossa is formed from above downwards by the popliteal surface of the femur, then the back of the capsule of the knee joint, and finally the fascia covering popliteus. The popliteal fascia (e) is the roof, and sartorius (c) takes no part in the fossa.
questions.keyConcept: Floor of the popliteal fossa from above downwards: popliteal surface of femur, knee joint capsule, fascia over popliteus.
options: Back of capsule of knee joint.

questions.text: As regards popliteal vessels, choose the CORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (B) because the popliteal artery lies on the floor of the fossa and is therefore its deepest structure, which is why its pulse is difficult to feel. Option (a) is wrong because the artery begins at the opening in adductor magnus, and (c) is wrong because it ends by dividing into the anterior and posterior tibial arteries. Option (d) is wrong because the popliteal vein lies superficial to the artery, and (e) is wrong because the vein becomes the femoral vein.
questions.keyConcept: The popliteal artery is the deepest structure in the popliteal fossa and divides into anterior and posterior tibial arteries.
options: Popliteal artery begins at distal border of Popliteus.
Popliteal artery is the deepest structure in popliteal fossa.
Popliteal artery ends by dividing into anterior & posterior peroneal arteries.
Popliteal vein runs deep to popliteal artery.
Popliteal vein ends by forming anterior tibial vein.

questions.text: As regards common peroneal nerve, choose INCORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (D) because this statement is incorrect: the deep peroneal nerve supplies the anterior compartment of the leg, the posterior compartment being supplied by the tibial nerve. The remaining statements are true, since the common peroneal nerve descends laterally along the medial border of biceps femoris and divides lateral to the neck of the fibula, its superficial branch supplying the lateral compartment.
questions.keyConcept: Deep peroneal nerve = anterior compartment of leg; superficial peroneal nerve = lateral compartment.
options: It descends downwards & laterally in popliteal fossa.
It runs close to biceps femoris muscle.
It ends lateral to neck of fibula.
Its deep peroneal branch supplies posterior compartment of leg.
Its superficial peroneal branch supplies lateral compartment of leg.

questions.text: As regards bones of leg, choose the INCORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (C) because this statement is incorrect: the head of the fibula forms the superior tibiofibular joint, while the inferior tibiofibular joint is formed by the lower end of the fibula. The remaining statements are true, since the anterior border and medial surface of the tibial shaft form the shin, the lower end of the tibia articulates with the fibula and the talus, the lower end of the fibula forms the lateral malleolus and the tibial condyles take part in the knee joint.
questions.keyConcept: The head of the fibula forms the superior tibiofibular joint; its lower end forms the inferior tibiofibular joint and the lateral malleolus.
options: Shaft of tibia forms the shin.
Lower end of tibia articulates with fibula & talus.
Head of fibula shares in formation of inferior tibiofibular joint.
Lower end of fibula forms lateral malleolus.
Condyles of tibia share in formation of knee joint.

questions.text: Deep peroneal nerve supplies all the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (C) because peroneus longus belongs to the lateral compartment of the leg and is supplied by the superficial peroneal nerve. Tibialis anterior, extensor hallucis longus, extensor digitorum longus and peroneus tertius are all anterior compartment muscles supplied by the deep peroneal nerve.
questions.keyConcept: Peroneus tertius is an anterior compartment muscle, whereas peroneus longus and brevis are lateral compartment muscles.

questions.text: The most medial structure deep to extensor retinacula is:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (E) because the structures deep to the extensor retinacula run, from medial to lateral, as tibialis anterior, extensor hallucis longus, the anterior tibial vessels with the deep peroneal nerve, extensor digitorum longus and peroneus tertius. Tibialis anterior is therefore the most medial and peroneus tertius the most lateral.
questions.keyConcept: In front of the ankle from medial to lateral: tibialis anterior, EHL, anterior tibial vessels and nerve, EDL, peroneus tertius.

questions.text: Choose the INCORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (D) because this statement is incorrect: the anterior tibial nerve, that is the deep peroneal nerve, begins on the lateral side of the neck of the fibula where the common peroneal nerve divides; it is the posterior tibial artery that begins at the distal border of popliteus. The remaining statements are true, since the anterior tibial artery crosses in front of the ankle midway between the malleoli and continues as the dorsalis pedis, and the nerve supplies the anterior compartment.
questions.keyConcept: The deep peroneal (anterior tibial) nerve begins lateral to the neck of the fibula.
options: Anterior tibial artery descends infront of ankle joint.
Anterior tibial artery passes midway between the 2 malleoli.
Anterior tibial artery continues as dorsalis pedis artery.
Anterior tibial nerve begins at distal border of Popliteus.
Anterior tibial nerve supplies muscles of anterior compartment of leg.

questions.text: Choose the CORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (A) because the dorsal venous arch of the foot is formed by the union of the dorsal metatarsal veins. Option (b) is wrong because the great saphenous vein begins from the medial end of the arch, and (c) is wrong because it ends in the femoral vein while the short saphenous vein ends in the popliteal vein. Option (d) is wrong because the short saphenous vein ascends in the back of the leg, and (e) is wrong because varicose veins result from defective, incompetent valves.
questions.keyConcept: The great saphenous vein arises from the medial end of the dorsal venous arch and ends in the femoral vein.
options: Dorsal venous arch is formed by union of metatarsal veins.
Great saphenous vein begins from lateral end of dorsal venous arch.
Great saphenous vein ends in popliteal vein.
Short saphenous vein ascends infront of leg.
Varicose veins are due to increased valves in superficial veins.

questions.text: Which listed intrinsic muscle has its belly on the dorsum of the foot?
questions.explanation: Extensor digitorum brevis is an intrinsic dorsal foot muscle. Extensor hallucis brevis is also present dorsally and is often described as its medial component. The other listed muscles have their bellies in the leg and reach the foot as tendons.
questions.keyConcept: Extensor digitorum brevis is the only muscle of the dorsum of the foot.

questions.text: As regards lateral compartment of leg, choose the INCORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (A) because this statement is incorrect: the lateral compartment contains peroneus longus and peroneus brevis, while peroneus tertius belongs to the anterior compartment. The remaining statements are true, since these muscles are supplied by the superficial peroneal nerve, which also supplies the skin of the dorsum and toes, and their tendons pass behind the lateral malleolus held by the peroneal retinacula.
questions.keyConcept: The lateral compartment of the leg contains peroneus longus and brevis, supplied by the superficial peroneal nerve.
options: It contains peroneus longus & peroneus tertius.
Its muscles are supplied by superficial peroneal nerve.
Its nerve supplies skin of dorsum & toes.
Its muscles lie behind lateral malleolus.
Its muscles are fixed by peroneal retinacula.

questions.text: Which one of the following is a superficial muscle in back of leg?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (B) because plantaris belongs, with gastrocnemius and soleus, to the superficial group of the calf. Popliteus, flexor hallucis longus, flexor digitorum longus and tibialis posterior make up the deep group of the back of the leg.
questions.keyConcept: Superficial calf muscles: gastrocnemius, soleus and plantaris.

questions.text: Which one of the following has 2 bellies?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (D) because gastrocnemius has two bellies, a medial and a lateral head, arising from the corresponding condyles of the femur and uniting to join the tendo calcaneus. The other muscles listed each have a single belly.
questions.keyConcept: Gastrocnemius has two heads arising from the femoral condyles.

questions.text: Choose the INCORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (C) because this statement is incorrect: the posterior tibial artery begins at the distal border of popliteus, where the popliteal artery divides, and only later passes deep to the flexor retinaculum. The remaining statements are true, since the posterior tibial nerve continues the tibial nerve, divides into medial and lateral plantar nerves, supplies the deep calf muscles, and the artery is a terminal branch of the popliteal artery.
questions.keyConcept: The posterior tibial artery begins at the distal border of popliteus.
options: Posterior tibial nerve is the continuation of the tibial nerve.
Posterior tibial nerve gives medial & lateral plantar nerves.
Posterior tibial artery begins deep to flexor retinaculum.
Posterior tibial artery is one of terminal branches of popliteal artery.
Posterior tibial nerve supplies deep muscles of back of leg.

questions.text: Deep to the flexor retinaculum at the ankle, which two structures lie immediately adjacent to the posterior tibial vessels on either side?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (C) because the structures passing deep to the flexor retinaculum are arranged from medial to lateral as tibialis posterior, flexor digitorum longus, the posterior tibial vessels, the tibial nerve and flexor hallucis longus. The vessels therefore lie between flexor digitorum longus and the tibial nerve.
questions.keyConcept: Behind the medial malleolus: tibialis posterior, FDL, posterior tibial vessels, tibial nerve, FHL.
options: Flexor digitorum longus & flexor hallucis longus.

questions.text: First layer of sole contains:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (E) because the first layer of the sole consists of abductor hallucis, flexor digitorum brevis and abductor digiti minimi. Flexor digitorum accessorius and the lumbricals belong to the second layer (c, d), while the long flexor tendons (a, b) reach the sole from the leg and lie in the second layer.
questions.keyConcept: First layer of the sole: abductor hallucis, flexor digitorum brevis, abductor digiti minimi.

questions.text: Second layer of sole contains:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (B) because the second layer of the sole contains flexor digitorum accessorius, also called quadratus plantae, together with the lumbricals and the long flexor tendons. Abductor hallucis, flexor digitorum brevis and abductor digiti minimi form the first layer (a, c, d), while adductor hallucis (e) belongs to the third layer.
questions.keyConcept: Second layer of the sole: flexor digitorum accessorius, lumbricals and the long flexor tendons.

questions.text: Third layer of sole contains:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (D) because the third layer of the sole comprises flexor hallucis brevis, adductor hallucis and flexor digiti minimi brevis. The plantar interossei (b) lie in the fourth layer with the tendons of tibialis posterior and peroneus longus (a, e), and flexor digitorum brevis (c) is in the first layer.
questions.keyConcept: Third layer of the sole: flexor hallucis brevis, adductor hallucis, flexor digiti minimi brevis.

questions.text: Match each joint in left column with its type in right column:
questions.explanation: The hip is the classical synovial ball and socket joint, the head of the femur fitting the acetabulum. The knee is a modified hinge, since rotation accompanies its flexion and extension, whereas the ankle is a pure hinge permitting only plantar flexion and dorsiflexion. The talocalcaneonavicular joint is also of the ball and socket variety, the head of the talus resting in a socket formed by the navicular, calcaneus and spring ligament.
questions.keyConcept: Hip and talocalcaneonavicular joints are ball and socket, the knee is a modified hinge and the ankle a simple hinge.

questions.text: Match each joint in left column with its appropriate movement in right column:
questions.explanation: Because it is a ball and socket joint, the hip permits circumduction, the sequential combination of flexion, abduction, extension and adduction. The knee undergoes locking by medial rotation of the femur in full extension and unlocking by popliteus, while the hinge-like ankle allows only plantar flexion and dorsiflexion. Inversion and eversion of the foot take place at the talocalcaneonavicular and subtalar joints.
questions.keyConcept: Inversion and eversion occur at the talocalcaneonavicular and subtalar joints, not at the ankle.

questions.text: Adduction of toes occurs in which direction?
questions.explanation: Toe adduction is toward the axis of the second toe.
questions.keyConcept: Movements of the Toes: Toe adduction is toward the axis of the second toe

questions.text: One of the following is biaxial joint:
questions.explanation: The source classifies the knee as biaxial because it permits flexion-extension with limited rotation.
questions.keyConcept: Knee Joint Classification: The source classifies the knee as biaxial because it permits flexion-extension with limited rotation

questions.text: Inversion means:
questions.explanation: Inversion is the movement that turns the sole medially toward the midline.
questions.keyConcept: Inversion turns the sole medially.
options: Moving foot so that sole faces medially.
Moving foot so that sole faces laterally.

questions.text: What is the type of the ankle joint?
questions.explanation: The talocrural ankle joint is a hinge synovial joint.
questions.keyConcept: Ankle Joint: The talocrural ankle joint is a hinge synovial joint

questions.text: The hip joint is:
questions.explanation: The hip is a multiaxial ball-and-socket joint.
questions.keyConcept: Hip Joint: The hip is a multiaxial ball-and-socket joint

questions.text: The sole of the foot is referred to as the ________ surface.
questions.explanation: The sole of the foot is the plantar surface.
questions.keyConcept: Plantar surface

questions.text: The patella is considered:
questions.explanation: The patella is a sesamoid bone embedded in the quadriceps tendon.
questions.keyConcept: Sesamoid bone

questions.text: The thigh consists of one bone the ___.
questions.explanation: The femur is the single bone of the thigh.
questions.keyConcept: The femur is the bone of the thigh.

questions.text: The leg consists of two bones the ___ medially and the ___ laterally.
questions.explanation: The tibia is medial and the fibula is lateral in the leg.
questions.keyConcept: Tibia is medial and fibula is lateral in the leg.

lectureNames: Sensory Nerve Supply of the Scalp

questions.text: All of the following are 2ry cartilaginous joints except:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (C) because the sacroiliac joint is a synovial joint between the auricular surfaces of the sacrum and the ilium, even though it becomes progressively fibrosed with age. The sternal angle (manubriosternal joint), the symphysis pubis and the intervertebral discs are all secondary cartilaginous joints, in which the bone ends are covered by hyaline cartilage and united by fibrocartilage.
questions.keyConcept: Secondary cartilaginous joints include the manubriosternal joint, symphysis pubis and intervertebral discs; the sacroiliac joint is synovial.

questions.text: Apex of the heart is formed by ___.
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the left ventricle, because the apex of the heart is formed entirely by the left ventricle and lies in the left fifth intercostal space about 9 cm from the midline. The right ventricle forms most of the anterior surface but does not reach the apex.
questions.keyConcept: The apex of the heart is formed by the left ventricle, in the left 5th intercostal space.

questions.text: The subarachnoid space lies between ___ and ___.
questions.explanation: The correct answers are the arachnoid mater and the pia mater, because the subarachnoid space is the interval between these two inner meninges and is the space that contains the cerebrospinal fluid. The subdural space, by contrast, lies between the dura and the arachnoid.
questions.keyConcept: The subarachnoid space lies between arachnoid and pia mater and contains the cerebrospinal fluid.

questions.text: Sternal angle opposite to which costal cartilage ___, at the level of disc between ___.
questions.explanation: The correct answers are the second costal cartilage and the disc between the fourth and fifth thoracic vertebrae, because the sternal angle marks the manubriosternal joint at the level of the second costal cartilages. It is the key surface landmark for the plane that separates the superior from the inferior mediastinum.
questions.keyConcept: The sternal angle lies at the 2nd costal cartilage, level with the T4/T5 disc.

questions.text: The vessels supplying the lung tissue are named ___.
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the bronchial arteries, because these branches of the descending thoracic aorta supply the lung tissue itself, that is the bronchi and connective tissue framework. The pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood for gas exchange and are functional rather than nutritive vessels.
questions.keyConcept: The bronchial arteries nourish the lung tissue; the pulmonary arteries serve gas exchange.

questions.text: In the usual right-dominant coronary circulation, the posterior interventricular artery arises from ___.
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the right coronary artery, because in the great majority of hearts the posterior interventricular (posterior descending) artery is its terminal branch, which defines a right-dominant circulation. It descends in the posterior interventricular groove to supply the posterior third of the interventricular septum.
questions.keyConcept: The posterior interventricular artery usually arises from the right coronary artery.

questions.text: Sensory nerve supply to the scalp behind the auricle by ___ while in front the auricle by ___.
questions.explanation: The correct answers are the lesser occipital nerve and the auriculotemporal nerve, because the scalp behind the auricle is supplied by the lesser occipital nerve from the cervical plexus, while the scalp in front of and above the auricle is supplied by the auriculotemporal branch of the mandibular nerve. This is the classic boundary between cervical and trigeminal territory on the scalp.
questions.keyConcept: Behind the auricle: lesser occipital nerve (C2). In front of the auricle: auriculotemporal nerve (V3).

questions.text: The peritoneal sac behind stomach is ___ while in front stomach is ___.
questions.explanation: The correct answers are the lesser sac and the greater sac, because the lesser sac (omental bursa) lies behind the stomach and lesser omentum while the greater sac lies in front of the stomach and forms the main part of the peritoneal cavity. The two communicate only through the epiploic foramen.
questions.keyConcept: Lesser sac lies behind the stomach, greater sac in front; they communicate at the epiploic foramen.

questions.text: The hilum of the liver is named ___ and lies on which surface? ___.
questions.explanation: The correct answers are the porta hepatis and the visceral surface, because the hilum of the liver is the transverse fissure on its visceral (inferior) surface through which the portal vein and hepatic artery enter and the hepatic ducts leave. It forms the horizontal bar of the H-shaped set of grooves on that surface.
questions.keyConcept: The porta hepatis is the hilum of the liver, on its visceral surface.

questions.text: The peritoneal fold between the spleen and left kidney is named ___, while the fold that encloses the jejunum and ileum is named ___.
questions.explanation: The correct answers are the lienorenal ligament and the mesentery, because the lienorenal ligament passes from the hilum of the spleen to the front of the left kidney and carries the splenic vessels and the tail of the pancreas. The jejunum and ileum are suspended by the mesentery, whose root runs obliquely across the posterior abdominal wall.
questions.keyConcept: Lienorenal ligament joins spleen to left kidney; the mesentery suspends jejunum and ileum.

questions.text: The vena caval opening of the diaphragm is located at the level of ___ and transmits ___ and ___.
questions.explanation: The correct answers are T8, the inferior vena cava and the right phrenic nerve, because the caval opening lies in the central tendon at the level of the eighth thoracic vertebra and transmits these two structures. Because it lies in the tendon, the opening is widened rather than closed when the diaphragm contracts, which aids venous return.
questions.keyConcept: The caval opening lies in the central tendon at T8 and transmits the IVC and right phrenic nerve.

questions.text: The cavity of the cerebral hemisphere is ___, while the cavity of the spinal cord is ___.
questions.explanation: The correct answers are the lateral ventricle and the central canal, because each cerebral hemisphere contains a lateral ventricle while the cavity of the spinal cord is the narrow central canal. Both are lined by ependyma and contain cerebrospinal fluid, and they are continuous through the third and fourth ventricles.
questions.keyConcept: Cavity of the cerebral hemisphere = lateral ventricle; cavity of the spinal cord = central canal.

questions.text: The esophagus passes through which parts of the mediastinum? ___ and ___.
questions.explanation: The correct answers are the superior and the posterior mediastinum, because the oesophagus enters the thorax behind the trachea in the superior mediastinum and then descends behind the pericardium in the posterior mediastinum to pierce the diaphragm at T10. It does not pass through the middle mediastinum, which is occupied by the heart and pericardium.
questions.keyConcept: The oesophagus traverses the superior and posterior mediastinum only.

questions.text: Urogenital triangle of perineum is divided into 2 pouches by ___.
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the perineal membrane, because this triangular sheet of deep fascia divides the urogenital triangle into a superficial perineal pouch below it and a deep perineal pouch above it. The two pouches have quite different contents, which is why the distinction matters in urethral rupture.
questions.keyConcept: The perineal membrane separates the superficial and deep perineal pouches.

questions.text: Ejaculatory duct ends at ___.
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the prostatic urethra, because each ejaculatory duct, formed by the union of the vas deferens and the duct of the seminal vesicle, opens on the posterior wall of the prostatic urethra on the colliculus seminalis beside the prostatic sinus. This is where the seminal and prostatic secretions join the urinary tract.
questions.keyConcept: The ejaculatory duct opens into the prostatic urethra.

questions.text: Triceps is supplied by the ___ nerve.
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the radial nerve, because all three heads of triceps brachii are supplied by the radial nerve, the nerve of the posterior compartment of the arm. This is why a lesion of the nerve high in the axilla weakens elbow extension as well as causing wrist drop.
questions.keyConcept: All three heads of triceps are supplied by the radial nerve.

questions.text: The plane that divides the body into a large right part & a small left part is:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is Left parasagittal because a parasagittal plane placed to the left of the median plane leaves a large right portion and a small left portion. The median plane would give two equal halves, and a right parasagittal plane would do the reverse, giving a small right part. Coronal and transverse planes divide the body front/back and upper/lower respectively.
questions.keyConcept: A left parasagittal plane lies left of the midline, so it cuts off a small left part and a large right part.

questions.text: Which of the following is responsible for the growth of the bone in length?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the epiphyseal plate because interstitial growth of its hyaline cartilage, followed by ossification on the diaphyseal side, lengthens the bone until the plate fuses. The periosteum adds bone appositionally and so increases diameter, not length. The endosteum lines the medullary cavity and remodels it rather than elongating the bone.
questions.keyConcept: Epiphyseal plate = growth in length; periosteum = growth in width.

questions.text: The parasagittal plane divides the body into:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is right & left unequal halves because a parasagittal plane is any vertical antero-posterior plane parallel to, but not through, the midline. Only the median (mid-sagittal) plane gives equal right and left halves. Anterior/posterior division is the coronal plane and upper/lower division is the transverse plane.
questions.keyConcept: Median plane = equal halves; parasagittal = unequal right and left parts.

questions.text: Which part of the bone is responsible for its growth in diameter (width)?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the Periosteum because its deep osteogenic layer lays down successive circumferential lamellae on the outer surface, thickening the shaft. The epiphyseal plate is responsible for length only. The primary centre converts the cartilaginous shaft into bone but does not govern subsequent appositional widening.
questions.keyConcept: Appositional growth in width comes from the osteogenic layer of the periosteum.

questions.text: The epidermis of the skin is thick in:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the Palm of hand because the palms and soles carry thick, hairless skin with a well-developed stratum corneum and stratum lucidum adapted to friction and pressure. The eyelid has the thinnest epidermis in the body. The arm, dorsum of hand and chest all carry thin hairy skin.
questions.keyConcept: Thick (glabrous) epidermis is found only on the palms and soles; the eyelid epidermis is the thinnest.

questions.text: A bone that ossifies from a membrane:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the Clavicle because it is the first bone in the body to ossify and does so mainly in membrane. The skull vault and facial bones are also membranous, but the skull base is cartilaginous. The scapula, hip bone and patella all ossify in cartilage.
questions.keyConcept: Membranous ossification: skull vault, facial bones and the clavicle; the skull base is cartilaginous.

questions.text: The epiphyseal plate of cartilage is:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is a primary cartilaginous joint because the bones are united by hyaline cartilage, it is immobile and it is temporary, disappearing when the epiphysis fuses. Secondary cartilaginous joints unite bones by fibrocartilage, lie in the midline and are permanent. It is not synovial as there is no joint cavity or synovial membrane.
questions.keyConcept: The epiphyseal plate is a temporary, immobile primary cartilaginous joint of hyaline cartilage.

questions.text: Superficial fascia is devoid of fat at:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the Eyelids because their superficial fascia is loose and fat-free, which is why oedema collects there so readily. Fat is also absent from the external ear, penis and scrotum. The thigh, arm, back of neck and palm all contain fat in the superficial fascia, the palm in the form of protective fibro-fatty pads.
questions.keyConcept: Superficial fascia is fat-free in the eyelids, external ear, penis and scrotum.

questions.text: Which of the following is a short bone?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is a Tarsal bone because tarsals, like carpals, are cuboidal with nearly equal length, breadth and thickness. The radius is a long bone, the sternum a flat bone, the vertebra an irregular bone and the maxilla a pneumatic bone.
questions.keyConcept: Short bones are cuboidal: the carpals and tarsals.

questions.text: Thick skin is present in:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the Palm of hand because palmar and plantar skin is thick, hairless, rich in sweat glands and firmly bound to the underlying aponeurosis. The face, dorsum of hand, abdomen and back all carry thin hairy skin, even though the skin of the back is tough and dermally thick, its epidermis is not of the thick glabrous type.
questions.keyConcept: Thick hairless skin is confined to the palms and soles.

questions.text: Thick cleavage (Langer's) lines of skin represent:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the direction of collagen fibers in the dermis because Langer's lines map the predominant orientation of dermal collagen bundles. Incisions made along these lines gape less and heal with a finer scar, which is their surgical importance. Skin creases over joints and finger prints are separate surface features unrelated to this fibre orientation.
questions.keyConcept: Langer's cleavage lines follow dermal collagen bundles, so incisions along them scar least.
options: Junctional lines between superficial & deep fascia
The direction of rows of elastic fibers in the dermis
The direction of collagen fibers in the dermis

questions.text: Regarding sesamoid bones, all the following statements are true EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is that they prevent obstruction of blood supply to a joint, because this is not a function of sesamoid bones. Their real roles are to reduce friction where a tendon crosses a bony surface, to alter the angle of pull and so increase the mechanical advantage of the muscle, and to resist pressure. The other four statements are all correct descriptions, the patella being the largest sesamoid bone.
questions.keyConcept: Sesamoid bones reduce friction and improve leverage; they have no role in protecting joint blood supply.
options: They develop within tendons of muscles
Patella is one of its examples
They prevent obstruction of blood supply to joint
They help to reduce friction of tendon

questions.text: In which one of the following cavities is yellow bone marrow found?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the Medullary cavity because the marrow cavity of the shaft of an adult long bone contains fatty yellow marrow. Red haemopoietic marrow persists instead in the flat bones, vertebrae and the ends of long bones. A joint cavity contains synovial fluid, and there is no such structure as an epiphyseal cavity.
questions.keyConcept: Yellow (fatty) marrow fills the medullary cavity of adult long bones.

questions.text: The presence of epiphyseal plate indicates that the bone is:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is increasing in length because an unfused epiphyseal plate means active interstitial cartilage growth is still elongating the bone. Once longitudinal growth ceases the plate ossifies and is replaced by the epiphyseal line. Growth in diameter depends on the periosteum and continues independently of the plate.
questions.keyConcept: An open epiphyseal plate means the bone is still growing in length; a fused epiphyseal line means growth has stopped.

questions.text: Tarsal bones are classified as:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is Short bones because the tarsals are cuboidal, with length, breadth and thickness nearly equal, and they are made of spongy bone with a thin compact shell. They are not developed in tendons, so they are not sesamoid. Their regular cuboidal outline excludes the irregular category.
questions.keyConcept: Tarsals and carpals are the classic short bones.

questions.text: Primary center of ossification of a long bone:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is that it changes the cartilaginous shaft into bone, because the primary centre appears in the middle of the cartilaginous diaphysis and ossifies it. It appears before birth, usually in the intrauterine period, so the option stating it appears after birth is wrong. Ossification of the epiphysis is the work of secondary centres, and growth in breadth is periosteal.
questions.keyConcept: The primary centre appears before birth in the diaphysis and ossifies the shaft; secondary centres ossify the epiphyses.

questions.text: What is the name of the vertical plane that divides the body into anterior & posterior parts?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is Coronal because the coronal (frontal) plane is a vertical plane running from side to side at right angles to the median plane, separating front from back. The median and parasagittal planes are also vertical but divide right from left. The transverse plane is horizontal and divides upper from lower.
questions.keyConcept: Coronal plane = vertical, side to side, dividing anterior from posterior.

questions.text: Which one of the following is not a part of the axial skeleton?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the Scapula because it belongs to the pectoral girdle and therefore to the appendicular skeleton. The axial skeleton consists of the skull, hyoid, vertebral column, ribs and sternum. The appendicular skeleton comprises the limb bones together with the pectoral and pelvic girdles.
questions.keyConcept: Axial skeleton = skull, hyoid, vertebrae, ribs and sternum; the girdles and limbs are appendicular.

questions.text: Which one of the following is a flat bone?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the Scapula because flat bones consist of two plates of compact bone enclosing a layer of spongy bone, exactly the structure of the scapula, ribs, sternum and skull vault. The vertebra is irregular, the humerus and clavicle are long bones and a carpal bone is short.
questions.keyConcept: Flat bones: scapula, ribs, sternum and bones of the skull vault.

questions.text: The metaphysis of the long bone is:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the part of the diaphysis near the epiphyseal plate, since the metaphysis is the flared end of the shaft immediately adjoining the growth plate. It is the most vascular and most metabolically active part of the bone, which is why acute osteomyelitis characteristically starts there. It belongs to the diaphysis, not to the epiphysis, and it is not the plate itself.
questions.keyConcept: The metaphysis is the diaphyseal side of the epiphyseal plate and is the usual site of acute osteomyelitis.
options: The part of the epiphysis near the epiphyseal plate
The part of the epiphysis away from the epiphyseal plate
The part of the diaphysis near the epiphyseal plate
The part of the diaphysis near the center of the bone
The place of the epiphyseal plate

questions.text: Which of the following is a characteristic of the long bone?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is that its shaft has a medullary cavity, which is a defining feature of a typical long bone and contains marrow. Length is gained from the epiphyseal plate, not the periosteum, and the outer covering is periosteum while endosteum lines the marrow cavity. The metaphysis belongs to the diaphysis, and the primary centre appears before birth.
questions.keyConcept: A long bone has a shaft with a medullary cavity, periosteum outside and endosteum lining the cavity.
options: Its shaft has a medullary cavity
It is covered from outside by endosteum
Its metaphysis is a part of its epiphysis
Its primary center of ossification appears after birth

questions.text: The skeleton of the hand includes all the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is seven carpal bones, because there are eight carpal bones arranged in two rows of four. The remaining statements are correct: five metacarpals, two phalanges in the thumb and three in each of the other four fingers, giving fourteen phalanges in all.
questions.keyConcept: The hand has 8 carpals, 5 metacarpals and 14 phalanges (2 in the thumb, 3 in each finger).

questions.text: Which one of the following is an irregular bone?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the Vertebra because its complex shape fits none of the other categories, which is the definition of an irregular bone. The scapula and skull cap are flat bones, the clavicle is a long bone and the patella is a sesamoid bone.
questions.keyConcept: Irregular bones include the vertebrae, hip bone and many bones of the skull base.

questions.text: The primary center of ossification of the long bone:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is that it changes the cartilaginous shaft into bone, since the primary centre arises in the middle of the diaphyseal cartilage model and spreads towards both ends. Centres appearing in the epiphyses are secondary centres, and the primary centre appears during intrauterine life rather than after birth. Growth in width is a periosteal function.
questions.keyConcept: Primary centre = diaphysis, before birth; secondary centres = epiphyses, mostly after birth.
options: Changes the cartilaginous shaft into bone
Appears at site of epiphyseal cartilage
Helps in growth of bone in width

questions.text: An example of secondary cartilaginous joint:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is Symphysis pubis because secondary cartilaginous joints (symphyses) unite bones by fibrocartilage, lie in the median plane and are permanent. The costochondral junction is a primary cartilaginous joint of hyaline cartilage. The sternocostal, sacroiliac and sternoclavicular joints are synovial.
questions.keyConcept: Secondary cartilaginous joints are midline, permanent and united by fibrocartilage: symphysis pubis, intervertebral discs, manubriosternal joint.

questions.text: An example of unipennate muscle:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the Palmar interosseous because its fibres arise from one side of a single tendon, like one half of a feather, which defines a unipennate muscle. The dorsal interossei and rectus femoris are bipennate, with fibres on both sides of a central tendon. Sartorius has parallel (strap) fibres and deltoid is multipennate.
questions.keyConcept: Unipennate = fibres on one side of the tendon: palmar interossei and flexor pollicis longus.

questions.text: Which of the following muscles is a bipennate muscle?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the 2nd dorsal interosseous because the dorsal interossei are bipennate, their fibres converging on both sides of a central tendon like a complete feather. Flexor pollicis longus and the palmar interossei are unipennate. Deltoid is multipennate and subscapularis is a multipennate/spiral flat muscle.
questions.keyConcept: Bipennate = complete feather pattern: dorsal interossei and rectus femoris.

questions.text: What is the type of the interphalangeal joints?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is Hinge because the interphalangeal joints are uniaxial synovial joints permitting only flexion and extension about a transverse axis. Condyloid (ellipsoid) joints such as the metacarpophalangeal joints are biaxial. Pivot joints allow rotation and saddle joints, like the carpometacarpal joint of the thumb, are biaxial with opposition.
questions.keyConcept: Interphalangeal joints are uniaxial hinge joints (flexion and extension only).

questions.text: What is the joint that contains a cartilaginous disc?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the Sternoclavicular joint because it contains a complete intra-articular fibrocartilaginous disc that divides the joint into two compartments and prevents medial dislocation of the clavicle. The other listed joints have no intra-articular disc. Other disc-containing joints include the temporomandibular joint and the inferior radioulnar joint.
questions.keyConcept: Intra-articular discs are found in the sternoclavicular, temporomandibular and inferior radioulnar joints.

questions.text: Which one of the following joints is the most moveable?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is Hinge because it is the only synovial joint in the list, and synovial joints are the freely movable (diarthrodial) class. Sutures and gomphoses are immobile fibrous joints and a syndesmosis permits only slight movement. Primary cartilaginous joints are immobile.
questions.keyConcept: Synovial joints are the freely movable class; fibrous and primary cartilaginous joints are essentially immobile.

questions.text: The function of the tendon is to link:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is a muscle to a bone because a tendon is a cord of dense regular collagen that transmits the pull of a muscle to the skeleton. Structures joining bone to bone are ligaments, which is the classic distractor here. Muscles that insert into skin do so directly by fleshy fibres, as in the muscles of facial expression, not by tendons.
questions.keyConcept: Tendon = muscle to bone; ligament = bone to bone.

questions.text: Which one of the following muscles is a multipennate muscle?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the Deltoid because its acromial part is built of several intramuscular septa with fibres arranged like a series of feathers, the definition of a multipennate muscle. Flexor pollicis longus is unipennate, while rectus femoris and the dorsal interossei are bipennate. Temporalis is a fan-shaped triangular muscle.
questions.keyConcept: Deltoid is the classic multipennate muscle, which is why it is so powerful.

questions.text: Match each joint in left column with its type in right column:
questions.explanation: The inferior tibiofibular joint is a fibrous joint of the syndesmosis type, held by the interosseous ligament. The intervertebral disc is a midline secondary cartilaginous joint of fibrocartilage. The interphalangeal joints are uniaxial hinges, the radioulnar joints are uniaxial pivots allowing pronation and supination, and the acromioclavicular joint is a plane synovial joint permitting gliding.
questions.keyConcept: Inferior tibiofibular = fibrous; IV disc = 2ry cartilaginous; IP = hinge; radioulnar = pivot; acromioclavicular = plane.

questions.text: The 2ry cartilaginous joint unites bones by:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is White fibrocartilage because in a symphysis the bone ends are capped with hyaline cartilage but are united by an intervening plate of white fibrocartilage. Union by hyaline cartilage alone defines a primary cartilaginous joint. Fibrous tissue unites fibrous joints and synovial fluid belongs to synovial joints.
questions.keyConcept: Secondary cartilaginous joint: hyaline-capped bone ends united by white fibrocartilage.

questions.text: The joints between the bones of the skull vault (cap) belong to:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is Sutures because the vault bones are joined edge to edge by a thin layer of fibrous tissue, forming immobile fibrous joints that later ossify. A syndesmosis is a fibrous joint with a longer intervening ligament, as between the tibia and fibula. A gomphosis is the peg-and-socket fibrous joint between a tooth and its alveolus.
questions.keyConcept: The three fibrous joints are sutures (skull vault), syndesmoses and gomphoses (teeth).

questions.text: Which one of the following muscles is a unipennate muscle?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is Flexor pollicis longus because its fleshy fibres arise from one side only of its long tendon. Tibialis anterior is described as circumpennate, the dorsal interossei are bipennate and deltoid is multipennate. Temporalis is a fan-shaped triangular muscle rather than a pennate one.
questions.keyConcept: Flexor pollicis longus is the standard example of a unipennate muscle.

questions.text: Which one of the following joints is a hinge synovial?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the Interphalangeal joint, a uniaxial hinge allowing flexion and extension only. The superior radioulnar joint is a pivot, the shoulder is a ball and socket, the wrist is ellipsoid and the acromioclavicular joint is plane.
questions.keyConcept: Hinge joints: elbow, ankle, knee (modified) and the interphalangeal joints.

questions.text: Primary cartilaginous joints:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is that they are usually temporary, because the epiphyseal plate, the commonest example, disappears when the epiphysis fuses with the shaft. They are immobile, not widely mobile, and they unite bones by hyaline cartilage rather than fibrous tissue. The tooth-and-jaw joint is a gomphosis and the lower tibiofibular union is a syndesmosis, both fibrous.
questions.keyConcept: Primary cartilaginous joints are immobile, hyaline and usually temporary (epiphyseal plate).
options: Unite lower ends of tibia & fibula

questions.text: In flexion of wrist, which muscle is a synergist?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is Flexor digitorum profundus because, although its main action is on the fingers, it crosses the wrist anteriorly and assists the prime mover in the same direction of movement, which is the definition of a synergist. Flexor carpi ulnaris is itself the agonist, and the extensors listed act in the opposite direction as antagonists. Triceps acts at the elbow and is unrelated to wrist flexion.
questions.keyConcept: A synergist assists the agonist in the same movement; the antagonist opposes it.

questions.text: Match each joint in left column with its type in right column:
questions.explanation: The inferior tibiofibular joint is a fibrous syndesmosis. The carpometacarpal joint of the thumb is the classic saddle joint, permitting opposition. The elbow is a uniaxial hinge, the epiphyseal plate is a temporary primary cartilaginous joint, and the metacarpophalangeal joints are biaxial ellipsoid joints.
questions.keyConcept: CMC of thumb = saddle; MCP = ellipsoid; elbow = hinge; epiphyseal plate = 1ry cartilaginous; inferior tibiofibular = syndesmosis.

questions.text: All the following are types of muscle attachments EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is Ligament because ligaments connect bone to bone and are not a mode of muscle attachment. Muscles attach by fleshy fibres, tendons, flattened aponeuroses, or raphes where two muscles interdigitate in a tendinous seam. The pharyngeal and pterygomandibular raphes are standard examples.
questions.keyConcept: Muscles attach by fleshy fibres, tendons, aponeuroses or raphes, never by ligaments.

questions.text: Match each muscle in left column with its appropriate definition in right column:
questions.explanation: The agonist (prime mover) initiates and carries out the movement, while the antagonist produces the opposite action and relaxes progressively to control it. A synergist assists the agonist in the same movement, and a fixator steadies a proximal joint or the origin of the prime mover so that its action is efficiently transmitted. These four roles are interchangeable depending on the movement being analysed.
questions.keyConcept: Agonist initiates, antagonist opposes, synergist assists, fixator stabilises.

pairs.premise: Muscle preventing movement of another joint
Muscle aiding another in the same movement

questions.text: An example of parallel type of muscle is:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is Sartorius because its long strap-like fibres run parallel to the line of pull, which gives a wide range of shortening but relatively little power. Rectus femoris and the dorsal interossei are bipennate, flexor pollicis longus is unipennate and deltoid is multipennate. Pennate arrangements pack in more fibres and so favour power over range.
questions.keyConcept: Parallel (strap) muscles such as sartorius favour range of movement; pennate muscles favour power.

questions.text: Symphysis pubis is:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is a Secondary cartilaginous joint because the two pubic bones are capped with hyaline cartilage and united by an interpubic fibrocartilaginous disc in the median plane. It is permanent and allows only slight movement, increasing in late pregnancy. It has no joint cavity or synovial membrane, so it is not synovial.
questions.keyConcept: Symphysis pubis is a permanent midline secondary cartilaginous joint.

questions.text: Match each muscle in left column with its example in right column:
questions.explanation: Flexor pollicis longus has fibres on one side of its tendon (unipennate) and the dorsal interossei have fibres on both sides (bipennate). Deltoid contains several tendinous septa and is multipennate, tibialis anterior has fibres converging around its tendon and is circumpennate, and sartorius has long parallel strap fibres. The printed premise 'Pcrollel fibers' is a scanning artefact of 'Parallel fibers' and has been normalised.
questions.keyConcept: Muscle fibre architecture: unipennate FPL, bipennate dorsal interosseous, multipennate deltoid, circumpennate tibialis anterior, parallel sartorius.

questions.text: Most of the joints that lie in the median plane of the body are:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is Secondary cartilaginous joint because symphyses are characteristically midline structures: the symphysis pubis, the intervertebral discs and the manubriosternal joint. Primary cartilaginous joints such as epiphyseal plates are not confined to the midline. Syndesmoses and gomphoses are fibrous joints found elsewhere.
questions.keyConcept: Midline joints are typically secondary cartilaginous (symphyses).

questions.text: All are characters of synovial joint EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is that the articular surfaces are covered by synovial membrane, because the articular surfaces are covered by hyaline articular cartilage; the synovial membrane lines the rest of the capsule but stops at the cartilage margins. All the other features are true: a cavity, a fibrous capsule, sometimes an intra-articular disc, and free mobility. This distinction explains why articular cartilage is avascular and nourished by synovial fluid.
questions.keyConcept: Synovial membrane lines everything inside the capsule except the articular cartilage.
options: A capsule binds its articulating bones
The articular surfaces are covered by synovial membrane

questions.text: Which of the following is a uniaxial joint?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the Interphalangeal joint because it is a hinge permitting movement about one axis only. The metacarpophalangeal joint and the wrist are biaxial ellipsoid joints and the hip is a multiaxial ball and socket. The intervertebral disc is a cartilaginous joint, not classified by axes in this way.
questions.keyConcept: Uniaxial = hinge and pivot; biaxial = ellipsoid and saddle; multiaxial = ball and socket.

questions.text: As regards the cartilaginous joints, choose the INCORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is that a syndesmosis is a type of primary cartilaginous joint, which is false: a syndesmosis is a fibrous joint in which bones are united by an interosseous ligament. The other statements are all true, since symphyses allow limited movement, lie in the median plane and have hyaline-covered bone ends united by fibrocartilage, while primary cartilaginous joints such as the epiphyseal plate are temporary.
questions.keyConcept: Syndesmosis is fibrous, not cartilaginous.
options: Secondary cartilaginous joints allow limited movement
Syndesmosis is a type of primary cartilaginous joint
Primary cartilaginous joints are usually temporary
Secondary cartilaginous joints lie usually in median plane
In secondary cartilaginous joints, articular surfaces are covered by hyaline cartilage

questions.text: Match each joint in left column with its type in right column:
questions.explanation: The elbow is a uniaxial hinge and the carpometacarpal joint of the thumb is the classic saddle joint. The wrist is a biaxial ellipsoid joint and the shoulder is a multiaxial ball and socket. Gomphoses and sutures are both fibrous joints, so the same target is legitimately used twice in this set.
questions.keyConcept: Elbow hinge, thumb CMC saddle, wrist ellipsoid, shoulder ball and socket, gomphosis and suture fibrous.

questions.text: As regards the muscles, choose the INCORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is that the most movable part of the muscle is its origin, which is false: the origin is the relatively fixed attachment and the insertion is the more movable one. A bipennate muscle does resemble a complete feather, a raphe is an interdigitating fleshy-tendinous seam, and muscles of facial expression are indeed inserted into skin. Most muscles do attach to bone through tendons.
questions.keyConcept: Origin = fixed end; insertion = movable end.
options: A bipennate muscle looks like a complete feather
The most movable part of the muscle is its origin
A raphe is a mixture of fleshy & tendinous fibers
The muscle may be inserted into the skin
Most muscles have tendons attached to bones

questions.text: As regards the skeletal muscles, choose the INCORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is that the origin is the most moveable end, which is incorrect because the origin is the fixed end and the insertion moves towards it. Contraction does approximate origin and insertion, intermuscular septa derived from deep fascia do divide limb muscles into compartments, and skeletal muscle is largely voluntary. Its nerve supply carries motor, sensory (proprioceptive) and autonomic vasomotor fibres.
questions.keyConcept: On contraction the insertion moves towards the fixed origin.
options: The origin is the most moveable end of the muscle
Contraction means approximation of origin & insertion
Septa from deep fascia divide them into groups
They are mostly under voluntary control
They are innervated by motor, sensory & autonomic nerve fibers

questions.text: Match each muscle in left column with its appropriate definition in right column:
questions.explanation: Trapezius has spiralling fibres and sternocleidomastoid is grouped with the cruciate muscles because the two muscles of opposite sides cross like a letter X. The palmar interossei and flexor pollicis longus are unipennate, the dorsal interossei and rectus femoris are bipennate, and deltoid is multipennate. Targets are legitimately reused because there are seven premises and only five categories.
questions.keyConcept: Fibre architecture: spiral trapezius, cruciate sternocleidomastoid, unipennate FPL and palmar interossei, bipennate dorsal interossei and rectus femoris, multipennate deltoid.

questions.text: Which part of the spinal nerve that does not contain motor fibers? OR Which part of the spinal nerve is formed of purely sensory fibers?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the Dorsal root because it carries only the central processes of the pseudounipolar sensory neurons whose cell bodies lie in the dorsal root ganglion. The ventral root is purely motor, and once the two roots unite the nerve trunk and both rami are mixed. This is the anatomical basis of the Bell-Magendie law.
questions.keyConcept: Dorsal root = purely sensory; ventral root = purely motor; trunk and rami = mixed.

questions.text: Which part of the spinal nerve is formed of purely motor fibers?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the Ventral root because it contains the axons of the anterior horn cells, together with preganglionic autonomic fibres in the appropriate segments. The dorsal root is purely sensory, and the nerve trunk and both rami are mixed after the roots join.
questions.keyConcept: The ventral root carries motor axons from anterior horn cells out of the cord.

questions.text: The sympathetic outflow is:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is Thoraco-lumbar because preganglionic sympathetic neurons lie in the lateral horn from T1 to L2 only. Cranio-sacral is the parasympathetic outflow, carried by cranial nerves III, VII, IX and X and by S2, S3 and S4. The sympathetic system nevertheless reaches every spinal nerve through grey rami communicantes.
questions.keyConcept: Sympathetic outflow = T1-L2 (thoraco-lumbar); parasympathetic = cranio-sacral.

questions.text: The parasympathetic outflow is:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is Cranio-sacral because parasympathetic preganglionic neurons lie in the brainstem nuclei of cranial nerves III, VII, IX and X and in the grey matter of sacral segments S2 to S4. Thoraco-lumbar describes the sympathetic outflow. Sacral alone is incomplete because it ignores the large cranial component, chiefly the vagus.
questions.keyConcept: Parasympathetic outflow: cranial nerves III, VII, IX, X and sacral segments S2-S4.

questions.text: Which ventral rami that do not form nerve plexuses?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the Thoracic rami because the ventral rami of T2 to T11 run independently as intercostal nerves and retain a strictly segmental distribution. The cervical, lumbar and sacral rami interlace to form the cervical, brachial, lumbar and sacral plexuses, and the coccygeal ramus joins the small coccygeal plexus.
questions.keyConcept: Thoracic ventral rami stay segmental as intercostal nerves and form no plexus.

questions.text: As regards the nervous system, choose the correct statement:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is that ganglia are groups of nerve cells outside the central nervous system, the standard definition, as opposed to nuclei which lie within the CNS. Plexuses are formed by ventral rami, dura mater is the outermost meninx and the sympathetic outflow is thoraco-lumbar. Ventral rami are mixed, not purely motor.
questions.keyConcept: Ganglion = collection of nerve cell bodies in the PNS; nucleus = the equivalent inside the CNS.
options: Nerve plexuses are formed by dorsal rami of spinal nerves
Pia mater is the outermost one of the meninges
Ganglia are groups of nerve cells outside CNS
Ventral rami of spinal nerves are purely motor

questions.text: Match each structure in the left column with its definition in the right column:
questions.explanation: Collections of neuronal cell bodies are called ganglia in the peripheral nervous system and nuclei in the central nervous system. Bundles of axons are called tracts centrally and nerves peripherally. The functional junction where one neuron communicates with another is the synapse.
questions.keyConcept: PNS: ganglion and nerve. CNS: nucleus and tract. Junction between neurons: synapse.

pairs.premise: A group of cell bodies in PNS
A group of cell bodies in CNS
A bundle of nerve fibers in CNS
A bundle of nerve fibers in PNS

questions.text: Cerebro-spinal fluid lies between:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is between the pia and the arachnoid mater, because cerebrospinal fluid fills the subarachnoid space. The space between dura and arachnoid is only a potential subdural space and contains no CSF normally. This is why a lumbar puncture needle must pass through the dura and arachnoid to reach the fluid.
questions.keyConcept: CSF occupies the subarachnoid space, between arachnoid and pia mater.

questions.text: As regards the spinal nerves, choose the INCORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is that nerve plexuses are formed by dorsal rami, which is false because all the great plexuses are formed by ventral rami; dorsal rami keep a segmental distribution to the back. The remaining statements are true: there are 3 1 pairs of spinal nerves, the dorsal roots are entirely sensory and bear ganglia, and the ventral rami are mixed.
questions.keyConcept: Plexuses are formed by ventral rami; dorsal rami supply the back segmentally.
options: Nerve plexuses are formed by dorsal rami of spinal nerves
Its dorsal roots are entirely sensory
Ventral rami of spinal nerves are mixed

questions.text: Sympathetic nervous system:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is that it is connected to all spinal nerves by grey rami communicantes, which is how sympathetic fibres reach the vessels, sweat glands and arrector pili of the whole body including the limbs. It stimulates rather than inhibits sweating, its outflow is thoraco-lumbar rather than cranio-sacral, and it dilates the pupil. Constriction of the pupil is parasympathetic.
questions.keyConcept: Every spinal nerve receives a grey ramus communicans, so sympathetic supply is body-wide.
