options: Is connected to all spinal nerves by gray rami communicans

questions.text: Which valve prevents the backward flow of the blood to the right atrium?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the Tricuspid valve because it guards the right atrioventricular orifice and closes during ventricular systole to stop regurgitation into the right atrium. The mitral valve performs the same duty on the left side. The pulmonary and aortic valves guard the outflow tracts, not the atrioventricular openings.
questions.keyConcept: Tricuspid = right AV valve; mitral = left AV valve.

questions.text: Lymph capillaries are absent from:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is Articular cartilage because it is avascular and alymphatic, being nourished by diffusion from synovial fluid. Bone, stomach, lung and lip all contain lymphatic capillaries. Avascularity is the general rule that predicts absence of lymphatics.
questions.keyConcept: Avascular tissues such as articular cartilage, cornea and epidermis have no lymphatics.

questions.text: Blood sinusoids are numerous in:
questions.explanation: Epiphyseal cartilage is avascular and receives nutrients by diffusion. Epiphyseal arterial branches supply the adjacent bony epiphysis; they do not form ordinary capillaries within the cartilage matrix.
questions.keyConcept: Sinusoids occur in liver, spleen, bone marrow, adrenal cortex and anterior pituitary.

questions.text: If the lymphatics of the upper limb become obstructed, the arm on that side is likely to:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is that it becomes oedematous, because lymphatics return protein-rich interstitial fluid to the blood and their blockage causes it to accumulate as lymphoedema. Arterial supply and venous drainage are unaffected, so the limb is neither ischaemic nor hyperaemic. This is the mechanism of arm swelling after axillary lymph node clearance.
questions.keyConcept: Lymphatic obstruction causes lymphoedema, classically after axillary node clearance.

questions.text: Match each description in the left column with its appropriate vessel in the right column:
questions.explanation: Veins, especially in the limbs, contain numerous valves that ensure one-way flow against gravity. Sinusoids are the wide exchange channels of the liver, while ordinary capillaries perform exchange throughout the body. Large arteries near the heart are rich in elastic tissue to smooth the pulse, and arteriovenous anastomoses in the skin regulate heat loss.
questions.keyConcept: Veins have valves, arteries are elastic, capillaries and hepatic sinusoids exchange, and A-V shunts control temperature.

pairs.premise: The abundant exchange vessels in liver
Plays role in control of body temperature

questions.text: The circulation that connects two sets of capillaries:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is Portal because by definition a portal vessel begins and ends in capillaries, linking two capillary beds in series. The systemic and pulmonary circulations each interpose the heart between their capillary beds. The hepatic portal and hypophyseal portal systems are the standard human examples.
questions.keyConcept: Portal circulation connects two capillary beds in series.

questions.text: Communication between arteries & veins in the tissues can be by:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is All of the above because arterial blood may reach the veins through ordinary capillaries, through wide sinusoids, through erectile cavernous tissue, or directly through arteriovenous anastomoses between arterioles and venules. Each route is found in particular tissues. All four are legitimate arteriovenous communications.
questions.keyConcept: Artery to vein routes: capillaries, sinusoids, cavernous tissue and direct A-V anastomoses.

questions.text: Choose the INCORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is that most veins have branches, which is incorrect terminology: veins receive tributaries, whereas arteries give branches. The other statements are true, since limb veins are richly valved, the portal system links two capillary beds, arteries convey blood away from the heart, and vessels such as the facial, splenic and uterine arteries are characteristically tortuous.
questions.keyConcept: Arteries have branches; veins have tributaries.
options: Portal circulation possesses two sets of capillaries
Arteries carry the blood away from the heart

questions.text: As regards anastomoses, choose the INCORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is that functional end arteries are sufficient to compensate a block, which is false: their anastomoses are too small to sustain the tissue, which is precisely why occlusion of a coronary or cerebral branch causes infarction. The remaining statements are all correct descriptions of anastomoses and end arteries.
questions.keyConcept: Functional end arteries cannot compensate for sudden occlusion, so infarction follows.
options: Arterio-venous anastomoses are numerous in skin of nose
Anatomical end artery has no anastomosis with other arteries
Arterio-venous anastomosis helps to control body temperature
Arterial anastomosis help to compensate a block in blood flow
Functional end arteries are sufficient to compensate a block of an artery

questions.text: As regards blood vessels, choose the INCORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is that venae comitantes accompany big veins, which is incorrect: venae comitantes are paired small veins that accompany a medium-sized or small artery within a common fascial sheath. All the other statements are true, since arteries branch, veins receive tributaries, limb veins are richly valved, and the wide irregular sinusoids slow the blood to allow exchange.
questions.keyConcept: Venae comitantes accompany arteries, not veins.
options: Valves are numerous in limb veins

questions.text: Which of the following is a tortuous artery?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is All of the above because each of these arteries is characteristically tortuous, an adaptation that allows the organ it supplies to move or to enlarge without stretching the vessel. The facial and lingual arteries accommodate movements of the face and tongue, the uterine artery accommodates pregnancy and the splenic artery accommodates changes in splenic size.
questions.keyConcept: Tortuous arteries (facial, lingual, uterine, splenic) supply mobile or distensible organs.

questions.text: Lymph capillaries are absent in:
questions.explanation: The relevant exception concerns conventional lymphatic vessels within central nervous system parenchyma. Meningeal lymphatic vessels are present, so the whole cranial compartment cannot be described as lacking lymphatic drainage.
questions.keyConcept: Conventional lymphatic vessels are absent from CNS parenchyma and avascular tissues; meninges have lymphatic vessels.

questions.text: Lymph capillaries:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is that they start blindly, because lymph capillaries begin as closed-ended endothelial tubes in the tissue spaces. They are not present in all tissues, they are wider and more permeable than blood capillaries, and their loose junctions admit large particles and even cells, which is how tumour cells and bacteria spread. Therefore the composite option is wrong.
questions.keyConcept: Lymph capillaries are blind-ended, wider and more permeable than blood capillaries.
options: Are present in all tissues of body
Are permeable to small particles only
Are smaller in caliber than blood capillaries

questions.text: As regards lymph vessels, choose the INCORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is that all of them end in the thoracic duct, which is false because lymph from the right side of the head and neck, the right upper limb and the right thorax drains through the right lymphatic duct. The other statements are true: lymph vessels are richly valved, accompany veins, are interrupted by nodes and finally empty into the great veins at the root of the neck.
questions.keyConcept: The right upper quadrant drains via the right lymphatic duct; the rest of the body drains via the thoracic duct.
options: All of them end in thoracic duct
Are interrupted by one or more lymph nodes

questions.text: As regards lymph nodes, choose the INCORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is that efferent vessels leave from the convex surface, which is incorrect because efferent lymphatics leave at the hilum, the concave surface, while numerous afferents enter over the convex surface. The other statements are true: nodes enlarge in inflammation, lie along lymph vessels and filter the lymph.
questions.keyConcept: Afferents enter a node over its convex surface; efferents leave at the concave hilum.
options: Each node receives several afferent lymphatics
Efferent lymph vessels leave the node from its convex surface
Lie along the course of lymph vessels

questions.text: Which of the following has rich lymphatics?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the Dermis of the skin, which contains a dense superficial and deep lymphatic plexus draining to the regional nodes. The spinal cord, like the rest of the central nervous system, has no lymphatics, and the eyeball and bone marrow are likewise devoid of them. The splenic pulp also lacks true lymphatic capillaries.
questions.keyConcept: The dermis carries a rich lymphatic plexus; CNS, eyeball, bone marrow and splenic pulp do not.

questions.text: What are the anatomical positions you know?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the anatomical position together with the supine, prone, lithotomy and lateral positions, because anatomical terminology is meaningless unless referred to a fixed standard posture. Note particularly that the palms face forwards, which is why the radius is lateral and the ulna medial.
questions.keyConcept: Anatomical position: erect, facing forward, arms at sides, palms forward, feet forward; all terms refer to it.
questions.modelAnswer: The standard anatomical position is the body standing erect, facing forwards, with the eyes looking to the horizon, the upper limbs by the sides and the palms facing forwards, and the lower limbs together with the feet pointing forwards. All anatomical descriptions of position and movement are made with reference to this position, whatever the actual posture of the patient. The two other positions in common use are the supine position, lying on the back with the face upwards, and the prone position, lying face downwards. The lithotomy position (supine with the hips and knees flexed and the thighs abducted) and the lateral (recovery) position are also described for clinical work.

questions.text: What are the anatomical planes?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is median/sagittal, coronal and transverse, because these three mutually perpendicular planes are the reference frame for description and for all cross-sectional imaging. Only the median plane gives equal halves; parasagittal planes give unequal parts.
questions.keyConcept: Median = equal right/left; parasagittal = unequal right/left; coronal = anterior/posterior; transverse = upper/lower.
questions.modelAnswer: There are three groups of planes. The median (midsagittal) plane is the vertical antero-posterior plane that divides the body into two equal right and left halves; a sagittal or parasagittal plane is any vertical plane parallel to it, dividing the body into unequal right and left parts. The coronal (frontal) plane is a vertical plane at right angles to the median plane, dividing the body into anterior and posterior parts. The transverse (horizontal or axial) plane is at right angles to both and divides the body into upper and lower parts.

questions.text: What are the Langer's lines?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is that Langer's lines represent the direction of the dermal collagen fibres, because this is what determines wound gaping and scarring. Incisions should therefore be planned parallel to them wherever possible.
questions.keyConcept: Langer's lines = direction of dermal collagen; incise parallel to them for a fine scar.
questions.modelAnswer: Langer's lines, also called cleavage or tension lines, are lines that indicate the predominant direction of the bundles of collagen fibres in the dermis. They run longitudinally in the limbs and transversely in the neck and trunk. A surgical incision made parallel to these lines separates the collagen bundles rather than cutting across them, so the wound gapes little and heals with a fine linear scar; an incision across them gapes widely and heals with a broad, ugly scar. They must be distinguished from skin creases, which are flexure lines at joints.

questions.text: What are the skin creases?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is that skin creases are flexure lines produced by firm attachment of the skin to deep structures at sites of movement. They differ from Langer's lines, which are invisible and reflect dermal collagen orientation.
questions.keyConcept: Skin creases are visible flexure lines where skin is tethered to deep fascia at joints.
questions.modelAnswer: Skin creases are permanent flexure lines of the skin that lie over or near joints, where the skin is firmly bound down to the underlying deep fascia or bone and where there is no fat in the superficial fascia. Familiar examples are the creases of the palm and the flexure lines of the fingers, wrist, elbow and knee. They allow the skin to fold neatly during flexion instead of being stretched, and they are useful surgical landmarks. Unlike Langer's lines they are visible on the surface and are not related to the direction of collagen bundles.

questions.text: Mention sites where the superficial fascia is firmly attached to the skin?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the scalp, palm, sole, skin creases and external ear, because in these sites fibrous septa tie the dermis to the deeper layers. The clinical importance is free bleeding and gaping of wounds and limited mobility of the skin.
questions.keyConcept: Skin is firmly bound in scalp, palm, sole and skin creases, so wounds there gape and bleed freely.
questions.modelAnswer: The superficial fascia is firmly bound to the skin in the scalp, where skin, superficial fascia and the epicranial aponeurosis move as one layer; in the palm of the hand and the sole of the foot, where dense fibrous septa anchor the skin for grip; and over the skin creases and other flexure lines. It is also firmly attached in the skin of the external ear and at the alae of the nose. This firm binding is why wounds of the scalp and palm gape widely and bleed freely, since the vessels are held open by the fibrous septa.

questions.text: Mention sites where the superficial fascia is loosely attached to the skin?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the dorsum of the hand and foot, penis, scrotum and eyelids, because loose areolar superficial fascia there permits free skin mobility. The clinical consequence is that these are the first sites to show swelling in oedema.
questions.keyConcept: Loose superficial fascia (dorsum of hand/foot, eyelids, scrotum, penis) means mobile skin and easy oedema.
questions.modelAnswer: The superficial fascia is loosely attached, so that the skin is freely mobile, over the dorsum of the hand and the dorsum of the foot, over the penis and scrotum, over the eyelids, and over the back of the neck and the loose areas of the trunk. In such places the loose areolar tissue allows the skin to be pinched up and slid over the deeper structures. Because the tissue planes are lax, oedema and extravasated blood or fluid collect readily in these sites, as in scrotal or eyelid oedema.

questions.text: Mention sites where the superficial fascia is devoid of fatty tissue?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the eyelids, auricle, penis and scrotum, because the superficial fascia in these regions is purely loose areolar tissue with no fatty layer. This is a constant examination point and contrasts with the thick fatty panniculus of the abdominal wall and buttock.
questions.keyConcept: No fat in superficial fascia of eyelids, auricle, penis and scrotum.
questions.modelAnswer: The superficial fascia contains no fat in the eyelids, the external ear (auricle), the penis and the scrotum. It is also fat-free at the skin creases and over the dorsum of the nose. The absence of fat in these sites keeps the part thin and mobile, which is functionally necessary for the eyelid and the auricle, and it explains why swelling there is due to fluid rather than to fat.

questions.text: Enumerate the functions of the superficial fascia?
questions.explanation: The correct answer covers fat storage, contour, insulation, protection, mobility, and the conveying of cutaneous vessels and nerves, because all of these depend on the areolar and adipose composition of the layer. Remember that the muscles of facial expression are the classic exception of muscle within superficial fascia.
questions.keyConcept: Superficial fascia: fat store, insulation, shock absorber, skin mobility, carries cutaneous vessels/nerves.
questions.modelAnswer: The superficial fascia stores fat, which is an energy reserve and gives the body its surface contour and the characteristic female form. Its fat is a thermal insulator that conserves body heat, and it acts as a shock absorber protecting the deeper structures. It allows the skin to move on the deeper structures and it carries the cutaneous vessels, cutaneous nerves, superficial lymphatics and superficial lymph nodes. In some regions it also contains muscles, namely the muscles of facial expression, platysma and dartos.

questions.text: Enumerate the functions of the deep fascia?
questions.explanation: The correct answer includes retention of muscles, compartmentation, retinacula and fibrous sheaths, vascular sheaths and the venous pump, because all arise from the tough, inelastic, well-organised nature of this layer. The compartment concept also explains compartment syndrome clinically.
questions.keyConcept: Deep fascia: holds muscles, forms compartments, retinacula, fibrous flexor sheaths and vascular sheaths, aids venous return.
questions.modelAnswer: The deep fascia keeps the muscles in position and gives origin to some muscle fibres, and it sends intermuscular septa that divide the limbs into functional compartments, each with its own nerve and blood supply. It condenses to form retinacula which hold tendons in place at the wrist and ankle, and fibrous flexor sheaths for the digital tendons, and it forms sheaths around vessels and nerves such as the carotid sheath. Together with the muscles it acts as a peripheral pump, since its tightness during muscular contraction compresses the deep veins and lymphatics and helps venous and lymphatic return. It also gives smoothness to the body contour and separates infection into compartments.

questions.text: What are the curves of the vertebral column?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is two primary curves (thoracic and sacral) and two secondary curves (cervical and lumbar), because the primary curves persist from the fetal C-shape while the secondary ones develop with head control and with walking. These curves give the column its resilience.
questions.keyConcept: Primary curves (thoracic, sacral) are fetal and concave forwards; secondary curves (cervical, lumbar) are acquired and convex forwards.
questions.modelAnswer: The adult vertebral column shows four antero-posterior curves. The cervical and lumbar curves are convex forwards (lordosis) and are secondary curves, acquired after birth when the infant begins to hold up the head and then to stand and walk. The thoracic and sacral (pelvic) curves are concave forwards (kyphosis) and are primary curves, present in the fetus and retained throughout life. A slight lateral curve may also be present, usually convex to the side of the dominant upper limb. Exaggeration of these curves produces the clinical deformities of kyphosis, lordosis and scoliosis.

questions.text: Classify the bones according to their shapes with examples for each type?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is long, short, flat, irregular, pneumatic and sesamoid bones with their examples, because this shape-based classification is the standard one used throughout the course. Sesamoid bones are noteworthy because they reduce friction and alter the angle of pull of a tendon.
questions.keyConcept: Bones by shape: long, short, flat, irregular, pneumatic and sesamoid.
questions.modelAnswer: Long bones have a shaft with a medullary cavity and two ends, for example the humerus, femur, tibia and also the miniature long bones, the metacarpals, metatarsals and phalanges. Short bones are roughly cuboidal with no medullary cavity, such as the carpal and tarsal bones. Flat bones consist of two plates of compact bone enclosing diploe, such as the scapula, sternum, ribs and the bones of the skull vault. Irregular bones have a complex shape, such as the vertebrae, the hip bone and the bones of the skull base. Two further types are described: pneumatic bones, which contain air sinuses, such as the maxilla and the ethmoid, and sesamoid bones, which develop within tendons, the largest being the patella.

questions.text: Describe the structure of a growing long bone. (A labelled diagram is required in the printed paper.)
questions.explanation: The correct answer must include the diaphysis, epiphysis, metaphysis, epiphyseal plate, medullary cavity, periosteum and endosteum, because the examiner's diagram is marked on these labels. The key functional pair is the epiphyseal plate for length and the periosteum for width.
questions.keyConcept: Growing long bone: diaphysis, metaphysis, epiphysis, epiphyseal plate (length), periosteum (width), medullary cavity with endosteum.
questions.modelAnswer: A growing long bone consists of a shaft or diaphysis, two ends or epiphyses, and between them the metaphysis, which is the part of the diaphysis adjoining the epiphyseal plate. The epiphyseal (growth) plate is a disc of hyaline cartilage between the epiphysis and the metaphysis; it is a primary cartilaginous joint and is responsible for growth of the bone in length, disappearing when growth ceases. The shaft is a tube of compact bone enclosing a medullary cavity that contains marrow whose red/yellow composition changes with age, with red marrow predominant in young children and is lined by endosteum, while the epiphyses are made of spongy bone containing red marrow and are covered at the joint by articular hyaline cartilage. The whole bone except the articular surfaces is covered by periosteum, which is responsible for growth in diameter and for the nutrition and repair of the bone. The bone is supplied by a nutrient artery to the shaft, together with periosteal, metaphyseal and epiphyseal vessels.

questions.text: Classify the fibrous joints with examples for each type?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is suture, syndesmosis and gomphosis with their examples, because these are the three recognised fibrous joints, all lacking a cavity. The inferior tibiofibular joint is the standard syndesmosis example and is frequently asked.
questions.keyConcept: Fibrous joints: suture (skull), syndesmosis (inferior tibiofibular), gomphosis (tooth in socket).
questions.modelAnswer: In a fibrous joint the bones are united by fibrous tissue and there is no joint cavity, so movement is absent or minimal. There are three types. A suture, found only between the bones of the skull, is united by a thin layer of fibrous tissue and is immovable; sutures ossify with age (synostosis). A syndesmosis is united by a larger amount of fibrous tissue, usually an interosseous ligament or membrane, and allows slight movement, as in the inferior tibiofibular joint and the interosseous membranes of the forearm and leg. A gomphosis is the peg-and-socket fixation of a tooth in its alveolus by the periodontal ligament.

questions.text: Classify the cartilaginous joints with examples for each type?
questions.explanation: The correct answer distinguishes primary (hyaline, temporary, may be lateral) from secondary (fibrocartilage, permanent, median plane) cartilaginous joints. Note that the manubriosternal joint and the symphysis pubis are the classic secondary examples.
questions.keyConcept: Primary cartilaginous = hyaline, temporary (epiphyseal plate); secondary = fibrocartilage, permanent, median (symphysis pubis, IV discs).
questions.modelAnswer: In a cartilaginous joint the bones are united by cartilage and there is no joint cavity. In a primary cartilaginous joint (synchondrosis) the union is by hyaline cartilage; such joints are usually temporary and are replaced by bone, the examples being the epiphyseal plate between the epiphysis and the diaphysis and the joint between the first rib and the sternum. In a secondary cartilaginous joint (symphysis) the bone ends are covered with hyaline cartilage and united by a disc of fibrocartilage; these joints are permanent, allow slight movement and lie almost always in the median plane, the examples being the symphysis pubis, the intervertebral discs, the manubriosternal joint and the sacrococcygeal joint.

questions.text: Classify the synovial joints with examples for each type?
questions.explanation: The correct answer groups the six types by the number of axes: hinge and pivot (uniaxial), ellipsoid and saddle (biaxial), ball-and-socket and plane (multiaxial). The carpometacarpal joint of the thumb as the saddle joint and the wrist as the ellipsoid joint are the most frequently examined examples.
questions.keyConcept: Synovial types: hinge, pivot (uniaxial); ellipsoid, saddle (biaxial); ball & socket, plane (multiaxial).
questions.modelAnswer: Synovial joints are classified by the shape of the articular surfaces and the axes of movement. Uniaxial joints are the hinge joint, moving about a transverse axis, such as the elbow, the ankle and the interphalangeal joints, and the pivot joint, moving about a vertical axis, such as the superior radioulnar and the atlanto-axial joints. Biaxial joints are the ellipsoid (condyloid) joint, such as the wrist and the metacarpophalangeal joints, and the saddle joint, the type example being the carpometacarpal joint of the thumb. Multiaxial joints are the ball and socket joint, such as the shoulder and the hip, and the plane (gliding) joint, such as the acromioclavicular joint and the intercarpal joints.

questions.text: What are the factors that maintain joint stability? Add a note on the ligaments.
questions.explanation: Joint stability depends on articular shape, ligaments and muscle tone. Most ligaments contain dense collagen and resist excessive movement, but some, such as vertebral elastic ligaments, can stretch and recoil. Healing and vascularity vary by ligament.
questions.keyConcept: Stability depends on bony fit, ligaments and muscle tone; most ligaments resist stretch, while some are elastic.
questions.modelAnswer: Joint stability depends on three groups of factors. The first is bony, that is the shape and mutual fit of the articular surfaces, which is the dominant factor in the hip. The second is ligamentous, the capsule and the intrinsic and extrinsic ligaments that check excessive movement. The third and most important in most joints is muscular, the tone of the muscles crossing the joint, which is why the shoulder, with shallow surfaces and lax ligaments, depends on the rotator cuff. Atmospheric pressure and the vacuum effect of the closed joint, and accessory structures such as labra and menisci, give additional stability. Ligaments are strong, mostly resistant to stretch, although some ligaments contain abundant elastic fibers bands of dense fibrous tissue that permit normal movement but resist abnormal movement; they are poorly vascular, so a torn ligament (sprain) heals slowly, and they carry proprioceptive nerve endings that reflexly protect the joint.

questions.text: Describe the structure of a typical synovial joint. (A labelled diagram is required in the printed paper.)
questions.explanation: The correct answer must name articular cartilage, fibrous capsule, synovial membrane, joint cavity with synovial fluid, and the accessory structures, since these are the marked labels. Remember that the synovial membrane never covers the articular cartilage, a common examination trap.
questions.keyConcept: Synovial joint = articular cartilage + capsule + synovial membrane (not over cartilage) + cavity with synovial fluid.
questions.modelAnswer: A typical synovial joint has articular surfaces covered by hyaline (articular) cartilage, which is smooth, avascular and nerve-free and reduces friction. The bones are united by a fibrous capsule attached to the periosteum around the articular margins, and the capsule is thickened in places to form ligaments. The capsule is lined internally by synovial membrane, which covers everything inside the joint except the articular cartilage and any intra-articular fibrocartilage, and secretes synovial fluid that lubricates and nourishes the cartilage. Between the surfaces there is a joint cavity containing this fluid, and some joints contain accessory structures such as intra-articular discs or menisci, labra, fat pads and intracapsular tendons. The joint is supplied by articular branches of the nerves supplying the muscles that move it (Hilton's law) and by an articular arterial anastomosis around it.

questions.text: Classify the skeletal muscles according to their shapes with examples for each type?
questions.explanation: The correct answer covers parallel, pennate (uni-, bi-, multi-, circum-), cruciate, spiral and sphincteric muscles with their standard examples, because the examiner's matching questions draw directly on this list. Pennate arrangement trades range of movement for power.
questions.keyConcept: Shapes: parallel (sartorius), unipennate (FPL), bipennate (dorsal interosseous), multipennate (deltoid), circumpennate (tibialis anterior), cruciate (SCM), spiral (trapezius).
questions.modelAnswer: Muscles with parallel fibres run in the long axis of the muscle and give a wide range of movement but less power; they may be strap-like as the sartorius, fusiform as the biceps brachii, quadrilateral as the pronator quadratus. Convergent muscles have fan-shaped fibres, as in the temporalis. Pennate muscles have fibres set obliquely on a tendon like a feather and are more powerful but shorter in range: unipennate, with the tendon on one side, as the flexor pollicis longus; bipennate, with the tendon in the middle, as the dorsal interossei and rectus femoris; multipennate, with several tendinous septa, as the deltoid; and circumpennate, with the fibres converging on a central tendon from all round, as the tibialis anterior. Other muscles are cruciate, with crossing fibres, as the sternocleidomastoid, or spiral, as the trapezius and latissimus dorsi. Sphincteric (circular) muscles such as the orbicularis oris surround an orifice and close it.

questions.text: Describe the structure of a typical spinal nerve. (A labelled diagram is required in the printed paper.)
questions.explanation: The correct answer must state that the dorsal root is sensory with a ganglion, the ventral root is motor, the trunk is mixed and divides into dorsal and ventral rami, and that white and grey rami communicantes connect it to the sympathetic chain. A common error is to attribute the plexuses to the dorsal rami; the plexuses are formed by ventral rami.
questions.keyConcept: Spinal nerve = sensory dorsal root (with ganglion) + motor ventral root, then a mixed trunk dividing into dorsal and ventral rami.
questions.modelAnswer: There are 3 1 pairs of spinal nerves, each formed within the intervertebral foramen by the union of a dorsal and a ventral root. The dorsal root is purely sensory and bears the dorsal root ganglion, which contains the cell bodies of the unipolar sensory neurons; the ventral root is purely motor and carries the axons of the anterior horn cells, together with preganglionic sympathetic fibres in the T1-L2 segments and preganglionic parasympathetic fibres in the S2, S3 and S4 segments. The resulting spinal nerve trunk is therefore mixed, and it is extremely short, dividing at once into a small dorsal ramus, which supplies the skin and the true muscles of the back, and a large ventral ramus, which supplies the rest of the trunk and the limbs and forms the nerve plexuses. The ventral ramus is connected to the sympathetic chain by a white ramus communicans (only T1-L2, carrying myelinated preganglionic fibres) and by a grey ramus communicans (present at every level, carrying non-myelinated postganglionic fibres).

questions.text: Describe the systemic circulation?
questions.explanation: The correct answer traces left atrium to left ventricle to aorta to body capillaries and back by the venae cavae to the right atrium. The contrast with the pulmonary circulation, in which the artery carries deoxygenated and the veins oxygenated blood, must be stated.
questions.keyConcept: Systemic: LA to LV to aorta to body to venae cavae to RA. Pulmonary: RA to RV to pulmonary trunk to lungs to pulmonary veins to LA.
questions.modelAnswer: The systemic (greater) circulation carries oxygenated blood from the left side of the heart to the whole body and returns deoxygenated blood to the right side. Oxygenated blood passes from the left atrium to the left ventricle, which pumps it into the aorta; the aorta and its branches distribute it to arteries, arterioles and finally to the capillary beds of all the tissues, where exchange of gases, nutrients and wastes takes place. The deoxygenated blood is collected by venules and veins, and returns to the right atrium through the superior and inferior venae cavae and the coronary sinus. From the right atrium it passes to the right ventricle to enter the pulmonary circulation, which carries it through the pulmonary trunk to the lungs and returns it, oxygenated, by the four pulmonary veins to the left atrium.

questions.text: Mention types of arteries?
questions.explanation: The correct answer gives both the structural classification (elastic, muscular, arterioles) and the functional one (anatomical and functional end arteries), because both are asked in the MCQ paper. The central artery of the retina and the coronary arteries are the required examples.
questions.keyConcept: Elastic, muscular and arteriolar by structure; anatomical (retinal) and functional (coronary, cerebral) end arteries by anastomosis.
questions.modelAnswer: Structurally, arteries are of three kinds: large elastic (conducting) arteries such as the aorta and its main branches, whose wall is rich in elastic tissue and converts the intermittent output of the heart into a continuous flow; medium muscular (distributing) arteries such as the brachial and femoral, whose wall is mainly smooth muscle and which regulate the distribution of blood; and arterioles, the smallest, which are the chief site of peripheral resistance and control blood pressure. Functionally, arteries are also classified according to their anastomoses into anatomical end arteries, which have no anastomosis at all with neighbouring arteries so that their occlusion causes infarction, the example being the central artery of the retina; and functional end arteries, in which anastomoses exist but are too small to maintain the circulation, examples being the coronary and cerebral arteries. Some arteries are tortuous, such as the uterine, splenic and facial arteries, to allow for movement or enlargement of the organ supplied.

questions.text: Mention types of arteriovenous connection?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is capillaries, sinusoids, cavernous tissue and arterio-venous anastomoses, because these are the four channels by which blood passes from the arterial to the venous side. The thermoregulatory role of the A-V anastomosis is the point most often examined.
questions.keyConcept: A-V connections: capillaries, sinusoids, cavernous tissue and arterio-venous anastomoses (thermoregulation).
questions.modelAnswer: Arteries and veins may be connected in four ways. Capillaries are the usual connection and are the exchange vessels of all tissues. Sinusoids are wide, irregular, thin-walled channels found in the liver, spleen, bone marrow and some endocrine glands, where they slow the flow and allow intimate exchange. Cavernous (erectile) tissue consists of large endothelium-lined spaces, as in the penis and in the nasal mucosa. Arterio-venous anastomoses are direct communications between arterioles and venules, bypassing the capillary bed; they are numerous in the skin of the nose, lips, ears and finger tips, and they play a major role in the control of body temperature.

questions.text: List 3 lymphatic aggregates?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the tonsils, the Peyer's patches of the ileum and the appendix, because these are the three aggregates named in the course; the thymus and spleen may be added. They are strategically placed at the entrances of the respiratory and alimentary tracts.
questions.keyConcept: Lymphatic aggregates: tonsils (Waldeyer's ring), Peyer's patches of ileum, and the appendix.
questions.modelAnswer: Aggregations of lymphoid tissue that are not encapsulated lymph nodes include the tonsils of Waldeyer's ring, that is the palatine, pharyngeal, lingual and tubal tonsils; the aggregated lymphoid follicles (Peyer's patches) of the ileum; and the lymphoid tissue of the vermiform appendix. The thymus and the spleen are the other large collections of lymphoid tissue, the spleen filtering blood rather than lymph. All these are guardians at sites where organisms readily gain entry.

questions.text: List 2 sites rich in lymphatics?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the dermis of the skin and the mucous (and serous) membranes, because these surfaces are the body's interfaces with the exterior and need efficient drainage and immune surveillance. It contrasts directly with the avascular structures and the CNS, which have none.
questions.keyConcept: Rich lymphatics: dermis of skin and the mucous and serous membranes.
questions.modelAnswer: The dermis of the skin carries a very rich lymphatic plexus, which is why cutaneous infection and cutaneous malignancy spread readily to the regional lymph nodes. The mucous membranes of the respiratory, alimentary and urogenital tracts are equally rich in lymphatics, and so are the serous membranes, the pleura and peritoneum. This abundance underlies the early lymphatic spread of carcinomas arising in skin and mucosa.

questions.text: Incisions must be made parallel to Langer's lines to ___. They run longitudinally in ___ and transversely in ___.
questions.explanation: The correct answers are that a parallel incision separates rather than cuts the dermal collagen bundles, so the wound does not gape and the scar is fine; the lines run longitudinally in the limbs and transversely in the neck and trunk. An incision across the lines gapes and heals with a wide scar.
questions.keyConcept: Langer's lines: longitudinal in limbs, transverse in neck and trunk; incise parallel for a fine scar.
blanks: avoid gaping of the wound so that it heals with a fine linear scar

questions.text: Factors maintaining stability of the joint are ___.
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the bony, ligamentous and muscular factors, since these are the three classical groups; muscle tone is the most important in mobile joints such as the shoulder, while bony fit dominates in the hip.
questions.keyConcept: Joint stability = articular shape + ligaments/capsule + muscle tone.
blanks: the shape and mutual fit of the articular surfaces (bony factor), the capsule and ligaments, and above all the tone of the muscles crossing the joint, assisted by atmospheric pressure and by accessory structures such as menisci and labra

questions.text: Torn ligament (sprain) heals slowly because the ligaments are ___.
questions.explanation: The correct answer is that ligaments are poorly vascular, so the repair process is slow; being dense inelastic fibrous tissue with few vessels, they also heal by fibrous scar rather than by regeneration.
questions.keyConcept: Ligaments are poorly vascular, so sprains heal slowly.
blanks: poorly vascular (they have a very poor blood supply)

questions.text: In a typical chemical connection between neurons, ___ of one neuron communicate with ___ of the next neuron at a site called ___.
questions.explanation: The correct answers are the axon terminals of one neuron, the dendrites or cell body of the next, and the synapse. Transmission at the synapse is chemical and one-way, which determines the direction of conduction in a nerve pathway.
questions.keyConcept: Synapse = site of contact between the axon of one neuron and the dendrites or cell body of another.
blanks: the dendrites or the cell body

questions.text: The CNS is covered by 3 meninges which are ___, ___, ___ with the CSF in the ___ space.
questions.explanation: Cerebrospinal fluid is in the subarachnoid space between arachnoid and pia. The cranial epidural space is normally potential, whereas the spinal epidural space is a real space containing fat and a venous plexus.
questions.keyConcept: Meninges: dura, arachnoid, pia; CSF lies in the subarachnoid space.

questions.text: Preganglionic neurons in spinal cord segments T1–L2 give rise to ___, while those in S2–S4 give rise to ___.
questions.explanation: The correct answers are the sympathetic (thoraco-lumbar) outflow from T1-L2 and the parasympathetic (sacral) outflow from S2, S3 and S4. The preganglionic sympathetic fibres leave in the ventral roots and reach the sympathetic chain through the white rami communicantes, which exist only at these levels.
questions.keyConcept: Sympathetic outflow = T1-L2 (thoraco-lumbar); parasympathetic = cranial nerves III, VII, IX, X and S2,3,4.
blanks: the sympathetic outflow, carrying preganglionic sympathetic fibres (thoraco-lumbar outflow, T1-L2)
the sacral part of the parasympathetic outflow (cranio-sacral outflow)

questions.text: The portal vein is the vein situated between ___.
questions.explanation: The correct answer is between two sets of capillaries, which is the defining feature of a portal circulation; the hepatic portal vein begins in the capillaries of the gut and ends in the sinusoids of the liver. The hypophyseal portal system is the other classical example.
questions.keyConcept: A portal vein connects two capillary beds instead of draining to the heart.
blanks: two sets of capillaries, that is it begins in capillaries and ends in capillaries instead of ending in the heart

questions.text: Anatomical end arteries are the arteries that have no ___ (e.g. ___).
questions.explanation: The correct answers are the complete absence of anastomosis and the central artery of the retina. Because no collateral channel exists, occlusion of such an artery causes infarction of the whole territory it supplies, in this case sudden blindness.
questions.keyConcept: Anatomical end artery = no anastomosis at all; occlusion causes infarction (central artery of retina).
blanks: anastomosis at all with the neighbouring arteries
the central artery of the retina

questions.text: Functional end arteries, the anastomosis are present but ___ (e.g. ___ and ___).
questions.explanation: The correct answers are that the anastomoses are inadequate, and the standard examples are the coronary and cerebral arteries. This is why coronary occlusion produces myocardial infarction and cerebral occlusion produces a stroke, even though small communications exist.
questions.keyConcept: Functional end arteries have anastomoses that are too small to compensate (coronary, cerebral).
blanks: insufficient, being too small to keep the tissue alive if the main artery is blocked

questions.text: Arterio-venous connection includes: ___.
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the four channels by which arterial blood reaches the veins. Capillaries are the usual route, sinusoids occur in liver, spleen and bone marrow, cavernous tissue in the penis and nasal mucosa, and A-V anastomoses bypass the capillary bed to regulate temperature.
questions.keyConcept: A-V connections: capillaries, sinusoids, cavernous tissue, arterio-venous anastomoses.
blanks: capillaries, sinusoids, cavernous (erectile) tissue and direct arterio-venous anastomoses

questions.text: Lymphatic aggregations are found in: ___.
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the tonsils, the Peyer's patches and the appendix, which are unencapsulated masses of lymphoid tissue guarding the entrances of the respiratory and alimentary tracts. The thymus and spleen are the encapsulated lymphoid organs.
questions.keyConcept: Lymphoid aggregates: tonsils, Peyer's patches of ileum, appendix.
blanks: the tonsils of Waldeyer's ring (palatine, pharyngeal, lingual and tubal), the aggregated lymphoid follicles (Peyer's patches) of the ileum, and the vermiform appendix, together with the thymus and spleen

questions.text: Avascular structures include ___.
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the epidermis, hair, nails, cornea, lens and articular cartilage, all of which are nourished by diffusion from neighbouring tissue fluid rather than by their own vessels. Being avascular they also have no lymphatics and heal poorly.
questions.keyConcept: Avascular: epidermis, hair, nails, cornea, lens, articular cartilage.
blanks: the epidermis, hair and nails, the cornea and lens of the eye, and the articular cartilage

questions.text: Sites rich in lymphatics include ___.
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the dermis and the mucous and serous membranes, the surfaces at which the body meets the exterior and needs both drainage and immune surveillance. This richness explains the early lymphatic spread of skin and mucosal carcinomas.
questions.keyConcept: Rich lymphatics: dermis of skin, mucous membranes, serous membranes.
blanks: the dermis of the skin and the mucous membranes of the respiratory, alimentary and urogenital tracts, together with the serous membranes

questions.text: In anatomical position, all the following statements are true EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: In anatomical position, the legs are straight and close to each other, not crossed.
questions.keyConcept: Anatomical position is erect with the upper limbs by the sides, palms forward, and lower limbs straight.
options: The arms are straight by the sides.

questions.text: The sagittal plane:
questions.explanation: A sagittal plane is vertical, lies parallel to the median plane, and divides the body into right and left parts.
questions.keyConcept: Sagittal planes divide the body into right and left portions.
options: Lies parallel to the median plane.
Divides the body into upper and lower parts.
Divides the body into anterior and posterior parts.

questions.text: A structure present towards the front of the body is described as:
questions.explanation: Anterior describes a position toward the front of the body.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior means toward the front of the body.

questions.text: A structure present in the sole of the foot is described as:
questions.explanation: Plantar refers to the sole of the foot.
questions.keyConcept: The plantar surface is the sole of the foot.

questions.text: A point present away from the origin of a structure is described as:
questions.explanation: Distal means farther from the origin or point of attachment of a structure.
questions.keyConcept: Distal means farther from a structure's origin or attachment.

questions.text: Approximation of two opposing surfaces is called:
questions.explanation: Flexion decreases the angle between articulating parts and approximates opposing surfaces.
questions.keyConcept: Flexion decreases the angle at a joint.

questions.text: Abduction of the fingers is movement away from the...... finger.
questions.explanation: The middle finger is the central axis of the hand; finger abduction is movement away from it.
questions.keyConcept: Finger abduction is measured from the middle finger.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a rotatory movement?
questions.explanation: Retraction is posterior movement of a structure rather than a rotatory movement.
questions.keyConcept: Retraction moves a structure posteriorly.

questions.text: Rotation of the foot to make the sole face medially is called:
questions.explanation: Inversion turns the sole of the foot medially.
questions.keyConcept: Inversion directs the sole medially.

questions.text: Which of the following is a combined movement?
questions.explanation: Circumduction combines flexion, abduction, extension, and adduction.
questions.keyConcept: Circumduction is a sequential combination of four angular movements.

questions.text: One of the following is an axial bone:
questions.explanation: The mandible belongs to the skull and therefore to the axial skeleton.
questions.keyConcept: The skull, including the mandible, is part of the axial skeleton.

questions.text: The shoulder girdle is formed by:
questions.explanation: The shoulder girdle consists of the clavicle and scapula.
questions.keyConcept: Each pectoral girdle contains a clavicle and scapula.

questions.text: Regarding ossification of bones, choose the correct statement:
questions.explanation: The clavicle ossifies predominantly in a connective-tissue membrane. Primary centers usually appear before birth in diaphyses; secondary centers usually appear after birth in epiphyses.
questions.keyConcept: The clavicle and skull vault are classic sites of intramembranous ossification.
options: Clavicle ossifies in a connective tissue membrane.
Skull vault bones ossify in cartilage models.
Primary centers of ossification appear in the epiphyses.
Secondary centers of ossification appear before birth.

questions.text: A sesamoid bone is:
questions.explanation: Both the patella and pisiform are sesamoid bones.
questions.keyConcept: Sesamoid bones develop within tendons; examples include the patella and pisiform.

questions.text: Regarding the two ends of a growing bone, choose the incorrect statement:
questions.explanation: Epiphyses do not enclose medullary cavities; the principal medullary cavity is in the diaphysis.
questions.keyConcept: The epiphyses form the ends of a long bone, while the medullary cavity lies mainly in the shaft.
options: They are covered by hyaline cartilage.
They ossify by secondary centers of ossification.

questions.text: A bone gets its blood supply through:
questions.explanation: Bone receives blood from nutrient, periosteal, and muscular arterial sources; the nutrient artery is the most important source.
questions.keyConcept: Long bones have nutrient, periosteal, metaphyseal, and epiphyseal arterial supplies.

questions.text: One of the following is NOT a cartilaginous joint:
questions.explanation: The inferior tibiofibular joint is a fibrous syndesmosis rather than a cartilaginous joint.
questions.keyConcept: The inferior tibiofibular joint is a syndesmosis.

questions.text: A pivot synovial joint is a...... joint.
questions.explanation: A pivot joint permits rotation around a single axis and is therefore uniaxial.
questions.keyConcept: Pivot joints are uniaxial rotational joints.

questions.text: An example of a hinge synovial joint is:
questions.explanation: The elbow and ankle are hinge joints. The superior radioulnar joint is pivot, while the sternoclavicular joint is saddle.
questions.keyConcept: The elbow and ankle are examples of hinge synovial joints.

questions.text: All the following combinations are true EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The middle radioulnar joint is a fibrous syndesmosis, not a pivot synovial joint.
questions.keyConcept: The middle radioulnar articulation is formed by the interosseous membrane and is fibrous.
options: Carpometacarpal joint of the thumb — saddle.

questions.text: Cardiac muscles are described as:
questions.explanation: Cardiac muscle fibers are striated, branched, and involuntary.
questions.keyConcept: Cardiac muscle is striated, branched, and involuntary.

questions.text: Regarding skeletal muscles, choose the correct statement:
questions.explanation: Skeletal muscle fibers are striated, voluntary, and normally unbranched.
questions.keyConcept: Skeletal muscle consists of voluntary, striated, unbranched fibers.
options: Their proximal attachment is the insertion.
They are supplied by the autonomic nervous system.

questions.text: A bipennate muscle is:
questions.explanation: Rectus femoris is bipennate; rectus abdominis is strap-like with intersections, deltoid is multipennate, and tibialis anterior is circumpennate in the source classification.
questions.keyConcept: Rectus femoris is a standard example of a bipennate muscle.

questions.text: One of the following is a parallel arrangement of skeletal muscle fibers:
questions.explanation: Fusiform muscles are a form of parallel muscle-fiber arrangement.
questions.keyConcept: Fusiform architecture is a parallel arrangement with a thick central belly.

questions.text: Regarding the deep fascia, choose the incorrect statement:
questions.explanation: Deep fascia does not cover the entire body; it is absent in areas including the face, scalp, and anterior abdominal wall.
questions.keyConcept: Deep fascia invests structures and forms retinacula but is not present over the whole body.
options: It is a dense inelastic fibrous membrane.
It gives attachment for some skeletal muscles.
It forms retinacula around the distal joints.

questions.text: Regarding the nerve cell, all the following statements are true EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: An axon transmits impulses away from the cell body, whereas dendrites transmit impulses toward it.
questions.keyConcept: Axons conduct away from the soma; dendrites conduct toward it.
options: The cell body contains the nucleus.
The axon is a single long process.
The junction between two cells is called a synapse.
The axon transmits impulses towards the cell body.

questions.text: The number of cervical spinal cord segments is:
questions.explanation: The spinal cord has 31 segments: 8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral, and 1 coccygeal.
questions.keyConcept: There are eight cervical spinal cord segments.

questions.text: The cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) circulates in:
questions.explanation: CSF circulates in the subarachnoid space and within the central canal of the spinal cord.
questions.keyConcept: CSF occupies the subarachnoid space and ventricular-central canal system.
options: Central canal of the spinal cord.

questions.text: One of the following is NOT a part of the brain stem:
questions.explanation: The brainstem consists of the midbrain, pons, and medulla oblongata; the diencephalon is not part of it.
questions.keyConcept: The brainstem comprises the midbrain, pons, and medulla.

questions.text: Regarding the spinal nerve, choose the incorrect statement:
questions.explanation: Dorsal rami are relatively small and generally do not form plexuses; the larger ventral rami tend to form plexuses.
questions.keyConcept: Ventral rami form the major nerve plexuses; dorsal rami generally remain segmental.
options: The dorsal ramus tends to form plexuses.

questions.text: In infants, the spinal cord ends at the level of the lower border of...... lumbar vertebra.
questions.explanation: In infants, the spinal cord terminates near the lower border of L3; in adults it ends near the lower border of L1 in the source explanation.
questions.keyConcept: The conus medullaris lies lower in infants than in adults.

questions.text: The preganglionic parasympathetic fibers arise with the following cranial nerves EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Preganglionic parasympathetic fibers arise with cranial nerves III, VII, IX, and X, but not with the trigeminal nerve.
questions.keyConcept: Cranial parasympathetic outflow travels with CN III, VII, IX, and X.

questions.text: One of the following is NOT a function of the parasympathetic system:
questions.explanation: The parasympathetic system does not stimulate all glands; sweat glands, for example, receive sympathetic stimulation.
questions.keyConcept: Parasympathetic activity supports rest-and-digest functions but does not innervate every gland.

questions.text: All the following statements are true regarding the systemic circulation EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood, while the pulmonary veins carry oxygenated blood.
questions.keyConcept: Pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood away from the right ventricle.
options: Superior and inferior venae cavae open into the right atrium.
Tricuspid valve lies between right atrium and right ventricle.
Left atrium receives blood from pulmonary veins.
Mitral valve lies between left atrium and left ventricle.

questions.text: The valve lying between the right ventricle and the artery leaving it is the...... valve.
questions.explanation: The pulmonary valve lies between the right ventricle and the pulmonary trunk.
questions.keyConcept: Blood exits the right ventricle through the pulmonary valve.

questions.text: Blood vessels that carry blood away from the heart are called:
questions.explanation: Arteries are defined as vessels that carry blood away from the heart.
questions.keyConcept: Arteries carry blood away from the heart regardless of oxygenation.

questions.text: The heart gets its arterial blood supply through:
questions.explanation: The myocardium receives arterial blood through the right and left coronary arteries; most venous drainage enters the coronary sinus.
questions.keyConcept: The right and left coronary arteries supply the myocardium.

questions.text: The circulation of the blood from the intestine to the liver is called:
questions.explanation: Blood from the intestine reaches the liver through the hepatic portal circulation.
questions.keyConcept: The hepatic portal system carries gut blood to the liver before systemic return.

questions.text: All the following statements are true about capillaries EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The cornea is avascular and contains no capillaries; capillaries are also absent from cartilage and the epidermis.
questions.keyConcept: The cornea, cartilage, and epidermis are avascular.

questions.text: Match each muscle form with its corresponding example.
questions.explanation: The printed key maps quadrilateral to quadratus lumborum, fusiform to biceps brachii, strap-like to sartorius, strap-like with tendinous intersections to rectus abdominis, and unipennate to flexor pollicis longus.
questions.keyConcept: Muscle architecture is classified by fiber direction and relationship to tendons.

questions.text: Match each bone with its definition.
questions.explanation: The humerus is the arm bone, the scaphoid is a carpal bone, the radius is lateral in the forearm, the femur is the thigh bone, and the ulna is medial in anatomical position.
questions.keyConcept: In anatomical position, the radius is lateral and the ulna is medial.

questions.text: The plane dividing the body vertically into a large right part and a small left part is:
questions.explanation: A left parasagittal plane is a vertical plane parallel to and left of the median plane, so it divides the body into a larger right part and a smaller left part. A right paramedian plane produces the opposite proportions. Coronal and horizontal planes divide the body into anterior-posterior and superior-inferior parts, respectively.
questions.keyConcept: A parasagittal plane divides the body into unequal right and left parts.

questions.text: Which of the following bones does not belong to the axial skeleton?
questions.explanation: The patella is part of the lower limb and therefore belongs to the appendicular skeleton. The maxilla is a skull bone, the sacrum is part of the vertebral column, and the floating ribs are part of the thoracic cage; all three belong to the axial skeleton.
questions.keyConcept: The patella is an appendicular bone of the lower limb.

questions.text: Regarding the clavicle, which statement is incorrect?
questions.explanation: The clavicle is predominantly ossified by intramembranous ossification, but it does not ossify completely from membrane because its ends have cartilaginous contributions. It forms the pectoral girdle with the scapula and is classified as a modified long bone.
questions.keyConcept: The clavicle is mainly, but not entirely, formed by intramembranous ossification.
options: It forms the pectoral girdle with the scapula
It is an example of a long bone
It does not participate significantly in blood-cell production

questions.text: Which term can be used to describe a structure on the sole of the foot?
questions.explanation: Plantar refers to the sole of the foot. Dorsal refers to the upper surface of the foot, distal describes position farther from the trunk or point of origin, and palmar refers to the palm of the hand.
questions.keyConcept: Plantar means relating to the sole of the foot.

questions.text: The nutrient artery is directed downward in all the following bones EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The nutrient canal of the ulna is directed toward the elbow and therefore upward. In the humerus it is directed downward toward the elbow, while in the tibia and fibula it is directed downward away from the knee. This follows the rule that nutrient canals are directed away from the more actively growing end.
questions.keyConcept: Nutrient canals point toward the elbow and away from the knee.

questions.text: Which of the following sites lacks conventional superficial fascia?
questions.explanation: The scrotum lacks the usual fat-containing superficial fascia. Its subcutaneous tissue is modified to form the dartos layer, which contains smooth muscle and no fat. The scalp, face, and back of the neck possess superficial fascial tissue.
questions.keyConcept: In the scrotum, ordinary superficial fascia is replaced by the dartos layer.

questions.text: Which of the following is the best example of a sesamoid bone?
questions.explanation: The pisiform is a sesamoid bone embedded in the tendon of flexor carpi ulnaris. The maxilla is an irregular bone, the clavicle is a modified long bone, and the scapula is a flat bone.
questions.keyConcept: The pisiform is a sesamoid bone within the flexor carpi ulnaris tendon.

questions.text: Choose the incorrect statement:
questions.explanation: In the anatomical position, the forearm is supinated and the palms face anteriorly; the hand is not pronated. False ribs do not attach directly to the sternum, the paired hip bones form the pelvic girdle, and the big toe has proximal and distal phalanges only.
questions.keyConcept: The forearm is supinated and the palms face forward in the anatomical position.
options: False ribs have costal cartilages that do not reach the sternum directly
The pelvic girdle is formed by the hip bones
In the anatomical position, the hand is pronated
The big toe has two phalanges

questions.text: Appositional growth of a long bone is a function of the:
questions.explanation: Appositional growth increases the thickness and diameter of a bone through osteogenic activity in the inner layer of the periosteum. Epiphyseal cartilage is responsible for longitudinal growth, while metaphysis and diaphysis are regions of the bone rather than the principal membrane responsible for appositional growth.
questions.keyConcept: Periosteal osteoblasts increase bone diameter by appositional growth.

questions.text: The most metabolically active part of a growing long bone is the:
questions.explanation: The metaphysis is highly vascular and undergoes active growth and remodeling adjacent to the epiphyseal plate. The diaphysis forms the shaft, the epiphysis forms the end of the bone, and the periosteum is important for appositional growth but is not the most active region in longitudinal growth.
questions.keyConcept: The metaphysis is the most active growth and remodeling region of a growing long bone.

questions.text: Regarding the foot, choose the incorrect statement:
questions.explanation: The axis for abduction and adduction of the toes passes through the second toe, not the middle or third toe. The foot has seven tarsal bones, plantar refers to the sole, and the big toe has two phalanges.
questions.keyConcept: Toe abduction and adduction are defined relative to the second toe.
options: The middle toe is the axis of abduction of the toes
A structure in the sole is described as plantar
The big toe has two phalanges

questions.text: The movement in which the radius and ulna become parallel is:
questions.explanation: During supination, the radius and ulna lie parallel. During pronation, the radius crosses anteriorly over the ulna. Inversion and eversion are movements of the foot rather than the forearm.
questions.keyConcept: The radius and ulna are parallel in supination and crossed in pronation.

questions.text: Which of the following joints does not belong to the cartilaginous type?
questions.explanation: The third sternocostal joint is a plane synovial joint. The symphysis pubis is a secondary cartilaginous joint, while the costochondral joints and epiphyseal cartilage are primary cartilaginous joints.
questions.keyConcept: The second through seventh sternocostal joints are synovial; costochondral joints are cartilaginous.

questions.text: The movement of a limb away from the trunk is:
questions.explanation: Abduction moves a limb away from the median plane of the body. Adduction moves it toward the median plane, flexion decreases the angle at a joint, and circumduction combines flexion, extension, abduction, and adduction.
questions.keyConcept: Abduction moves a limb away from the body's median plane.

questions.text: Regarding the fifth rib, choose the incorrect statement:
questions.explanation: The fifth rib is a true rib because its costal cartilage attaches directly to the sternum. Its costochondral joint is primary cartilaginous, and the rib articulates posteriorly with the thoracic vertebral column.
questions.keyConcept: Ribs 1–7 are true ribs with direct cartilaginous attachment to the sternum.
options: It articulates with its costal cartilage by a primary cartilaginous joint
Its costal cartilage reaches the sternum
It articulates with the vertebral column posteriorly

questions.text: Which of the following joints does not belong to the synovial variety?
questions.explanation: The inferior tibiofibular joint is a fibrous syndesmosis. Intercarpal joints are plane synovial joints, the first carpometacarpal joint is a saddle synovial joint, and the inferior radioulnar joint is a pivot synovial joint.
questions.keyConcept: The inferior tibiofibular joint is a fibrous syndesmosis, not a synovial joint.

questions.text: Regarding sutures, select the incorrect statement:
questions.explanation: Sutures are essentially immobile fibrous joints and do not permit a wide range of movement. They occur between skull bones and may later ossify to form synostoses.
questions.keyConcept: Sutures are fibrous joints with little or no movement.
options: They have a wide range of movement

questions.text: All the following are examples of pinnate muscles EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Rectus abdominis is a parallel, strap-like muscle interrupted by tendinous intersections rather than a pinnate muscle. Tibialis anterior and flexor pollicis longus have unipennate architecture, while the deltoid is multipennate.
questions.keyConcept: Rectus abdominis is a parallel muscle; the deltoid is multipennate.

questions.text: During a surgical operation, a longitudinal incision could be made at which of the following sites?
questions.explanation: Skin cleavage lines in the limbs generally run longitudinally, so a longitudinal incision is suitable in the forearm. Cleavage lines over the neck and trunk are predominantly transverse, making transverse incisions more favorable at those sites.
questions.keyConcept: Cleavage lines are generally longitudinal in the limbs and transverse on the neck and trunk.

questions.text: As regards the neurons, choose the CORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: Bundles of axons in the peripheral nervous system are called nerves. A neuron's nucleus is in its cell body, dendrites generally conduct toward the cell body and the usually single axon conducts away.
questions.keyConcept: Axon bundles are nerves in the PNS and tracts in the CNS.
options: Axons carry nerve impulses towards cell bodies.
Dendrites carry nerve impulses away from cell bodies.
Bundles of axons outside CNS form nerves.

questions.text: Menisci are present in:
questions.explanation: The knee contains medial and lateral fibrocartilaginous menisci that improve congruity, distribute load and absorb shock.
questions.keyConcept: The knee contains medial and lateral menisci.

questions.text: All the following lie within the grey matter of the spinal cord EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Ascending tracts are bundles of axons in the spinal cord's white matter. The horns and grey commissure are grey matter, which surrounds the central canal.
questions.keyConcept: Spinal tracts lie in white matter; neuronal horns lie in grey matter.

questions.text: One of the following joints is uniaxial:
questions.explanation: The elbow is a uniaxial hinge joint whose principal movements are flexion and extension around a transverse axis.
questions.keyConcept: Hinge joints such as the elbow are uniaxial.

questions.text: The long fibrous cord for attachment of muscles is called:
questions.explanation: A tendon is a cord of dense collagen that attaches a muscle to bone. An aponeurosis is a broad, flat tendinous sheet.
questions.keyConcept: Tendon is a cord-like muscle attachment; aponeurosis is sheet-like.

questions.text: The medial structure is the structure that lies:
questions.explanation: Medial describes a structure positioned closer to the body's median plane.
questions.keyConcept: Medial means toward the median plane.
options: Closer to the upper end of the body.
Closer to the lower end of the body.
Closer to the front of the body.
Closer to the back of the body.
Closer to the median plane of the body.

questions.text: All the following contain mixed nerve fibers EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The dorsal and ventral roots are not mixed: the dorsal root is sensory and the ventral root is motor. The spinal nerve trunk and both rami are mixed.
questions.keyConcept: Roots are functionally separate; the spinal nerve and its rami are mixed.

questions.text: What is the type of joint that connects the roots of the teeth to their sockets?
questions.explanation: A gomphosis is a peg-and-socket fibrous joint connecting a tooth root to its alveolus through the periodontal ligament.
questions.keyConcept: Tooth-to-socket joint is a fibrous gomphosis.

questions.text: The wrist joint is:
questions.explanation: The radiocarpal joint is a biaxial ellipsoid joint permitting flexion, extension, abduction, adduction and circumduction.
questions.keyConcept: The wrist is an ellipsoid synovial joint.

questions.text: The intermuscular septa and interosseous membranes:
questions.explanation: Intermuscular septa and interosseous membranes help divide the limbs into osteofascial compartments containing muscle groups with related actions.
questions.keyConcept: Intermuscular septa separate functional muscle compartments.
options: Surround the muscles of the upper and lower limbs.
Separate different groups of muscles which have different actions.
Are transverse thickened bands of deep fascia present at wrist joint.
Form tough sheaths around big blood vessels.

questions.text: What is the type of joint of the intervertebral discs?
questions.explanation: Adjacent vertebral bodies are united through intervertebral discs as secondary cartilaginous joints, or symphyses.
questions.keyConcept: Intervertebral discs form secondary cartilaginous joints.

questions.text: Which one of the following joints is a hinge synovial?
questions.explanation: The elbow is a hinge synovial joint. The superior radioulnar joint is pivot, the shoulder is ball-and-socket, the wrist is ellipsoid and the acromioclavicular joint is plane.
questions.keyConcept: The elbow is a hinge synovial joint.

questions.text: Choose the correct arrangement from outside inwards:
questions.explanation: From outside inward, the sequence is dura, potential subdural space, arachnoid, CSF-filled subarachnoid space and pia.
questions.keyConcept: Meningeal order: dura → arachnoid → pia, with CSF between arachnoid and pia.
options: Pia mater, subarachnoid space, arachnoid mater, subdural space & dura mater.
Dura mater, subdural space, pia mater, subarachnoid space & arachnoid mater.
Arachnoid mater, subdural space, pia mater, subarachnoid space & dura mater.
Dura mater, subdural space, arachnoid mater, subarachnoid space & pia mater.
Dura mater, subdural space, subarachnoid space, pia mater & arachnoid mater.

questions.text: As regards the cartilaginous joints, choose INCORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: A syndesmosis is a fibrous joint, not a primary cartilaginous joint. The remaining statements describe primary or secondary cartilaginous joints correctly.
questions.keyConcept: Syndesmosis is a fibrous joint.
options: Secondary cartilaginous joints allow limited movement.
Syndesmosis is a type of primary cartilaginous joint.
Primary cartilaginous joints are usually temporary.
Secondary cartilaginous joints lie usually in median plane.
In secondary cartilaginous joints, articular surfaces are connected by fibrocartilage.

questions.text: What is the type of joint present at the ends of the growing long bones?
questions.explanation: The epiphyseal plate is a temporary primary cartilaginous joint (synchondrosis).
questions.keyConcept: Cartilaginous Joints: The epiphyseal plate is a temporary primary cartilaginous joint (synchondrosis)

questions.text: The smooth muscles are:
questions.explanation: Smooth muscle is involuntary and forms part of vessel walls.
questions.keyConcept: Smooth Muscle: Smooth muscle is involuntary and forms part of vessel walls
options: Present in the wall of blood vessels.

questions.text: Cervical segments of spinal cord are:
questions.explanation: There are eight cervical spinal cord segments.
questions.keyConcept: Spinal Cord Segments: There are eight cervical spinal cord segments

questions.text: Which one of the following is an ellipsoid joint?
questions.explanation: The radiocarpal (wrist) joint is an ellipsoid/condyloid joint.
questions.keyConcept: Synovial Joint Classification: The radiocarpal (wrist) joint is an ellipsoid/condyloid joint

questions.text: Which one of the following structures never lies inside synovial cavity?
questions.explanation: The fibrous capsule encloses the joint rather than occupying its cavity.
questions.keyConcept: Synovial Joint Structure: The fibrous capsule encloses the joint rather than occupying its cavity

questions.text: Intra-membranous ossification occurs in:
questions.explanation: The clavicle ossifies predominantly by intramembranous ossification.
questions.keyConcept: Intramembranous Ossification: The clavicle ossifies predominantly by intramembranous ossification

questions.text: The example of the muscle that is inserted in a raphe is:
questions.explanation: Pharyngeal constrictors insert posteriorly into the pharyngeal raphe.
questions.keyConcept: Muscle Attachments: Pharyngeal constrictors insert posteriorly into the pharyngeal raphe

questions.text: An example of a triangular muscle is:
questions.explanation: Temporalis is a convergent, triangular muscle.
questions.keyConcept: Muscle Architecture: Temporalis is a convergent, triangular muscle

questions.text: Intra-cartilaginous ossification occurs in:
questions.explanation: Vertebrae develop mainly by endochondral (intracartilaginous) ossification.
questions.keyConcept: Endochondral Ossification: Vertebrae develop mainly by endochondral (intracartilaginous) ossification

questions.text: As regards the skeletal muscle, choose the INCORRECT statement.
questions.explanation: The origin is usually the less movable attachment.
questions.keyConcept: Skeletal Muscle: The origin is usually the less movable attachment
options: The origin is the most movable end of the muscle.
Contraction means approximation of origin and insertion.
Septa from deep fascia divide them into groups.
They are mostly under voluntary control.
They are innervated by motor, sensory and autonomic nerve fibers.

questions.text: Appendicular skeleton is formed of:
questions.explanation: The appendicular skeleton includes limbs and their girdles.
questions.keyConcept: Appendicular Skeleton: The appendicular skeleton includes limbs and their girdles
options: Bones of the upper and lower limbs.

questions.text: One of the functions of superficial fascia is:
questions.explanation: Superficial fascia contains or supports cutaneous muscles in certain regions.
questions.keyConcept: Superficial Fascia: Superficial fascia contains or supports cutaneous muscles in certain regions

questions.text: The skeletal muscles are:
questions.explanation: Most skeletal muscles attach to bones and produce voluntary movement.
questions.keyConcept: Skeletal Muscle: Most skeletal muscles attach to bones and produce voluntary movement
options: Present in the wall of blood vessels.

questions.text: The articular surface of the synovial joint is covered by:
questions.explanation: Synovial joint surfaces are usually covered by hyaline articular cartilage.
questions.keyConcept: Synovial Joint Structure: Synovial joint surfaces are usually covered by hyaline articular cartilage

questions.text: One of the functions of deep fascia is that it:
questions.explanation: Deep fascia contributes to strong interosseous membranes.
questions.keyConcept: Deep Fascia: Deep fascia contributes to strong interosseous membranes
options: Facilitates the movement of the skin.
Prevents heat loss from the body.

questions.text: Which part of the spinal nerve does not contain motor fibers?
questions.explanation: The dorsal root carries sensory afferent fibers only.
questions.keyConcept: Spinal Nerve Roots: The dorsal root carries sensory afferent fibers only

questions.text: Secondary cartilaginous joints:
questions.explanation: Symphyses unite bones partly by fibrocartilage and permit limited movement.
questions.keyConcept: Secondary Cartilaginous Joints: Symphyses unite bones partly by fibrocartilage and permit limited movement
options: Include epiphyseal plate of long bones.

questions.text: In which of the following cavities is yellow bone marrow found?
questions.explanation: Yellow marrow occupies the medullary cavity of adult long bones.
questions.keyConcept: Bone Marrow: Yellow marrow occupies the medullary cavity of adult long bones

questions.text: Which of the following is (are) not striated?
questions.explanation: Smooth muscle is non-striated; skeletal and cardiac muscle are striated.
questions.keyConcept: Muscle Tissue: Smooth muscle is non-striated; skeletal and cardiac muscle are striated

questions.text: Which of the following positions describes anatomical position?
questions.explanation: The anatomical position is the standard erect standing posture used for anatomical description.
questions.keyConcept: Standard anatomical position
options: Curled into a ball, as a baby in the uterus.
Sitting comfortably with your hands on your knees.
The eyes looking to the side.

questions.text: The following is a feature of anatomical position:
