questions.explanation: In anatomical position the upper limbs lie by the sides and the palms face forward.
questions.keyConcept: Palms face forward
options: Palms of the hands directed medially.
Has upper limbs by side, and the palms facing forward.

questions.text: The vertical plane that divided the body into anterior and posterior parts is:
questions.explanation: A coronal plane divides the body into anterior and posterior parts.
questions.keyConcept: Coronal plane

questions.text: Regarding the anatomical planes, choose the correct answer:
questions.explanation: The coronal plane separates anterior from posterior parts of the body.
questions.keyConcept: Plane definitions
options: Sagittal plane divides body into anterior and posterior halves.
Coronal plane is a horizontal plane.
Parasagittal plane is perpendicular to median plane.
Coronal plane divides body into anterior and posterior parts.
Transverse plane divides the body into right and left parts.

questions.text: Regarding the anatomical planes, one of the following is true:
questions.explanation: The median plane intersects the anterior surface along the anterior median line.
questions.keyConcept: Median plane
options: The median plane cuts the anterior surface of the body along the anterior median line.
Coronal plane is a horizontal plane at right angle to the sagittal plane.
The terms proximal and distal are used in limbs in place of anterior and posterior.
Horizontal planes are drawn parallel to the coronal plane.

questions.text: ________ plane passes through the midline of the body, dividing it into right and left halves.
questions.explanation: The midsagittal plane passes through the midline and divides the body into equal right and left halves.
questions.keyConcept: Midsagittal plane

questions.text: The following term is correct:
questions.explanation: Distal means farther from the root or point of attachment of a limb.
questions.keyConcept: Distal means farther from the root or point of attachment of a limb
options: Peripheral means near the center of the body.
Proximal means away from the trunk.
Inferior means nearer to the head.
Distal means away from the root of the limb.
Lateral means nearer to the median plane.

questions.text: Which directional term best describes the position of the phalanges with respect to carpal bones:
questions.explanation: Phalanges are farther from the limb root than the carpal bones, so they are distal to them.
questions.keyConcept: Distal relationship

questions.text: Which directional term best describes the position of the radius bone to phalanges:
questions.explanation: The radius is nearer the root of the upper limb than the phalanges, so it is proximal to them.
questions.keyConcept: Proximal relationship

questions.text: Regarding the movements, the correct statement is:
questions.explanation: Eversion means turning the sole of the foot outward.
questions.keyConcept: Eversion means turning the sole of the foot outward
options: Adduction: Movement away from the midline of the body
Flexion: Increase the angle between two bones
Eversion: Turning of the sole of the foot outward.

questions.text: The following statement regarding the fascia is true:
questions.explanation: The fat in superficial fascia contributes to the rounded contour of the body.
questions.keyConcept: Superficial fascia
options: Deep fascia acts as a heat insulator.
Deep fascia is a transparent weak membrane.
Superficial fascia gives the body its round contour.

questions.text: Regarding the retinacula, they:
questions.explanation: Retinacula are transverse thickenings of deep fascia at the wrist and ankle that hold tendons in place.
questions.keyConcept: Retinacula are transverse thickenings of deep fascia at the wrist and ankle that hold tendons in place
options: Are tight sheets of deep fascia around the muscles of limbs and neck.
Are partitions of deep fascia separating groups of muscles.
Are transverse thickenings of deep fascia around the wrist and ankle.
Are strong sheaths of deep fascia investing large vessels and nerves.
Are strong bands of superficial fascia giving attachments to muscles.

questions.text: Regarding the skeletal muscles, one of the following is true:
questions.explanation: The deltoid is classically described as a multipennate muscle.
questions.keyConcept: Multipennate muscle
options: Tibialis anterior is a bipennate muscle.
Extensor digitorum longus is multipennate muscle.
Rectus femoris is a parallel muscle.

questions.text: Regarding the metaphysis of long bone, it is:
questions.explanation: The metaphysis is the expanded part of the shaft adjacent to the epiphyseal cartilage.
questions.keyConcept: The metaphysis is the expanded part of the shaft adjacent to the epiphyseal cartilage
options: The part of the diaphysis near the center of the bone.
The part of the diaphysis close to the epiphyseal cartilage.
The cartilaginous plate separating the epiphysis and diaphysis of a long bone.

questions.text: The site of growth of long bone in length is due to the activity of:
questions.explanation: Growth in length of a long bone occurs at the epiphyseal cartilage.
questions.keyConcept: Epiphyseal cartilage

questions.text: Which function of the skeleton is performed by providing a system of levers for skeletal muscles?
questions.explanation: The skeleton acts as a lever system for muscles and therefore contributes to locomotion.
questions.keyConcept: The skeleton acts as a lever system for muscles and therefore contributes to locomotion

questions.text: A vertebra is considered:
questions.explanation: A vertebra is an irregular bone because its shape is complex and specialized for protection of the spinal cord and articulation with adjacent vertebrae.
questions.keyConcept: Vertebrae are classified as irregular bones.

questions.text: The epiphyseal plate is an example of:
questions.explanation: The epiphyseal plate is a primary cartilaginous joint.
questions.keyConcept: Primary cartilaginous joint

questions.text: Which synovial joint type allows a wide range of flexion, extension, abduction, adduction, and medial and lateral rotation?
questions.explanation: Ball-and-socket joints are polyaxial and allow medial rotation.
questions.keyConcept: Ball-and-socket joint

questions.text: An example of secondary cartilaginous joints is:
questions.explanation: Intervertebral joints between vertebral bodies are secondary cartilaginous joints.
questions.keyConcept: Secondary cartilaginous joint
options: Joints between adjacent vertebral bodies through intervertebral discs

questions.text: The stability of joints depends upon:
questions.explanation: The shape and congruence of the articulating surfaces are major determinants of joint stability.
questions.keyConcept: Articular congruence

questions.text: Regarding the synovial joints, choose the correct answer:
questions.explanation: Synovial joints are defined by the presence of a joint cavity separating the articulating bones.
questions.keyConcept: Joint cavity
options: They are joints of limited movements.
Their never be intracapsular tendon of a muscle.
Synovial membrane connects the articulating bones.
The articulating bones are separated by a joint cavity.
The articulating bones are covered with a synovial membrane.

questions.text: Regarding the veins, one is correct:
questions.explanation: Systemic veins return deoxygenated blood from the body to the right atrium, whereas pulmonary veins are the main exception because they carry oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium.
questions.keyConcept: Systemic veins return deoxygenated blood to the right atrium.
options: Veins are vessels that carry blood out of the heart.
Systemic veins return deoxygenated blood from the body to the right atrium.
Pulmonary veins return oxygenated blood from the lungs to the right atrium.
All systemic veins have no valves.
Venules are the smallest veins which arise from the arteries.

questions.text: Regarding the arteries, one is correct:
questions.explanation: An anastomosis is a joining or communication between branches of arteries.
questions.keyConcept: Arterial anastomosis
options: Arteries are vessels that carry blood back to the heart.
Arterioles are the largest arteries, which open in the capillaries.
Anastomosis is the joining of branches of arteries.

questions.text: Which organ systems function to control other organ systems?
questions.explanation: The nervous and endocrine systems regulate and coordinate the activities of other organ systems.
questions.keyConcept: Nervous and endocrine control

questions.text: Which statement correctly gives the number of pairs of spinal nerves in a region?
questions.explanation: Only the cervical group has 8 pairs; thoracic, lumbar, sacral, and coccygeal counts make the other options incorrect.
questions.keyConcept: There are 8 pairs of cervical spinal nerves.

questions.text: Regarding the spinal cord, one is correct:
questions.explanation: In the newborn, the spinal cord ends around the level of L3; the other statements are anatomically incorrect.
questions.keyConcept: The newborn spinal cord ends around L3.
options: Length is 35 cm in the male and 30 cm in female
Location is in the upper third of the vertebral canal
It begins as the continuation of the pons.
It ends in the newborn at the level of the third lumbar vertebra.

questions.text: Regarding the autonomic nervous system, one is correct:
questions.explanation: The sympathetic system mediates the emergency or fight-or-flight response.
questions.keyConcept: Sympathetic activity prepares the body for emergencies.
options: It is concerned with innervation of voluntary structures.
Sympathetic system Prepare the body for an emergency.
Sympathetic system increases the peristalsis and glandular activity and open sphincters.
Parasympathetic system it increases the heart rate, raises the blood pressure.
Sympathetic system Responsible for conserving and restoring energy.

questions.text: Regarding the skin appendages, one is correct:
questions.explanation: Sebaceous glands usually discharge into hair follicles.
questions.keyConcept: Sebaceous glands typically open into hair follicles.
options: The sebaceous gland opens into the hair follicles.
The sweat glands present over the surface of the lips.
The root of nail is its distal edge.
The hair follicles are projections from the dermis.
The arrector pili muscle connects the hair follicles to each others.

questions.text: Trunk of the human body formed of thorax, ___ and pelvis.
questions.explanation: The trunk is classically divided into thorax, abdomen, and pelvis.
questions.keyConcept: The trunk consists of thorax, abdomen, and pelvis.

questions.text: Coronal plane divides the body into ___ and ___ parts.
questions.explanation: A coronal plane separates the body into anterior and posterior parts.
questions.keyConcept: A coronal plane divides the body into anterior and posterior parts.

questions.text: ___ is toward the head while ___ is toward the feet.
questions.explanation: Superior means toward the head and inferior means toward the feet.
questions.keyConcept: Superior is toward the head; inferior is toward the feet.

questions.text: ___ is toward the front while ___ is toward the back of the body.
questions.explanation: Anterior refers to the front and posterior to the back of the body.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior is front; posterior is back.

questions.text: ___ is toward the midline while ___ is toward the side of the body.
questions.explanation: Medial means toward the midline and lateral means away from it.
questions.keyConcept: Medial is toward the midline; lateral is toward the side.

questions.text: Palmar is ___ of the hand while plantar is ___ of the foot.
questions.explanation: Palmar refers to the anterior surface of the hand, while plantar refers to the sole of the foot.
questions.keyConcept: Palmar = anterior hand; plantar = sole of foot.

questions.text: Vertebral column is formed of ___ vertebrae.
questions.explanation: The vertebral column is formed from 33 vertebrae.
questions.keyConcept: The vertebral column is formed by 33 vertebrae.

questions.text: Vertebrae are classified into 7 ___ vertebrae, 12 ___ vertebrae, 5 ___ vertebrae, 5 ___ vertebrae and 4 ___ vertebrae.
questions.explanation: The vertebral column is divided into cervical, thoracic, lumbar, sacral, and coccygeal regions.
questions.keyConcept: Vertebral regions are cervical, thoracic, lumbar, sacral, and coccygeal.

questions.text: According to shape femur is ___ bone and scapula is ___ bone.
questions.explanation: The femur is a long bone and the scapula is a flat bone.
questions.keyConcept: Femur is long; scapula is flat.

questions.text: Blood transported by the pulmonary veins returns to the:
questions.explanation: The four pulmonary veins carry oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium. Blood then passes through the mitral valve into the left ventricle.
questions.keyConcept: Pulmonary veins return oxygenated blood to the left atrium.

questions.text: The joint between the manubrium and body of the sternum is:
questions.explanation: The manubriosternal joint is a secondary cartilaginous joint (symphysis) united by fibrocartilage. It forms the palpable sternal angle.
questions.keyConcept: The manubriosternal joint is a secondary cartilaginous joint at the sternal angle.

questions.text: The number of spinal cord segments is:
questions.explanation: The spinal cord has 31 segments: 8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral, and 1 coccygeal. Each segment gives rise to a pair of spinal nerves.
questions.keyConcept: There are 31 spinal cord segments and 3 1 pairs of spinal nerves.

questions.text: For proper healing of a wound in the skin of the leg, the incision should be made:
questions.explanation: Langer's lines generally run longitudinally in the limbs. An incision parallel to these collagen lines gapes less and heals with a finer scar.
questions.keyConcept: In limbs, incisions parallel to longitudinal Langer's lines heal best.

questions.text: An example of a strap-like muscle is:
questions.explanation: Sartorius is a long, narrow muscle with parallel fibers and is the classic strap muscle. Temporalis is fan-shaped, deltoid is multipennate, and biceps is fusiform.
questions.keyConcept: Sartorius is the classic strap-like parallel muscle.

questions.text: Which one of the following structures has no lymphatics?
questions.explanation: Brain parenchyma has no conventional lymphatic vessels; interstitial fluid drains through perivascular and cerebrospinal-fluid pathways. The liver, skin, intestine, and pleura all have lymphatic vessels.
questions.keyConcept: The brain has no conventional intraparenchymal lymphatics.

questions.text: Cerebrospinal fluid lies between:
questions.explanation: Cerebrospinal fluid fills the subarachnoid space between the arachnoid and pia mater. The subdural space between dura and arachnoid is only a potential space.
questions.keyConcept: CSF occupies the subarachnoid space between arachnoid and pia.

questions.text: Which one of the following joints is the most movable?
questions.explanation: A hinge joint is synovial and therefore freely movable. Syndesmoses, sutures, and gomphoses are fibrous joints, while primary cartilaginous joints are essentially immobile.
questions.keyConcept: Synovial joints are freely movable; hinge is the only synovial option here.

questions.text: During an operation to remove a swelling from the back under general anesthesia, the patient should be placed in which position?
questions.explanation: The prone position places the patient face down and exposes the posterior surface of the trunk for surgery. Supine would place the back against the operating table.
questions.keyConcept: Prone position provides surgical access to the back.

questions.text: A piece of glass lacerated the wrist of a teenager. The tendons crossing the wrist were no longer held in place during movement. Which structure was most likely cut?
questions.explanation: Retinacula are localized thickenings of deep fascia that hold tendons close to the skeleton at the wrist and prevent bowstringing. Cutting one allows the tendons to displace during movement.
questions.keyConcept: Retinacula hold tendons in place at joints and prevent bowstringing.

questions.text: A patient sustained a fracture of the lateral bone of the leg. The affected bone is the:
questions.explanation: The fibula is the slender lateral bone of the leg, while the tibia is the larger medial weight-bearing bone. Radius is in the forearm, patella at the knee, and talus in the foot.
questions.keyConcept: Fibula is lateral; tibia is medial in the leg.

questions.text: A patient has severe forearm pain with inability to pronate and supinate the radius over the ulna. The affected type of joint is:
questions.explanation: Pronation and supination occur at the proximal and distal radioulnar joints, both pivot synovial joints. Pivot joints permit rotation around a longitudinal axis.
questions.keyConcept: Radioulnar joints are pivot joints that permit pronation and supination.

questions.text: Which type of bone makes the skull lighter and more resonant?
questions.explanation: Pneumatic bones contain air-filled sinuses, reducing skull weight and adding resonance to the voice. Examples include the frontal, ethmoid, sphenoid, and maxilla.
questions.keyConcept: Air-filled pneumatic bones lighten the skull and increase resonance.

questions.text: During elbow flexion, which term describes the muscles that initiate the movement?
questions.explanation: The muscle chiefly responsible for initiating and producing a movement is the prime mover, or agonist. Synergists assist it, antagonists oppose it, and fixators stabilize proximal parts.
questions.keyConcept: Prime mover (agonist) initiates; synergist assists; antagonist opposes; fixator stabilizes.

subjects.name: Anatomy
subjects.lectures: Spermatogenesis, Ovulation, Gametogenesis, Female Reproductive Cycles, Oogenesis, Introduction to Embryology, Fertilization, Implantation, Cleavage, Decidua, Twinning, Fetal Membranes, Bilaminar Germ Disc, Gastrulation, Neurulation, Somites, Intraembryonic Mesoderm, Germ Layer Derivatives, Folding, Placenta, Amniotic Fluid, Umbilical Cord, Fetal Circulation, Chromosomal Anomalies, Birth Defects & Teratology, Placental Barrier, Chorion, Chorionic Villi, Placental Endocrinology, Extraembryonic Mesoderm, Placental Circulation, Abnormal Implantation

questions.text: Sperm can retain fertilizing capacity in the female reproductive tract for up to approximately:
questions.explanation: Under favorable conditions sperm can remain capable of fertilization for up to about 5 days. An oocyte is generally fertilizable for about 24 hours after ovulation, producing a fertile window that includes the five preceding days.
questions.keyConcept: Sperm can remain fertile for up to about 5 days; an oocyte for about 24 hours.

questions.text: Ovulation is the process of liberation of:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the Secondary oocyte because at ovulation the cell released is arrested in metaphase of the second meiotic division. It becomes a mature ovum only if a sperm penetrates it and the second meiotic division is completed. The primary oocyte and oogonium are earlier stages that remain in the ovary.
questions.keyConcept: Ovulation releases a secondary oocyte arrested in metaphase II.

questions.text: Which of the following cells contains 23 chromosomes?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the Secondary spermatocyte because it is produced by the first meiotic (reduction) division and therefore carries the haploid number of 23 chromosomes, although each still has two chromatids. Spermatogonia, oogonia and primary spermatocytes are all diploid with 46 chromosomes.
questions.keyConcept: The first meiotic division halves the chromosome number, so secondary spermatocytes are haploid.

questions.text: Until approximately when is the corpus luteum the predominant progesterone source before placental production takes over?
questions.explanation: The corpus luteum is predominant in very early pregnancy. Production shifts toward the placenta around gestational weeks 7–9, and the placenta is the major definitive source beyond 1 0 weeks; this corresponds approximately to the 2–3-month option.
questions.keyConcept: Luteal-placental progesterone transition occurs in the first trimester, around weeks 7–9.

questions.text: Which of the following cells is diploid?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the Primary spermatocyte because it is formed from a spermatogonium by mitosis and has not yet undergone the reduction division, so it retains 46 chromosomes. The secondary oocyte, spermatid and sperm are all haploid, having completed the first meiotic division.
questions.keyConcept: Diploid germ cells: spermatogonia, oogonia, primary spermatocytes and primary oocytes.

questions.text: Which of the following is a diploid cell?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the Primary oocyte because it arises from an oogonium by mitosis and remains arrested in prophase of the first meiotic division with 46 chromosomes until puberty. Secondary spermatocytes, spermatids, sperms and polar bodies are all haploid products of meiosis.
questions.keyConcept: The primary oocyte is diploid and stays arrested in prophase I from fetal life until puberty.

questions.text: Necrospermia means:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is Dead sperms because necrospermia denotes semen in which the spermatozoa present are non-viable. Complete absence of sperms is azoospermia, a low count is oligospermia and an excess of abnormal forms is teratospermia. Distinguishing these terms matters because each points to a different cause of infertility.
questions.keyConcept: Necrospermia = dead sperms; azoospermia = none; oligospermia = few; teratospermia = abnormal forms.

questions.text: The corpus luteum of pregnancy is maintained by a hormone secreted from:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the Chorion because human chorionic gonadotrophin, produced by the syncytiotrophoblast of the chorion, rescues and maintains the corpus luteum during early pregnancy. Pituitary luteinising hormone maintains the corpus luteum only in the ordinary menstrual cycle. This is also the hormone detected by pregnancy tests.
questions.keyConcept: Chorionic gonadotrophin from the syncytiotrophoblast maintains the corpus luteum of pregnancy.

questions.text: The acrosome of the sperm is derived from:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the Golgi apparatus because during spermiogenesis the Golgi complex of the spermatid forms the acrosomal vesicle that spreads as a cap over the nucleus. The mitochondria instead form the helical sheath of the middle piece and the centriole gives rise to the axoneme of the tail.
questions.keyConcept: Acrosome from Golgi, middle-piece sheath from mitochondria, tail from the centriole.

questions.text: The acrosome is formed from which part of the spermatid?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the Golgi complex, whose vesicles coalesce into the acrosomal granule and then flatten over the anterior two thirds of the nucleus. The acrosome is effectively a large lysosome, containing hyaluronidase and acrosin used to penetrate the corona radiata and zona pellucida. The nucleus itself merely condenses.
questions.keyConcept: The acrosome is a Golgi-derived lysosome-like cap carrying hyaluronidase and acrosin.

questions.text: The oocyte completes the first meiotic division at:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is Ovulation because the primary oocyte, arrested since fetal life in prophase I, completes the first meiotic division just before ovulation under the influence of the luteinising hormone surge, extruding the first polar body. The second meiotic division is completed only at fertilization.
questions.keyConcept: Meiosis I is completed just before ovulation; meiosis II only on fertilization.

questions.text: The largest cell of the spermatogenic series is:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the Primary spermatocyte because it is the largest cell of the series, having grown considerably during the growth phase before entering the long prophase of the first meiotic division. Each subsequent stage is smaller, culminating in the spermatid and the highly condensed mature sperm.
questions.keyConcept: The primary spermatocyte is the largest cell of the spermatogenic series.

questions.text: The oocyte remains arrested until puberty in:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is prophase of the first meiotic division, specifically the diplotene or dictyotene stage, in which all primary oocytes are held from fetal life until puberty. The second meiotic arrest, in metaphase II, occurs later and is broken only by fertilization. This prolonged arrest is thought to underlie the increased risk of non-disjunction in older mothers.
questions.keyConcept: Primary oocytes are arrested in prophase I (dictyotene) from fetal life until puberty.

questions.text: Complete absence of sperms in semen is called:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is Azoospermia because the prefix a- denotes complete absence of spermatozoa from the ejaculate. Oligospermia is a reduced count, necrospermia means the sperms present are dead and teratospermia means an excess of abnormal forms. Azoospermia may be obstructive or non-obstructive in origin.
questions.keyConcept: Azoospermia = no sperms at all in the semen.

questions.text: The normal diploid number of chromosomes in the human somatic cell is:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is 44 autosomes plus 2 sex chromosomes that may be the same or different, giving the total of 46. The two sex chromosomes are identical (XX) in the female but different (XY) in the male, so any option insisting they are identical is wrong. Options quoting 46 autosomes ignore that the sex chromosomes are included in the 46.
questions.keyConcept: 46 = 44 autosomes + 2 sex chromosomes (XX in the female, XY in the male).
options: 44 autosomes + 2 sex chromosomes (may be same or different)

questions.text: Match each cell in the left column with its chromosomal formula in the right column:
questions.explanation: The oogonium and the primary spermatocyte are diploid, so they carry 44 autosomes with XX and XY respectively. After the reduction division the secondary spermatocyte and the sperm are haploid and may carry either an X or a Y, which is why the father determines the sex of the child. The secondary oocyte can only carry an X.
questions.keyConcept: Female gametes are always 22X; male gametes are 22X or 22Y, so paternal chromosomes determine sex.

questions.text: The chromosomal formula of the first polar body is:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is 22+X because the first polar body is the small haploid cell extruded when the primary oocyte completes the first meiotic division, and every female gamete carries an X chromosome. It can never carry a Y, and it is not diploid because the reduction division has already occurred.
questions.keyConcept: All oocyte-derived cells, including polar bodies, carry 22 autosomes and an X chromosome.

questions.text: Which of the following cells does not undergo cell division?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the Spermatid because it is the end product of meiosis and merely transforms into a spermatozoon during spermiogenesis without dividing again. Primary and secondary spermatocytes divide in meiosis I and II respectively, and both oocyte stages retain the capacity to complete their meiotic divisions.
questions.keyConcept: The spermatid does not divide; it only differentiates into a sperm (spermiogenesis).

questions.text: Spermiogenesis includes all the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is that the Golgi material forms the tail, which is false because the Golgi complex forms the acrosome while the tail develops from the centriole. The other four events are genuine features of spermiogenesis: acrosome formation, nuclear condensation, the mitochondrial helix of the middle piece and shedding of surplus cytoplasm as the residual body.
questions.keyConcept: In spermiogenesis the Golgi makes the acrosome and the centriole makes the tail.
options: Formation of a mitochondrial helical sheath

questions.text: Before fertilization the sperm must undergo:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is Capacitation because the sperm must spend several hours in the female genital tract, during which a glycoprotein coat and seminal proteins are removed from the acrosomal membrane, before it can undergo the acrosome reaction and fertilise. Spermiogenesis and acrosome formation are completed earlier, in the testis. The sperm keeps its tail until it enters the oocyte.
questions.keyConcept: Capacitation in the female tract must precede the acrosome reaction and fertilization.

questions.text: The chromosomal formula of the secondary oocyte is:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is 22 autosomes plus one X chromosome because the secondary oocyte is haploid, having completed the first meiotic division, and every oocyte carries an X. A Y chromosome can only be carried by a sperm, and 44XX would be the diploid formula of the oogonium or primary oocyte.
questions.keyConcept: Secondary oocyte = 22 + X (haploid).

questions.text: The non-cellular layer that surrounds the ovum is:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the Zona pellucida because it is an acellular glycoprotein coat secreted around the oocyte, unlike the corona radiata, cumulus oophorus and stratum granulosum, which are all layers of follicular cells. The theca folliculi is a cellular condensation of ovarian stroma outside the follicle. The zona carries the sperm receptors and mediates the zona reaction that blocks polyspermy.
questions.keyConcept: The zona pellucida is the acellular glycoprotein coat of the oocyte and blocks polyspermy.

questions.text: Zona pellucida is:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is a membrane that surrounds the ovum, since the zona pellucida is deposited immediately around the oocyte between it and the follicular cells. The surface covering of the ovary is the germinal epithelium and that of the testis is the tunica albuginea. The clear area on the head of the sperm is the acrosome.
questions.keyConcept: The zona pellucida lies immediately around the oocyte, inside the corona radiata.
options: A membrane that surrounds the Graafian follicle
A membrane that surrounds the ovum
The surface covering of the ovary
A clear area on the head of the sperm
The surface covering of the testis

questions.text: In a regular28-day menstrual cycle, which statement best describes ovulation?
questions.explanation: Ovulation may cause mittelschmerz in some women. The LH surge triggers ovulation; it is expected around day14 in a regular28-day cycle, but timing varies in other cycles. The sustained basal-temperature rise follows ovulation. MeiosisII is completed upon fertilization.
questions.keyConcept: Ovulation timing depends on cycle length; LH surge triggers it and some women experience pain.
options: Occurs 3 weeks after start of menstruation
Is accompanied by completion of the 2nd meiotic division
Is accompanied by pain in some women
Is accompanied by a fall in basal temperature

questions.text: The second meiotic division of the ovum occurs:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is on fertilization because the secondary oocyte is arrested in metaphase II and completes that division only when a sperm penetrates it, extruding the second polar body. If fertilization does not occur the oocyte degenerates still arrested. The first meiotic division, by contrast, is completed just before ovulation.
questions.keyConcept: Meiosis II of the oocyte is completed only on fertilization, releasing the second polar body.

questions.text: On ovulation, the ovary discharges:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is a secondary oocyte with its corona radiata, because the first meiotic division is completed just before ovulation and the oocyte is shed still surrounded by the innermost layer of follicular cells. A primary oocyte is never released, and the Graafian follicle itself remains in the ovary to become the corpus luteum.
questions.keyConcept: Ovulation discharges a secondary oocyte clothed in its corona radiata.

questions.text: If fertilization does not occur, the corpus luteum starts to regress after:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is 12-1 4 days because in the absence of chorionic gonadotrophin the corpus luteum of menstruation degenerates about two weeks after ovulation, and the resulting fall in progesterone precipitates menstruation. Only if implantation occurs is it rescued and maintained for months as the corpus luteum of pregnancy.
questions.keyConcept: Without fertilization the corpus luteum regresses after about 12-1 4 days, causing menstruation.

questions.text: The sources of progesterone secreted during pregnancy include:
questions.explanation: Both corpus luteum and placenta produce progesterone during pregnancy. The corpus luteum predominates early; production shifts toward the placenta around gestational weeks 7–9, and placenta is the major definitive source beyond 1 0 weeks. The pituitary secretes gonadotrophins, not progesterone.
questions.keyConcept: Corpus luteum supplies progesterone early; placenta predominates after the first-trimester luteal-placental shift.

questions.text: Contraceptive pills act by:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is suppressing follicle maturation, because the oestrogen and progestogen in the pill inhibit pituitary gonadotrophin release, so no follicle ripens and ovulation does not occur. The pill is neither spermicidal nor abortifacient, and withdrawal bleeding still takes place each month.
questions.keyConcept: Oral contraceptives suppress gonadotrophins, so follicles do not mature and ovulation is prevented.

questions.text: The follicular phase of the ovarian cycle is under the control of:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is pituitary FSH because follicle stimulating hormone drives the growth and maturation of the ovarian follicles in the first half of the cycle. Luteinising hormone triggers ovulation and then maintains the corpus luteum, whose progesterone governs the luteal phase.
questions.keyConcept: FSH governs the follicular phase; LH triggers ovulation and the luteal phase.

questions.text: A newly-married wife noticed a delay in her expected menstrual cycle for two weeks. A pregnancy test confirmed her pregnancy.
questions.explanation: With a regular28-day cycle and a period two weeks overdue, fertilization was approximately four weeks earlier. hCG from syncytiotrophoblast maintains the early corpus luteum; placental progesterone production becomes predominant during the first trimester.
questions.keyConcept: Two weeks overdue implies about four weeks since fertilization in a regular28-day cycle; hCG maintains early corpus luteum.

subQuestions.text: How old is the baby (from the day of fertilization)?
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Approximately four weeks after fertilization, assuming a regular28-day cycle: fertilization occurs about two weeks before the expected period, which is now two weeks overdue.

subQuestions.text: Which term is proper for that baby (embryo or fetus)?
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Embryo, because the embryonic period lasts from fertilization until the end of the 8th week; only after that is the term fetus used.

subQuestions.text: What is the hormone measured in the pregnancy test?
How long does the corpus luteum persist under the effect of that hormone?
subQuestions.modelAnswer: hCG supports the corpus luteum in early pregnancy. Progesterone production shifts toward the placenta around gestational weeks 7–9, with placenta the major definitive source beyond 1 0 weeks.

questions.text: A placenta covering the internal cervical os results from implantation in which part of the uterus?
questions.explanation: Placenta praevia is a placenta covering the internal cervical os. Low implantation can produce this condition, but a merely low-lying placenta does not necessarily cover the os. Accreta and percreta instead describe abnormal depth of placental attachment.
questions.keyConcept: Placenta praevia covers the internal cervical os.

questions.text: The commonest site of ectopic pregnancy is:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the uterine tube because the great majority of ectopic pregnancies implant in the tube, most often in its ampulla, where fertilization itself takes place. Ovarian, peritoneal and cervical implantations are all rare. The tube cannot expand, so tubal pregnancy usually ruptures with severe haemorrhage.
questions.keyConcept: The uterine tube, especially the ampulla, is the commonest site of ectopic pregnancy.

questions.text: The cell that is fertilized by the sperm is the:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the secondary oocyte because the cell released at ovulation and penetrated by the sperm is arrested in metaphase II; it becomes a mature ovum only after the sperm triggers completion of that division. The primary oocyte never leaves the ovary and the polar bodies are non-functional.
questions.keyConcept: The sperm fertilizes a secondary oocyte, which then completes meiosis II to become the ovum.

questions.text: A placenta implanted in the lower uterine segment and covering the internal cervical os is called placenta:
questions.explanation: Placenta praevia is a placenta covering the internal cervical os. Low implantation can produce this condition, but a merely low-lying placenta does not necessarily cover the os. Accreta and percreta instead describe abnormal depth of placental attachment.
questions.keyConcept: Placenta praevia covers the internal cervical os.

questions.text: Enlargement of the cleaving zygote is prevented by:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the zona pellucida because it persists during cleavage and confines the dividing cells, so that the blastomeres become smaller with each division and the whole conceptus does not grow. The corona radiata and follicular cells are shed soon after fertilization. The zona is lost only just before implantation.
questions.keyConcept: The zona pellucida keeps the cleaving zygote the same size, so blastomeres get progressively smaller.

questions.text: Prevents enlargement of the dividing zygote:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the zona pellucida, the tough glycoprotein coat that surrounds the conceptus throughout cleavage and restricts its overall size. The vitelline membrane is the oocyte's own plasma membrane and does not constrain growth, and the tubal lumen plays no part in limiting the size of the conceptus.
questions.keyConcept: Cleavage occurs inside an unchanging zona pellucida, so total size stays constant.

questions.text: The process of sperm capacitation takes place within the:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the female genital tract because capacitation is the removal of a glycoprotein coat and seminal plasma proteins from the sperm surface, and it requires several hours of exposure to the secretions of the uterus and uterine tube. It cannot occur in the testis or male urethra, and it must be completed before the acrosome reaction.
questions.keyConcept: Capacitation occurs only in the female genital tract and precedes the acrosome reaction.

questions.text: No sperm can penetrate the oocyte after fertilization due to:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the zona reaction because release of the cortical granules changes the zona pellucida so that its sperm receptors are inactivated and it becomes impenetrable, thus blocking polyspermy. Hyaluronidase in fact helps sperms to penetrate, and there is no antibody or chemotactic mechanism involved.
questions.keyConcept: The cortical granule release causes the zona reaction, the definitive block to polyspermy.

questions.text: Sperm capacitation occurs in the:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the uterus because it is the only part of the female genital tract offered, and capacitation takes place in the uterus and uterine tube. The seminiferous tubules, rete testis, epididymis and vas deferens are all male passages, where the sperm matures but is not yet capacitated.
questions.keyConcept: Capacitation takes place in the uterus and uterine tube, not anywhere in the male tract.

questions.text: The site of acrosomal reaction is:
questions.explanation: The acrosomal reaction releases enzymes and alters sperm membranes to facilitate penetration of the oocyte investments. In normal reproduction this process occurs in association with the cumulus–oocyte complex in the uterine tube; it should not be defined as invariably beginning at first zona-pellucida contact.
questions.keyConcept: The acrosome reaction happens at the zona pellucida in the uterine tube.
options: In the seminiferous tubules of the testes

questions.text: Where does the process of sperm capacitation take place?
questions.explanation: Sperm acquire motility and functional maturation during epididymal passage. Further capacitation in the female tract or suitable culture conditions is required before fertilization. Sperm leaving the testis have not yet undergone epididymal maturation.
questions.keyConcept: Freshly ejaculated sperms cannot fertilize until capacitated in the female tract.

questions.text: What is the result of the zona reaction (cortical reaction)?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is that sperms can no longer enter the egg, because the cortical granules discharge enzymes that inactivate the sperm receptors of the zona and harden it. The zona pellucida and corona radiata are formed long before, in the ovary, and the reaction does not remove acrosomes.
questions.keyConcept: The zona (cortical) reaction seals the oocyte against any further sperm.
options: Sperms can now enter the egg
Sperms can no longer enter the egg

questions.text: The stage that implants into the uterus is:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the blastocyst because implantation is carried out by its trophoblast after the zona pellucida has been shed, on about the sixth day. The zygote and the 2-cell and 4-cell stages are still in the uterine tube, and the morula only reaches the uterine cavity, where it cavitates into a blastocyst before implanting.
questions.keyConcept: Only the zona-free blastocyst can implant, using its trophoblast.

questions.text: Results of fertilization include all the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is beginning of implantation because that occurs about six days later, after cleavage and blastocyst formation, and is not an immediate result of fertilization. Fertilization itself restores the diploid number, determines sex, triggers completion of meiosis II with extrusion of the second polar body, and initiates cleavage.
questions.keyConcept: Fertilization restores diploidy, completes meiosis II, determines sex and starts cleavage; implantation comes days later.
options: Restoration of diploid number of chromosomes

questions.text: The first stage that reaches the uterine lumen after fertilization is:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the morula because cleavage takes place as the conceptus travels along the uterine tube, and it enters the uterine cavity about the fourth day as a solid ball of cells. Fluid then accumulates within it and it becomes a blastocyst inside the uterus, so the blastocyst is not the first stage to arrive.
questions.keyConcept: The morula enters the uterine cavity on about day 4 and there becomes a blastocyst.

questions.text: The sex of the embryo is determined at the time of:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is fertilization because the genetic sex is settled at the moment the sperm, carrying either an X or a Y chromosome, unites with the always-X oocyte. Gonadal and phenotypic differentiation occur weeks later and merely express that already-determined chromosomal sex.
questions.keyConcept: Genetic sex is decided at fertilization by the sex chromosome carried by the sperm.

questions.text: Only one sperm can penetrate the oocyte membrane due to:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the zona reaction because cortical granule enzymes render the zona pellucida impenetrable once the first sperm has entered. Hyaluronidase and capacitation assist penetration rather than prevent it, and extrusion of the second polar body is a consequence of fertilization, not a barrier to polyspermy.
questions.keyConcept: The zona reaction is the definitive barrier that permits monospermic fertilization.

questions.text: Normal site of fertilization is:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the lateral part of the uterine tube, that is the ampulla, where the sperm meets the oocyte within about a day of ovulation. Fertilization in the uterus itself is too late, because the oocyte survives only some 24 hours, and fertilization on the ovarian surface would give an ovarian ectopic pregnancy.
questions.keyConcept: Fertilization normally occurs in the ampulla, the lateral part of the uterine tube.

questions.text: Implantation of blastocyst begins in which post-fertilization day?
questions.explanation: Implantation begins around day6–7 after fertilization and is completed by the middle of the second week. Different intermediate stages include attachment, burial and closure of the endometrial surface.
questions.keyConcept: Implantation starts on day 6 and finishes about day 9-10.

questions.text: Which listed site is the usual implantation site on the posterior wall of the upper uterine body?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the posterior wall of the body of the uterus, the usual site of normal implantation in the upper part of the uterine body. Implantation in the lower uterus gives placenta praevia, and implantation in the cervix or on the ovary is ectopic.
questions.keyConcept: Normal implantation is in the upper part of the uterine body, usually the posterior wall.
options: Anterior wall of body of uterus
Posterior wall of body of uterus

questions.text: Which of the following could not be a place for ectopic pregnancy?
questions.explanation: Tubal implantation is ectopic. Implantation in the lower uterine cavity is intrauterine; it can produce a low-lying placenta or placenta praevia if the placenta covers the internal cervical os.
questions.keyConcept: Ectopic means implantation outside the uterine cavity; a low intrauterine implantation is praevia, not ectopic.
options: Lower part of body of uterus

questions.text: Which part of the decidua lies between the embryonic pole of the blastocyst & the endometrium?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the decidua basalis because it is the part deep to the embryonic pole, between the conceptus and the myometrium, and it forms the maternal part of the placenta. The decidua capsularis covers the conceptus superficially and the decidua parietalis lines the rest of the uterine cavity.
questions.keyConcept: Decidua basalis lies deep to the embryo and becomes the maternal placenta; capsularis covers it; parietalis lines the rest.

questions.text: A newly-married woman had a delayed menstrual period & her pregnancy test was positive. Two weeks later, she got bleeding & abdominal pain. In the hospital, she was diagnosed to have ectopic pregnancy.
questions.explanation: The correct answers follow from the anatomy of the uterine tube and the behaviour of the trophoblast: the narrow, non-distensible tube is eroded and stretched, giving pain and bleeding and often rupture, while normal implantation occurs high in the uterine body where the endometrium can undergo the decidual reaction.
questions.keyConcept: Tubal pregnancy erodes and ruptures the non-distensible tube; normal implantation is high on the posterior uterine wall.

subQuestions.modelAnswer: The tube cannot expand as the conceptus grows, so its distension and the erosion of its wall by the trophoblast cause pain and bleeding, and may end in tubal rupture with intraperitoneal haemorrhage. The vaginal bleeding comes from breakdown of the decidua in the uterus as hormonal support falls.

subQuestions.text: What are the common sites of ectopic pregnancy?
subQuestions.modelAnswer: The uterine tube is by far the commonest, especially the ampulla, then the isthmus and interstitial part; less often the ovary, the peritoneal or abdominal cavity, and the cervix.

subQuestions.text: What is the normal site of implantation?
subQuestions.modelAnswer: The upper part of the body of the uterus, usually on the posterior wall.

questions.text: A 27-year-old wife discovered that she had a positive pregnancy test but the level of the hormones was lower than expected. Later she got unilateral abdominal pain suggestive of appendicitis with mild vaginal bleeding. In the hospital, she knew that she had disturbed tubal pregnancy.
questions.explanation: A zona-free blastocyst implants in the endometrium, normally in the upper uterine body. Implantation is completed by the middle of the second week. A tubal pregnancy cannot normally accommodate the growing conceptus and may rupture; low intrauterine implantation is not ectopic and is praevia only when placenta covers the internal os.
questions.keyConcept: Implantation finishes in the middle of week 2; tubal implantation is ectopic; praevia covers internal os.

subQuestions.text: Why can a tubal pregnancy not normally reach full term?
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Because the uterine tube has a narrow lumen, a thin wall and no proper decidua, so it cannot enlarge with the conceptus and its eroded wall ruptures early, usually within the first two months.

subQuestions.text: Which structure should disappear for implantation to occur?
subQuestions.modelAnswer: The zona pellucida, which must be shed (hatching) before the trophoblast can contact and invade the endometrium.

subQuestions.text: What is the normal site of implantation?
subQuestions.modelAnswer: The upper part of the body of the uterus, usually the posterior wall.

subQuestions.text: What is the embryonic stage that is implanted?

subQuestions.modelAnswer: Implantation is completed by the middle of the second week after fertilization.

subQuestions.text: Can you consider implantation in the lower uterus ectopic?
subQuestions.modelAnswer: No. It is within the uterine cavity. It may produce a low-lying placenta or placenta praevia if the placenta covers the internal cervical os.

questions.text: Define spermatogenesis and mention its steps?
questions.explanation: The correct answer must define the process and name the four phases of proliferation, growth, maturation and transformation. Note that only the maturation phase is meiotic and that the growth and transformation phases involve no cell division at all.
questions.keyConcept: Spermatogenesis (60-6 4 days) = proliferation, growth, maturation (meiosis) and transformation (spermiogenesis).
questions.modelAnswer: Spermatogenesis is the sequence of events by which the primitive germ cells of the seminiferous tubules, the spermatogonia, are converted into mature spermatozoa; it begins at puberty and continues throughout life, and it takes about 60-6 4 days. It passes through four phases. In the proliferation phase the spermatogonia multiply repeatedly by mitosis. In the growth phase one daughter cell enlarges to become the primary spermatocyte, the largest cell of the series. In the maturation phase the primary spermatocyte undergoes the first meiotic (reduction) division to give two haploid secondary spermatocytes, each of which divides again in the second meiotic division to give two spermatids, so that four spermatids arise from each primary spermatocyte. In the transformation phase (spermiogenesis) each spermatid is remodelled, without further division, into a spermatozoon.

questions.text: Define spermiogenesis and describe the changes that occur to the spermatid during this process?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is that the Golgi forms the acrosome, the nucleus condenses, the centriole forms the tail, the mitochondria form the middle-piece helix and the excess cytoplasm is shed. The trap is to attribute the tail to the Golgi; the Golgi makes only the acrosome.
questions.keyConcept: Spermiogenesis: Golgi to acrosome, nucleus condenses, centriole to tail, mitochondria to middle piece, cytoplasm shed.
questions.modelAnswer: Spermiogenesis is the transformation phase of spermatogenesis, in which the non-dividing spermatid is remodelled into a mature spermatozoon. The Golgi apparatus forms the acrosomal vesicle, which flattens as the acrosomal cap over the anterior two thirds of the nucleus and contains hyaluronidase and acrosin. The nucleus condenses and elongates to form the head, while one centriole gives rise to the axoneme of the tail. The mitochondria migrate and arrange themselves as a helical sheath around the proximal part of the tail, forming the middle piece that supplies the energy for motility. Finally most of the cytoplasm is shed as a residual body and is phagocytosed by the Sertoli cells.

questions.text: Mention 2 cells that have the diploid number of chromosomes in spermatogenesis?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the spermatogonium and the primary spermatocyte, since the first meiotic division that halves the chromosome number takes place only when the primary spermatocyte divides. Their formula is 44XY.
questions.keyConcept: Diploid in spermatogenesis: spermatogonium and primary spermatocyte (44XY).
questions.modelAnswer: The spermatogonium (both the stem and the daughter spermatogonium) and the primary spermatocyte are diploid, each carrying 46 chromosomes, that is 44 autosomes with an X and a Y (44XY). They are diploid because they arise by mitosis and have not yet passed through the reduction division. Every later cell of the series, namely the secondary spermatocyte, the spermatid and the sperm, is haploid.

questions.text: Mention 3 cells that have the haploid number of chromosomes in spermatogenesis?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the secondary spermatocyte, the spermatid and the sperm, all produced after the reduction division. Their formula 22X or 22Y is the reason the father determines the sex of the child.
questions.keyConcept: Haploid in spermatogenesis: secondary spermatocyte, spermatid and sperm (22X or 22Y).
questions.modelAnswer: The secondary spermatocyte, the spermatid and the mature spermatozoon are all haploid, each carrying 23 chromosomes, that is 22 autosomes with either an X or a Y (22X or 22Y). The secondary spermatocyte becomes haploid as soon as the first meiotic (reduction) division is complete, although its chromosomes still have two chromatids each. Because the male gamete may carry either an X or a Y, it is the sperm that determines the genetic sex of the embryo.

questions.text: Define oogenesis and mention its steps?
questions.explanation: The correct answer must contrast oogenesis with spermatogenesis: it starts in fetal life, has two long arrests, has no transformation phase, and produces one ovum instead of four gametes. The two arrests (prophase I until puberty, metaphase II until fertilization) are the most examined points.
questions.keyConcept: Oogenesis: prenatal proliferation, arrest in prophase I until puberty, meiosis I before ovulation, meiosis II only on fertilization; one ovum per primary oocyte.
questions.modelAnswer: Oogenesis is the sequence of events by which the primitive germ cells of the ovary, the oogonia, are converted into mature ova. It begins in intrauterine life, is arrested from before birth until puberty, and is completed only if fertilization occurs. In the proliferation phase, entirely prenatal, the oogonia multiply by mitosis. In the growth phase each enlarges into a primary oocyte, which then remains arrested in the prophase of the first meiotic division from fetal life until puberty. In the maturation phase, just before ovulation, the primary oocyte completes the first meiotic division to give one large secondary oocyte and a small first polar body; the secondary oocyte is arrested in metaphase of the second meiotic division and completes it, extruding the second polar body, only when a sperm penetrates it. There is no transformation phase, and each primary oocyte yields only one functioning ovum plus polar bodies.

questions.text: Mention 2 cells that have the diploid number of chromosomes in oogenesis?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the oogonium and the primary oocyte, with the formula 44XX, since the reduction division is only completed just before ovulation. Every female cell of the series carries two X chromosomes at this stage.
questions.keyConcept: Diploid in oogenesis: oogonium and primary oocyte (44XX).
questions.modelAnswer: The oogonium (including the daughter oogonium) and the primary oocyte are diploid, each with 46 chromosomes, that is 44 autosomes and two X chromosomes (44XX). Both are formed by mitosis, and the primary oocyte remains diploid throughout its long arrest in the prophase of the first meiotic division. All later cells, the secondary oocyte, the polar bodies and the mature ovum, are haploid.

questions.text: Mention 3 cells that have the haploid number of chromosomes in oogenesis?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the secondary oocyte, the polar bodies and the mature ovum, all with the formula 22X. The polar bodies are haploid but non-functional and eventually degenerate.
questions.keyConcept: Haploid in oogenesis: secondary oocyte, polar bodies and mature ovum (22X).
questions.modelAnswer: The secondary oocyte, the polar bodies (first and second) and the mature ovum are all haploid, each with 23 chromosomes, that is 22 autosomes and one X chromosome (22X). They arise after the first meiotic division, which is completed just before ovulation. Because the female gamete can only carry an X chromosome, the sex of the embryo is determined by the sperm and not by the ovum.

questions.text: Mention the 2 uterine phases and the 2 ovarian phases of the female cycle?
questions.explanation: The correct answer pairs the ovarian follicular and luteal phases with the uterine proliferative and secretory phases, since each uterine change is the endometrial response to the ovarian hormone of that phase. Ovulation on day 14 is the dividing line.
questions.keyConcept: Ovary: follicular then luteal. Uterus: proliferative (oestrogen) then secretory (progesterone). Ovulation divides them on day 14.
questions.modelAnswer: The ovarian cycle has two phases separated by ovulation. The follicular (pre-ovulatory) phase occupies days 1 to 14, is controlled by pituitary FSH and is characterised by growth and maturation of the ovarian follicles with secretion of oestrogen. The luteal (post-ovulatory) phase occupies days 15 to 28, follows the LH surge, and is characterised by the corpus luteum secreting progesterone and oestrogen. The uterine (menstrual) cycle likewise has a proliferative (follicular) phase, days 5 to 14, in which the endometrium regenerates and thickens under oestrogen, and a secretory (luteal) phase, days 15 to 28, in which under progesterone the glands become tortuous and secretory and the endometrium is prepared for implantation; this is preceded by the menstrual phase of days 1 to 4 when the endometrium is shed.

questions.text: What is the expected day of ovulation? What are its results?
questions.explanation: The oocyte is generally fertilizable for about 24 hours after ovulation. Under favorable conditions sperm can retain fertilizing capacity for up to 5 days, so intercourse before ovulation can lead to pregnancy.
questions.keyConcept: Ovulation on day 14 releases a secondary oocyte in its corona radiata and leaves the corpus luteum behind.
questions.modelAnswer: Ovulation occurs on the 14th day of a regular 28-day cycle, that is 1 4 days before the first day of the next period, under the influence of the luteinising hormone surge. Its results are the rupture of the mature Graafian follicle and the discharge of a secondary oocyte, arrested in metaphase of the second meiotic division and surrounded by the zona pellucida and the corona radiata, into the peritoneal cavity, whence it is picked up by the fimbriae of the uterine tube. The remains of the follicle are converted into the corpus luteum, which secretes progesterone. Ovulation is accompanied by a slight rise in basal body temperature and, in some women, by mid-cycle pain (mittelschmerz), and the oocyte remains fertilizable for only about 24 hours.

questions.text: What is the pregnancy hormone?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is human chorionic gonadotrophin, produced by the syncytiotrophoblast, because it is both the hormone detected by pregnancy tests and the hormone that maintains the corpus luteum. Progesterone is the hormone of pregnancy maintenance, but hCG is the hormone that signals pregnancy.
questions.keyConcept: hCG supports the early corpus luteum; the progesterone shift to placenta occurs in the first trimester.
questions.modelAnswer: Human chorionic gonadotrophin (hCG) is secreted by syncytiotrophoblast and is detected in standard pregnancy tests. It supports the corpus luteum in early pregnancy. Progesterone production shifts toward the placenta around gestational weeks 7–9, and the placenta becomes the major definitive source beyond 1 0 weeks.

questions.text: The normal haploid chromosome number of the human is:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is 22 autosomes + a male or female sex chromosome because the haploid gamete carries exactly half of the 46 somatic chromosomes, that is 22 autosomes plus a single sex chromosome (X or Y). Options containing two sex chromosomes describe the diploid somatic pattern, not a gamete. The options quoting 23 autosomes are wrong because only 22 of the 23 haploid chromosomes are autosomes.
questions.keyConcept: Haploid gamete = 22 autosomes + one sex chromosome (X or Y); diploid somatic cell = 44 autosomes + 2 sex chromosomes.
options: 23 autosomes + a male or female sex chromosome
22 autosomes + a male or female sex chromosome

questions.text: Production of mature sperm by meiotic spermatogenesis normally begins at:
questions.explanation: Meiotic spermatogenesis leading to mature sperm normally begins at puberty. Earlier primordial germ-cell differentiation and establishment of the male germ-cell lineage occur during fetal development, so these are not equivalent milestones.
questions.keyConcept: Mature sperm production begins at puberty; germ-cell lineage differentiation starts earlier.

questions.text: Which of the following cells are not capable of cell division and increasing the number of male germ cells?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the Spermatid because it is the end product of the maturation divisions and undergoes only spermiogenesis, a process of transformation without any further cell division. Spermatogonia divide mitotically, while primary and secondary spermatocytes divide by the first and second meiotic divisions respectively, so all three of them still increase cell number.
questions.keyConcept: The spermatid never divides; it only transforms into a sperm by spermiogenesis.

questions.text: As regards spermiogenesis, all are true EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is that the cytoplasm forms the head of the sperm, because during spermiogenesis most of the cytoplasm is actually shed as a residual body; it is the condensed nucleus capped by the acrosome that forms the head. The other statements are all correct features of spermiogenesis: the spermatid nucleus is haploid, the Golgi zone becomes the acrosome, the mitochondria form the helical sheath of the middle piece and the centrioles give the axial filament of the tail.
questions.keyConcept: In spermiogenesis the head is the condensed nucleus plus acrosome; the cytoplasm is shed, not retained.
options: The nucleus contains half the number of chromosomes
Mitochondria form the bulk of the middle piece
The centrioles form the axial filament
Cytoplasm forms the head of the sperm

questions.text: When the 2ry oocyte is ovulated, it is surrounded by:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is B and C only because the ovulated secondary oocyte carries with it the non-cellular zona pellucida immediately around it and the innermost layer of follicular cells, the corona radiata, outside that. The theca interna is a vascular endocrine layer of the wall of the Graafian follicle that stays behind in the ovary and contributes to the corpus luteum, so it is not shed with the oocyte.
questions.keyConcept: The ovulated oocyte carries the zona pellucida and corona radiata; the theca interna remains in the ovary.

questions.text: During the progestational (secretory) phase of the menstrual cycle:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is that the arteries become tortuous because under the influence of progesterone from the corpus luteum the spiral arteries of the endometrium elongate and coil. Follicle maturation belongs to the preceding follicular phase, the glands dilate and become tortuous rather than constrict, progesterone is at its peak rather than dropping, and the endometrium is thick and oedematous rather than thin.
questions.keyConcept: Secretory phase: progesterone thickens the endometrium, coils the spiral arteries and dilates the glands.

questions.text: The spermatid contains:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is 23 chromosomes because the spermatid is produced by the second meiotic division of the secondary spermatocyte and is therefore haploid, carrying 22 autosomes plus one sex chromosome. Forty-six is the diploid somatic number found in spermatogonia and primary spermatocytes, and 44 counts only the autosomes while ignoring the sex chromosomes.
questions.keyConcept: The spermatid is haploid: 23 chromosomes (22 autosomes + 1 sex chromosome).

questions.text: Concerning the spermatogenesis, all of the following are true except:
questions.explanation: Spermatogenesis occurs in seminiferous tubules and includes mitosis, meiosis and spermiogenesis. One primary spermatocyte yields four spermatids. It begins at puberty and can continue into old age; menopause is a female reproductive event.
questions.keyConcept: Spermatogenesis begins at puberty and continues into old age; there is no male menopause.
options: It occurs in the seminiferous tubules of the testis
It includes mitotic and meiotic divisions
It starts from puberty until menopause
One primary spermatocyte gives rise to four spermatids

questions.text: The first meiotic division occurs in the:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the Primary spermatocyte because it is the diploid cell that undergoes the first (reduction) meiotic division to give two haploid secondary spermatocytes. The secondary spermatocyte performs the second meiotic division, while the spermatid and the mature sperm never divide at all.
questions.keyConcept: First meiotic division: primary spermatocyte to two secondary spermatocytes.

questions.text: The second meiotic division occurs in the:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the Secondary spermatocyte because it divides by the second (equational) meiotic division to give two spermatids, so that each primary spermatocyte finally yields four spermatids. The primary spermatocyte performs the first meiotic division, and neither the spermatid nor the sperm divides.
questions.keyConcept: Second meiotic division: each secondary spermatocyte gives two spermatids.

questions.text: Oligospermia is:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is a decreased number of sperms in the semen, since the prefix oligo- means few and refers to the sperm count, not to the volume of the ejaculate. Dead sperms in the semen is necrospermia and complete absence of sperms is azoospermia.
questions.keyConcept: Oligospermia = low sperm count; necrospermia = dead sperms; azoospermia = no sperms.
options: Decreased number of sperms in semen
No sperms are found in the semen

questions.text: All are true about the sperm except:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is that the sperm is a diploid cell, because it is in fact haploid, carrying only 23 chromosomes after the two meiotic divisions. The remaining statements are true: the sperm is actively motile by its tail, it penetrates the oocyte at fertilisation, and it is structurally divided into a head, a middle piece and a tail.
questions.keyConcept: The mature sperm is a haploid, motile cell with head, middle piece and tail.
options: Formed of head, middle piece and tail

questions.text: Oogenesis:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is that it starts in the intrauterine life of the female, because the oogonia multiply and enter the first meiotic division as primary oocytes before birth, then arrest in prophase until puberty. Only the completion of oogenesis, not its beginning, occurs between puberty and menopause, and it takes place in the ovary rather than in the fallopian tube.
questions.keyConcept: Oogenesis begins before birth; the primary oocyte is arrested in prophase I until puberty.
options: Starts at the puberty until the menopause
Starts at the intrauterine life of the female

questions.text: The corpus luteum is the remaining part of the Graafian follicle after ovulation, it secrets mainly:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is Progesterone because the luteinised granulosa cells of the corpus luteum are the main source of progesterone, which prepares and maintains the secretory endometrium. Oestrogen is secreted in smaller amounts and is mainly a product of the maturing follicle, while human chorionic gonadotrophin comes from the syncytiotrophoblast of the chorion, not from the corpus luteum.
questions.keyConcept: The corpus luteum secretes mainly progesterone; hCG comes from the trophoblast.

questions.text: The uni-ovular twins results from:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is fertilisation of one ovum by one sperm with subsequent division of the zygote into two embryos, because uni-ovular (identical, monozygotic) twins arise from a single zygote and are therefore genetically identical and always of the same sex. Fertilisation of two ova by two sperms produces bi-ovular (fraternal) twins, and fertilisation of one ovum by two sperms is an abnormal, non-viable event.
questions.keyConcept: Uni-ovular twins: one ovum, one sperm, one zygote that splits; always identical and same sex.
options: Fertilization of one ovum with 2 sperms
Fertilization of two ovum with 2 sperms
Fertilization of one ovum with one sperm and the resulting zygote is divided into 2 embryos

questions.text: All about the bi-ovular twins are true except:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is that the incidence is 30%, which is far too high; bi-ovular twinning is an uncommon event and nothing approaching a third of pregnancies. The other statements are correct, since bi-ovular twins arise from two ova fertilised by two sperms, may differ in appearance and sex, and each has its own placenta, amnion and umbilical cord.
questions.keyConcept: Bi-ovular twins: two ova, two sperms, separate placentas and membranes; may differ in sex.
options: They are formed from fertilization of 2 ova with 2 sperms
They are different in shape or sex
They have double placenta, amnion & umbilical cords

questions.text: The zona pellucida disappears at the:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the 5th day because the zona pellucida must be shed before the blastocyst can attach to the endometrium, and this hatching occurs on about day five, shortly before implantation begins on day six. Persistence of the zona to day six or seven would prevent implantation, while day four is still the morula stage when the zona is intact.
questions.keyConcept: The blastocyst hatches from the zona pellucida on about day 5, just before implantation.

questions.text: The decidua in which implantation occurs is:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the decidua basalis because it is the part of the endometrium lying deep to the implanted blastocyst, between the embryonic pole and the uterine wall, and it later forms the maternal part of the placenta. The decidua capsularis is the thin layer that covers the conceptus superficially, and the decidua parietalis lines the rest of the uterine cavity.
questions.keyConcept: Decidua basalis lies deep to the conceptus and forms the maternal placenta.

questions.text: The decidua that covers the blastocyst after implantation is:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the decidua capsularis because after interstitial implantation the blastocyst becomes buried in the endometrium and the overlying superficial layer closes over it as a thin capsule. The decidua basalis lies deep to the conceptus and the decidua parietalis lines the remainder of the uterine cavity.
questions.keyConcept: Decidua capsularis is the thin layer covering the implanted conceptus.

questions.text: The rest of the uterine endometrium after implantation is now called:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the decidua parietalis because this is the name given to the decidualised endometrium lining the whole of the rest of the uterine cavity away from the implantation site. The basalis lies deep to the conceptus and the capsularis covers it; as pregnancy advances the capsularis fuses with the parietalis and the uterine cavity is obliterated.
questions.keyConcept: Decidua parietalis lines the rest of the uterus and later fuses with the capsularis.

questions.text: The layer of the chorion that forms the fetal blood vessels is:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the extra-embryonic mesoderm because the mesodermal core that grows into the villus differentiates into the fetal capillaries, converting a secondary villus into a tertiary villus. The cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast are the two epithelial trophoblastic layers of the villus and are not angiogenic.
questions.keyConcept: Fetal vessels of the placenta arise from the extra-embryonic mesodermal core of the villus.

questions.text: The embryonic disc becomes bilaminar at the:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the 2nd week because during the second week the inner cell mass differentiates into the epiblast and the hypoblast, forming the bilaminar germ disc; this is why the second week is called the week of twos. The first week is occupied by fertilisation and cleavage, while the third week is the week of gastrulation when the disc becomes trilaminar.
questions.keyConcept: Week 2 = bilaminar disc (epiblast + hypoblast); week 3 = trilaminar disc.

questions.text: Which layer of the bilaminar embryonic disc forms the floor of the amniotic cavity?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the Epiblast because it is the dorsal layer of the bilaminar disc and its upper surface forms the floor of the amniotic cavity. The hypoblast is the ventral layer facing the yolk sac, Heuser's membrane lines the primary yolk sac, and the amniogenic epithelium forms the roof and walls of the amniotic cavity rather than the disc itself.
questions.keyConcept: Epiblast faces the amniotic cavity; hypoblast faces the yolk sac.

questions.text: The primary yolk sac is roofed by:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the Hypoblast because the primary yolk sac lies immediately beneath the disc and its roof is formed by the hypoblast, while its walls and floor are lined by the exocoelomic (Heuser's) membrane. The epiblast forms the floor of the amniotic cavity above, and the amniogenic epithelium belongs to the amnion.
questions.keyConcept: Primary yolk sac: roofed by hypoblast, lined elsewhere by Heuser's membrane.

questions.text: The cavity between the 2 layers of the primary mesoderm is:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the extra-embryonic coelom because cavitation within the extra-embryonic (primary) mesoderm splits it into a somatopleuric layer lining the trophoblast and amnion and a splanchnopleuric layer covering the yolk sac, and the cleft between them is the extra-embryonic coelom or chorionic cavity. The intra-embryonic coelom appears later within the lateral plate mesoderm of the embryo itself.
questions.keyConcept: Splitting of extra-embryonic mesoderm creates the extra-embryonic coelom (chorionic cavity).

questions.text: The neuro-enteric canal is a temporary canal that connects the:
questions.explanation: The notochordal canal communicates caudally with the primitive pit. Cranially, the notochordal process extends toward the prechordal plate.
questions.keyConcept: The neurenteric canal is a temporary communication between the amniotic cavity and the yolk sac.
options: Yolk sac with the extra-embryonic coelom

questions.text: The posterior (Caudal) neuropore is closed at:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the 27th day because closure of the neural tube proceeds in both directions from the cervical region, the cranial neuropore closing about day 25 and the caudal neuropore about two days later on day 27. Failure of closure of this caudal neuropore produces spina bifida, just as failure of the cranial neuropore produces anencephaly.
questions.keyConcept: Cranial neuropore closes about day 25, caudal neuropore about day 27.

questions.text: The embryonic disc becomes trilaminar at the:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the 3rd week because gastrulation, the process by which epiblast cells migrate through the primitive streak to form the three definitive germ layers, takes place during the third week. The disc is bilaminar in the second week, and by the fourth week folding and organogenesis are already under way.
questions.keyConcept: Gastrulation in week 3 converts the bilaminar disc into a trilaminar disc.

questions.text: The secondary mesoderm develops between the ectoderm and the endoderm except in:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is all of the above because the intraembryonic mesoderm spreads everywhere between the ectoderm and endoderm apart from three sites: the oropharyngeal (oral) membrane and the cloacal membrane, where ectoderm and endoderm remain in direct contact, and the midline occupied by the notochord. These are precisely the regions where the two outer germ layers stay apposed.
questions.keyConcept: Intraembryonic mesoderm is absent at the oral membrane, cloacal membrane and notochord.

questions.text: The intra-embryonic coelom is developed within the:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the lateral plate mesoderm because clefts appear within it and coalesce to split it into a somatic (parietal) and a splanchnic (visceral) layer, the cavity between them being the intra-embryonic coelom that becomes the pericardial, pleural and peritoneal cavities. The paraxial mesoderm segments into somites and the intermediate mesoderm forms the urogenital system, neither of which cavitates in this way.
questions.keyConcept: The intra-embryonic coelom forms by splitting of the lateral plate mesoderm into somatic and splanchnic layers.

questions.text: The diaphragm is derived from:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the septum transversum because it forms the central tendon of the diaphragm, to which the pleuroperitoneal membranes, the dorsal mesentery of the oesophagus and the body wall musculature are subsequently added. The cardiogenic plate forms the heart, while sclerotomes form vertebrae and dermomyotomes form dermis and trunk muscles.
questions.keyConcept: The septum transversum forms the central tendon of the diaphragm.
