questions.text: The urogenital system is derived from:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the intermediate plate mesoderm because this column, lying between the paraxial mesoderm and the lateral plate, forms the nephrogenic cord from which the kidneys, ureters and the genital ridges develop. The paraxial mesoderm gives somites, the lateral plate gives the body wall and serous membranes, and the cardiogenic mesoderm gives the heart.
questions.keyConcept: Intermediate (nephrogenic) mesoderm forms the urinary and genital systems.

questions.text: The visceral layer of the lateral plate mesoderm forms which of the following:
questions.explanation: The splanchnic layer of lateral plate mesoderm forms connective tissue and smooth muscle of the gut wall. Limb and trunk skeletal muscles arise from somite myotomes; somatic lateral plate forms limb connective tissue and skeletal elements.
questions.keyConcept: Splanchnic lateral plate mesoderm forms the smooth muscle and connective tissue of the gut.

questions.text: The vertebral column is derived from which of the following:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is A and B because the bodies and arches of the vertebrae are formed by the sclerotomes of the somites, while the notochord persists between them as the nucleus pulposus of each intervertebral disc. Dermomyotomes give the dermis and the segmental muscles, not the vertebrae themselves.
questions.keyConcept: Vertebrae come from sclerotomes; the notochord persists as the nucleus pulposus.

questions.text: As a result of the head fold, the most cranial structure of the embryo will be:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the forebrain because the head fold rotates the cranial end of the disc through nearly 180 degrees, so that the rapidly growing forebrain overhangs everything else and comes to lie most cranially. In doing so it carries the oral membrane, the cardiogenic plate and the septum transversum backwards beneath it, reversing their original order.
questions.keyConcept: Head folding places the forebrain most cranial, with the heart and septum transversum swept ventrocaudally.

questions.text: As a result of the tail fold, the connecting stalk becomes:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is ventral to the embryo because the tail fold swings the caudal end of the disc forwards and downwards, carrying the connecting stalk from its original caudal position onto the ventral aspect of the embryo where it joins the yolk sac to form the umbilical cord. It never comes to lie dorsally or cranially.
questions.keyConcept: Tail folding brings the connecting stalk ventrally, where it forms part of the umbilical cord.

questions.text: As a result of the 2 lateral folds, the yolk sac becomes:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is that it is compressed inside the endoderm to form the gut tube, because the two lateral folds meet ventrally and pinch the wide communication between the embryo and the yolk sac into a narrow vitello-intestinal duct, incorporating the dorsal part of the yolk sac as the primitive gut. It is the amnion, not the yolk sac, that expands to surround the embryo.
questions.keyConcept: Lateral folding incorporates the roof of the yolk sac as the gut tube and narrows the vitello-intestinal duct.
options: Compressed inside the endoderm to form the gut tube

questions.text: The chorion frondosum is facing the:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the decidua basalis because the villi related to the deep, well-vascularised decidua basalis continue to proliferate and form the bushy chorion frondosum, which becomes the fetal part of the placenta. The villi facing the poorly supplied decidua capsularis atrophy instead to form the smooth chorion laeve.
questions.keyConcept: Chorion frondosum faces the decidua basalis and forms the placenta.

questions.text: The chorion laeve is facing the:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the decidua capsularis because the villi on the superficial pole of the conceptus are compressed and poorly supplied as the capsularis stretches, so they degenerate leaving the smooth chorion laeve. The chorion frondosum, in contrast, faces the richly vascular decidua basalis.
questions.keyConcept: Chorion laeve faces the decidua capsularis and is smooth and avillous.

questions.text: The primary chorionic villus is formed of:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is cytotrophoblast plus syncytiotrophoblast because the primary villus consists only of a cytotrophoblastic core covered by syncytiotrophoblast. When extra-embryonic mesoderm invades that core it becomes a secondary villus, and when blood vessels differentiate within the mesoderm it becomes a tertiary villus.
questions.keyConcept: Primary villus = trophoblast only; secondary = plus mesoderm; tertiary = plus fetal vessels.
options: Cytotrophoblast, Syncytiotrophoblast, Mesodermal core + fetal blood vessels

questions.text: The sources of the amniotic fluid is:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is all of the above because amniotic fluid is contributed to by the amniogenic epithelium and maternal tissue fluid early on, and increasingly by fetal urine and by secretions of the fetal respiratory and gastrointestinal tracts as pregnancy advances. This is why obstruction of the fetal gut causes hydramnios and renal agenesis causes oligohydramnios.
questions.keyConcept: Amniotic fluid comes from amniogenic epithelium, fetal urine and fetal GIT secretions.
options: Secretions of the GIT of the fetus

questions.text: All are the contents of the umbilical cord at birth except:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is two umbilical veins because only one umbilical vein, the left, persists to term while the right umbilical vein disappears early in development. The cord at birth normally contains two umbilical arteries, one umbilical vein and Wharton's jelly, together with the vestigial remnants of the allantois and vitello-intestinal duct.
questions.keyConcept: Umbilical cord at term: 2 arteries, 1 (left) vein, Wharton's jelly.

questions.text: The medial umbilical ligament is the remnant of:
questions.explanation: The medial umbilical ligaments are obliterated distal umbilical arteries. The median umbilical ligament is the urachus remnant. Lateral umbilical folds contain inferior epigastric vessels.
questions.keyConcept: Medial umbilical ligaments are umbilical-artery remnants; median ligament is urachus.

questions.text: The ligamentum teres of the liver is the remnant of:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the left umbilical vein because after birth it is obliterated and persists in the free margin of the falciform ligament as the ligamentum teres of the liver. The ductus venosus that bypassed the liver becomes the ligamentum venosum, while the umbilical arteries and allantois form the umbilical ligaments of the anterior abdominal wall.
questions.keyConcept: Left umbilical vein becomes the ligamentum teres; ductus venosus becomes the ligamentum venosum.

questions.text: The median umbilical ligament id the remnant of the:
questions.explanation: The distal umbilical arteries become the paired medial umbilical ligaments. The urachus becomes the median umbilical ligament. Lateral umbilical folds contain inferior epigastric vessels.
questions.keyConcept: Allantois to urachus to median umbilical ligament (single, midline).

questions.text: All of the following anomalies might be fatal to the embryo except:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is false knots because they are merely local accumulations of Wharton's jelly or tortuosities of the umbilical vessels and do not obstruct the circulation. A true knot can tighten and occlude the vessels, and an excessively long cord may prolapse or coil around the fetal neck, both of which can be fatal.
questions.keyConcept: False knots are harmless swellings of Wharton's jelly; true knots can be fatal.
options: True knot of the umbilical cord
False knots of the umbilical cord

questions.text: When the villi are invading deep into the endometrium the placenta will be:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is placenta accreta because in this condition the chorionic villi invade abnormally deeply and adhere directly to the myometrium owing to a deficient decidua basalis, so the placenta fails to separate after delivery and causes severe haemorrhage. Placenta membranacea, bipartite and accessory placenta are anomalies of placental shape rather than of depth of invasion.
questions.keyConcept: Placenta accreta: villi invade too deeply and the placenta cannot separate after birth.

questions.text: One of the following veins carries oxygenated blood:
questions.explanation: The umbilical vein carries relatively oxygenated blood from placenta to fetus. Umbilical arteries return relatively deoxygenated blood to placenta. It is incorrect to call the umbilical vein the only oxygenated vein in the body, since pulmonary veins also carry oxygenated blood.
questions.keyConcept: The umbilical vein carries oxygenated blood; the umbilical arteries carry deoxygenated blood.

questions.text: Down's syndrome is due to:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is trisomy of chromosome 21 because Down syndrome results from an extra copy of chromosome 21, usually through non-disjunction during maternal meiosis, giving 47 chromosomes. Trisomy 18 is Edward syndrome and trisomy 13 is Patau syndrome, while there is no chromosome 23 in the numbered autosomal series.
questions.keyConcept: Down syndrome = trisomy 21 (47 chromosomes).

questions.text: Klinefelter's syndrome is due to:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is trisomy involving the X chromosome because Klinefelter syndrome has the karyotype 47,XXY, that is an extra X chromosome in a male, giving 44 autosomes plus XXY. Trisomy 18 is Edward syndrome and trisomy 21 is Down syndrome, and an extra Y alone produces the 47,XYY supermale rather than Klinefelter.
questions.keyConcept: Klinefelter syndrome = 47,XXY (44 + XXY): an extra X in a male.
options: An extra X chromosome in a male, usually47,XXY

questions.text: The zona pellucida is produced by the activity of:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the ovum and the follicular cells together because the glycoprotein layer of the zona pellucida is secreted jointly by the oocyte and by the surrounding granulosa (follicular) cells as the primary follicle grows. The corpus luteum is an endocrine structure that only forms after ovulation and plays no part in secreting the zona.
questions.keyConcept: The zona pellucida is secreted by the oocyte together with the follicular cells.

questions.text: Extra-embryonic coelom will form:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is none of the above because the pericardial, pleural and peritoneal cavities are all derived from the intra-embryonic coelom formed within the lateral plate mesoderm. The extra-embryonic coelom is the chorionic cavity outside the embryo, and it is progressively obliterated as the amnion expands.
questions.keyConcept: Serous cavities come from the intra-embryonic coelom; the extra-embryonic coelom is the chorionic cavity.

questions.text: At the caudal end of the primitive streak, the ectoderm & the endoderm meet at:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the cloacal membrane because it is the bilaminar area at the caudal end of the disc where ectoderm and endoderm remain in direct contact with no intervening mesoderm. The corresponding site at the cranial end is the oropharyngeal or oral membrane, and the notochord is a midline mesodermal rod rather than a membrane.
questions.keyConcept: Cloacal membrane caudally and oropharyngeal membrane cranially: ectoderm meets endoderm directly.

questions.text: Regarding the amnion, all of the following are true except:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is that it prevents fetal movements, because the amniotic fluid does exactly the opposite and permits free symmetrical movement of the fetus, which is essential for normal musculoskeletal development. The other statements are true: the cavity contains watery fluid, oesophageal atresia prevents swallowing and causes hydramnios, and renal agenesis abolishes fetal urine and causes oligohydramnios.
questions.keyConcept: Amniotic fluid permits fetal movement, cushions the fetus and equalises pressure.
options: Hydramnios may be due to esophageal atresia
Oligohydramnios may be due to renal agenesis (Failure of formation of the kidneys)

questions.text: Drugs will produce a great teratogenic effect during which period of pregnancy:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the first 10-1 2 weeks because this covers the embryonic period of organogenesis, when the primordia of all the organ systems are being laid down and are maximally susceptible to teratogens. In the first week the conceptus tends to respond in an all-or-none fashion, while after the first trimester the fetus is growing and maturing rather than forming organs, so defects are functional rather than gross structural.
questions.keyConcept: Maximum teratogenic susceptibility is the embryonic period, the first trimester (weeks 3-12).
options: During the first 10-1 2 weeks of pregnancy

questions.text: A woman who believes she is pregnant complains of edema and vaginal bleeding. Examination reveals high plasma hCG concentrations and placental tissue, but no evidence of an embryo. How would you explain this condition?
questions.explanation: A positive hCG test with no intrauterine pregnancy seen raises concern for an ectopic pregnancy, but can also represent an early intrauterine pregnancy. Confirmation requires clinical assessment and appropriate ultrasound and serial hCG evaluation; an adnexal gestational sac supports the ectopic diagnosis.
questions.keyConcept: Hydatidiform mole: placental tissue and very high hCG with no embryo; risk of choriocarcinoma.
questions.modelAnswer: This is a hydatidiform (vesicular) mole, an abnormal pregnancy in which the trophoblast proliferates but no embryo develops. It arises when an ovum that has lost its nucleus is fertilised, so that all the chromosomes are of paternal origin; the trophoblast, which is under paternal genetic control, therefore grows excessively while the inner cell mass fails to form. The chorionic villi degenerate into grape-like vesicles and the exuberant syncytiotrophoblast secretes very large amounts of human chorionic gonadotrophin, which explains the abnormally high plasma hCG. Clinically the uterus is larger than expected for the dates, there is vaginal bleeding, and no fetal parts or fetal heart can be demonstrated on ultrasound. The condition must be evacuated and followed up with serial hCG measurements, because a proportion of moles progress to invasive mole or choriocarcinoma.

questions.text: A young woman who has missed two menstrual periods complains of intense abdominal pain. What might an initial diagnosis be, and how would you confirm it?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is ectopic (tubal) pregnancy because amenorrhoea plus acute abdominal pain in a woman of reproductive age is ectopic until proven otherwise. A positive hCG with an empty uterus on ultrasound confirms it.
questions.keyConcept: Ectopic pregnancy: positive hCG with an empty uterine cavity on ultrasound; rupture is a surgical emergency.
questions.modelAnswer: The most likely initial diagnosis is an ectopic pregnancy, most commonly a tubal pregnancy implanted in the ampulla of the uterine tube. Amenorrhoea of about two months followed by severe abdominal pain is the classical presentation, and the pain is caused by distension and eventual rupture of the tube, which cannot expand to accommodate the growing conceptus. Confirmation is by measuring plasma human chorionic gonadotrophin, which will be positive and thus establishes that the patient is pregnant, combined with transvaginal ultrasonography, which shows an empty uterine cavity with an adnexal gestational sac. Rupture is a surgical emergency because it causes severe intraperitoneal haemorrhage and shock.

questions.text: On ultrasound examination, it was determined that a fetus had well-developed facial and thoracic regions, but caudal structures were abnormal. Kidneys were absent, lumbar and sacral vertebrae were missing. What process may have been disturbed to cause such defects?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is a disturbance of gastrulation in the caudal region because the absent kidneys and missing lumbar and sacral vertebrae are all derivatives of caudal mesoderm, while the normally formed cranial structures show that early gastrulation proceeded correctly.
questions.keyConcept: Caudal dysgenesis (sirenomelia): insufficient caudal mesoderm at gastrulation; linked to maternal diabetes.
questions.modelAnswer: The process that has been disturbed is gastrulation, specifically the formation of mesoderm in the caudal region of the embryo during the third week. Cells migrating through the caudal part of the primitive streak normally give rise to the intermediate mesoderm that forms the kidneys and to the sclerotomes that form the lumbar and sacral vertebrae. If too few cells migrate through the caudal streak the result is caudal dysgenesis, also known as caudal regression syndrome or, in its extreme form with fused lower limbs, sirenomelia. Because gastrulation proceeds in a craniocaudal sequence, the cranial structures such as the face and thorax are already established normally and are therefore spared. The condition is strongly associated with maternal diabetes mellitus.

questions.text: A 22-year-old woman consumes large quantities of alcohol at a party and loses consciousness; 3 weeks later, she misses her second consecutive period. A pregnancy test is positive. Should she be concerned about the effects of her binge-drinking episode on her baby?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is yes because the exposure coincided with the third week of development, a highly sensitive stage, and alcohol is a well-established teratogen causing fetal alcohol spectrum disorder.
questions.keyConcept: Alcohol is a teratogen; third-week exposure risks fetal alcohol spectrum disorder and holoprosencephaly.
questions.modelAnswer: Yes, she has real cause for concern. Working back from a second missed period, the binge occurred at around the third week of development, which is the period of gastrulation and the very beginning of organogenesis and one of the most teratogen-sensitive stages of the whole of development. Alcohol is a proven human teratogen and is the commonest preventable cause of intellectual disability. Exposure at this stage can produce fetal alcohol spectrum disorder, whose features include growth retardation, microcephaly and intellectual disability, midfacial hypoplasia with short palpebral fissures, a smooth philtrum and a thin upper lip, and cardiac septal defects; severe third-week exposure has also been linked to holoprosencephaly. There is no established safe threshold, so she should be counselled to abstain completely for the remainder of the pregnancy and be offered detailed antenatal ultrasound follow-up.

questions.text: The primitive streak develops in which of the following layers?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the Epiblast because the primitive streak appears as a thickening in the caudal midline of the epiblast, and it is epiblast cells that invaginate through it to form all three definitive germ layers. The hypoblast is displaced by these migrating cells rather than giving rise to the streak, and the amnion, yolk sac and trophoblast lie outside the embryonic disc altogether.
questions.keyConcept: The primitive streak arises from the epiblast, and all three germ layers come from epiblast cells.

questions.text: Which of the following is derived from somites:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the Dermis because each somite differentiates into a sclerotome, a myotome and a dermatome, and it is the dermatome that forms the dermis of the skin. Ganglia are neural crest derivatives, the pleura comes from the lateral plate mesoderm, the lining of the lungs is endodermal and the kidneys arise from the intermediate cell mass.
questions.keyConcept: Somite = sclerotome (bone) + myotome (muscle) + dermatome (dermis).

questions.text: Which syndrome has 47,XXY chromosomes?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is Klinefelter's syndrome because its karyotype is 44 autosomes plus XXY, an extra X chromosome in a phenotypic male, producing tall stature, small testes, gynaecomastia and infertility. Turner's syndrome is 44+XO, Down's is trisomy 21, Edward's is trisomy 18 and cri du chat is a deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5.
questions.keyConcept: Klinefelter's syndrome = 44 + XXY.

questions.text: An umbilical cord attached to the margin of the placenta is called:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is Battledore placenta because that is the term for marginal insertion of the umbilical cord at the edge of the placental disc rather than centrally. Velamentous insertion is attachment to the membranes outside the placenta, placenta accreta is abnormally deep villous invasion, and succenturiate placenta is an accessory lobe.
questions.keyConcept: Battledore placenta = marginal insertion of the umbilical cord.

questions.text: The major source of the intraembryonic mesoderm is:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the primitive streak because the bulk of the intraembryonic mesoderm is formed by epiblast cells invaginating through it, with smaller contributions from the primitive node and the notochord. The endoderm is itself a product of this migration rather than a source of mesoderm, and the neurenteric canal is only a transient communication between the amniotic cavity and the yolk sac.
questions.keyConcept: Sources of intraembryonic mesoderm: primitive streak, primitive node and notochord.

questions.text: Which of the following syndromes is caused by chromosomal monosomy?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is Turner's syndrome because its karyotype is 44+XO, a monosomy in which only a single X chromosome is present and the total count is 45. Down's and Edward's syndromes are trisomies of chromosomes 21 and 18, Klinefelter's has an extra X, and cri du chat is a partial deletion rather than a whole-chromosome monosomy.
questions.keyConcept: Turner's syndrome = monosomy X = 44 + XO = 45 chromosomes.

questions.text: Which of the following syndromes has the genotype 44 + XXY?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is Klinefelter's syndrome, defined by the presence of an extra X chromosome in a male giving 44 autosomes plus XXY. The superfemale carries 44+XXX, Turner's carries 44+XO, and Down's and Edward's syndromes are autosomal trisomies of chromosomes 21 and 18 respectively.
questions.keyConcept: 44 + XXY is Klinefelter's; 44 + XXX is superfemale; 44 + XYY is supermale.

questions.text: The kidneys develop from which part of the intraembryonic mesoderm?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the intermediate cell mass because this nephrogenic column between the paraxial mesoderm and the lateral plate gives rise to the pronephros, mesonephros and metanephros as well as to the gonads. The somites form the axial skeleton, muscles and dermis, while the two layers of the lateral plate form the body wall and the viscera.
questions.keyConcept: Kidneys develop from the intermediate cell mass (nephrogenic mesoderm).
options: Visceral layer of lateral plate mesoderm
Somatic layer of lateral plate mesoderm

questions.text: Which of the following is not found in the umbilical cord at full term?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the right umbilical vein because it degenerates early in development, leaving only the left umbilical vein to carry oxygenated blood from the placenta to the fetus. At term the cord contains two umbilical arteries, the single left umbilical vein, Wharton's jelly and the vestigial remnants of the allantois and vitello-intestinal duct.
questions.keyConcept: The right umbilical vein disappears; only the left umbilical vein persists to term.

questions.text: Which part of the skin is mesodermal in origin?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the dermis because it is derived from the dermatome of the somites and from lateral plate mesoderm, whereas the epidermis and all of its appendages are ectodermal. Nails and hairs are epidermal appendages and the pigment cells are melanocytes derived from the neural crest, which is also ectodermal.
questions.keyConcept: Skin is dual in origin: epidermis and appendages from ectoderm, dermis from mesoderm.

questions.text: The epithelial lining of the lower respiratory tract (larynx, trachea, bronchi and alveoli) develops principally from:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is Endoderm because the respiratory diverticulum buds from the ventral wall of the foregut, so the entire epithelial lining of the larynx, trachea, bronchi and alveoli is endodermal. The surrounding cartilage, smooth muscle and connective tissue come from splanchnic mesoderm, but the lining itself does not.
questions.keyConcept: Respiratory epithelium is endodermal; the supporting cartilage and muscle are mesodermal.

questions.text: Oligohydramnios in a pregnant female suggests which of the following anomalies?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is renal agenesis because fetal urine is the major contributor to amniotic fluid in the later part of pregnancy, so failure of kidney formation results in a severely reduced fluid volume. The other options obstruct swallowing or increase fluid production and therefore cause hydramnios, the opposite abnormality.
questions.keyConcept: Renal agenesis causes oligohydramnios; failure to swallow causes hydramnios.

questions.text: Which of the following syndromes has the genotype 44 + XO?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is Turner's syndrome, in which a single X chromosome is present with 44 autosomes, giving a total of 45 and a phenotypic female with short stature, webbed neck, streak gonads and coarctation of the aorta. Klinefelter's is 44+XXY, the superfemale 44+XXX and the supermale 44+XYY.
questions.keyConcept: Turner's syndrome = 44 + XO, the only viable human monosomy.

questions.text: Which of the following is derived from the paraxial mesoderm?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the dermis of the skin because it arises from the dermatome portion of the somites, which are the segmented derivatives of the paraxial mesoderm. The spinal cord is neuroectodermal, cardiac muscle comes from splanchnic mesoderm, the kidneys from intermediate mesoderm and the pleura from the lateral plate.
questions.keyConcept: Paraxial mesoderm forms the somites, hence axial skeleton, trunk muscle and dermis.

questions.text: The anterior neuropore closes on day:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is day 25 because closure of the neural tube begins in the cervical region and proceeds in both directions, with the cranial (anterior) neuropore closing on about the twenty-fifth day and the caudal neuropore about two days later. Failure of the anterior neuropore to close results in anencephaly.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior neuropore closes on day 25; failure causes anencephaly.

questions.text: Klinefelter's syndrome has a genotype of:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is 44 + XXY because Klinefelter's syndrome results from non-disjunction of the sex chromosomes producing an extra X in a male. The genotype 44+XY is normal male, 44+XXX is the superfemale, 44+X is Turner's syndrome and 44+XYY is the supermale.
questions.keyConcept: Klinefelter's = 44 + XXY, caused by sex chromosome non-disjunction.

questions.text: The vertebrae and ribs develops from:
questions.explanation: Somites arise from paraxial mesoderm; their sclerotomes form vertebrae and ribs. The entire axial skeleton is not uniformly somite-derived: skull regions have other cranial mesoderm and neural crest contributions.
questions.keyConcept: Paraxial mesoderm forms somites, whose sclerotomes contribute vertebrae and ribs.

questions.text: The genotype of Klinefelter's syndrome is:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is 44 + XXY, the karyotype of Klinefelter's syndrome, in which an affected male has an additional X chromosome and a total of 47 chromosomes. Option 44+X is Turner's, 44+XYY is the supermale, 44+XY is a normal male and 44+XXX is the superfemale.
questions.keyConcept: Klinefelter's syndrome: 47 chromosomes, 44 + XXY.

questions.text: The allantois is present in the:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the connecting stalk because the allantois is a small endodermal diverticulum from the caudal part of the yolk sac that grows into the extra-embryonic mesoderm of the connecting stalk. Its blood vessels become the umbilical vessels, and its intra-embryonic part becomes the urachus.
questions.keyConcept: The allantois lies in the connecting stalk; its vessels become the umbilical vessels.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT derived from the ectoderm?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the adrenal cortex because it develops from coelomic (mesodermal) epithelium, in contrast to the adrenal medulla which is a neural crest derivative and therefore ectodermal. The spinal cord and sensory epithelia come from neuroectoderm, the epidermis and its appendages from surface ectoderm, and the neural crest is itself ectodermal.
questions.keyConcept: Adrenal cortex is mesodermal; adrenal medulla is neural crest (ectodermal).

questions.text: The vertebrae and ribs is derived from:
questions.explanation: Somites arise from paraxial mesoderm; their sclerotomes form vertebrae and ribs. The entire axial skeleton is not uniformly somite-derived: skull regions have other cranial mesoderm and neural crest contributions.
questions.keyConcept: Paraxial mesoderm forms somites, whose sclerotomes contribute vertebrae and ribs.

questions.text: Which of the following is endodermal in origin?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the bronchial tree because its epithelial lining develops as an outgrowth of the endodermal foregut. The brain and the eye are neuroectodermal, the heart is derived from splanchnic mesoderm and the dermis from the somites and lateral plate mesoderm.
questions.keyConcept: The bronchial tree epithelium is an endodermal outgrowth of the foregut.

questions.text: Oligohydramnios could indicate:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is renal agenesis because the fetal kidneys produce most of the amniotic fluid in later pregnancy, so their absence gives a markedly reduced volume, a combination known as Potter sequence with pulmonary hypoplasia and limb deformities. Maternal diabetes and oesophageal atresia produce hydramnios instead, and cord knots do not alter the fluid volume.
questions.keyConcept: Oligohydramnios points to renal agenesis; hydramnios points to failure of fetal swallowing.

questions.text: Which of the following is ectodermal in origin:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the Brain because the entire central nervous system develops from the neuroectoderm of the neural plate and neural tube. The heart arises from splanchnic mesoderm, the lung and liver are endodermal outgrowths of the foregut, and the kidney develops from the intermediate mesoderm.
questions.keyConcept: The brain and spinal cord are neuroectodermal derivatives of the neural tube.

questions.text: Hydramnios could indicate which abnormality in the fetus?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is oesophageal atresia because the fetus normally swallows amniotic fluid, and an atretic oesophagus blocks this route of removal so that fluid accumulates. Agenesis of the kidneys abolishes fetal urine and therefore causes the opposite condition, oligohydramnios, while organomegaly and cardiac anomalies are not classical causes.
questions.keyConcept: Hydramnios follows failure of fetal swallowing, classically oesophageal atresia or anencephaly.

questions.text: Which of the following is derived from the intermediate cell mass of intraembryonic mesoderm?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the Kidneys because the intermediate cell mass forms the nephrogenic cord and the urogenital ridge, from which the urinary system and the gonads develop. The heart and blood vessels come from splanchnic mesoderm, while the dermis and the trunk muscles come from the dermatomes and myotomes of the somites.
questions.keyConcept: Intermediate cell mass = urogenital system.

questions.text: The earliest somites begin to appear on day:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is day 20 because the first pair of somites forms in the occipital region on the twentieth day, after which new pairs appear craniocaudally at a rate of about three per day. Days 15 and 18 fall in the period of gastrulation before segmentation begins, and by day 25 to 28 many pairs are already present.
questions.keyConcept: The first pair of somites appears on day 20 in the occipital region.

questions.text: The neural crest cells give rise to the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the retina of the eye because it develops from the optic vesicle, an outgrowth of the neural tube itself, and not from the neural crest. Melanocytes, the dorsal root and autonomic ganglia and the chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla are all classical neural crest derivatives.
questions.keyConcept: The retina comes from the neural tube (optic vesicle), not from neural crest.

questions.text: The vessels of the umbilical cord are:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is two arteries and one vein because the right umbilical vein degenerates, leaving the paired umbilical arteries carrying deoxygenated blood to the placenta and the single left umbilical vein returning oxygenated blood to the fetus. A single umbilical artery is an important anomaly associated with other congenital defects.
questions.keyConcept: Umbilical cord vessels: 2 arteries and 1 vein.

questions.text: Nucleus pulposus of intervertebral disc develops from the:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the Notochord because it is the sole adult remnant of the notochord, persisting as the gelatinous nucleus pulposus at the centre of each intervertebral disc. The sclerotomes of the somites form the vertebral bodies and the surrounding annulus fibrosus, but not the nucleus itself.
questions.keyConcept: The notochord persists only as the nucleus pulposus of the intervertebral disc.

questions.text: Which germ layer forms most of the epithelial lining of the gastrointestinal tract, excluding the oral and distal anal ectodermal regions?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is Endoderm because the epithelial lining of the gut tube and of its derived glands, including the liver and pancreas, is endodermal. The muscular and connective tissue coats of the gut are supplied by the splanchnic layer of the lateral plate mesoderm, but the question asks for the layer that forms the tract itself.
questions.keyConcept: Endoderm forms the epithelial lining of the gut and its glands.

questions.text: Pigment cells of the skin (melanocytes) are derived from the:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the Neural crest because melanoblasts arise from neural crest cells that migrate extensively to reach the basal layer of the epidermis, where they differentiate into melanocytes. The surrounding keratinocytes come from surface ectoderm and the dermis from the dermomyotome, but neither produces the pigment cells.
questions.keyConcept: Melanocytes are neural crest cells that migrate into the epidermis.

questions.text: Induces embryonic development of the nervous system:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the Notochord because it induces the overlying ectoderm to thicken into the neural plate, which is the first step of neurulation. The primitive streak generates the mesoderm and endoderm, the hypoblast is displaced during gastrulation and the connecting stalk is an extra-embryonic structure.
questions.keyConcept: The notochord induces the overlying ectoderm to form the neural plate.

questions.text: Turner's syndrome has the following genotype:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is 44 + X because Turner's syndrome is a monosomy in which only one sex chromosome, an X, is present, giving a total of 45 chromosomes. The genotype 44+XXY is Klinefelter's, 44+XXX is the superfemale, 44+XYY is the supermale and 44+XY is a normal male.
questions.keyConcept: Turner's syndrome = 44 + X (45,XO).

questions.text: On what week of intrauterine life does gastrulation occur?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the 3rd week because gastrulation, the formation of the trilaminar germ disc through the primitive streak, is the defining event of the third week of development. The first week is cleavage and implantation, the second week produces the bilaminar disc, and by the fourth week folding and organogenesis are already in progress.
questions.keyConcept: Gastrulation occurs in the third week of intrauterine life.

questions.text: Somites may differentiate into all of the following except:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the epidermis of the skin because it is a surface ectodermal derivative, whereas the somite forms only mesodermal tissues. The sclerotome gives bone and cartilage, the myotome gives skeletal muscle and the dermatome gives the dermis and its connective tissue.
questions.keyConcept: Somites give bone, cartilage, muscle and dermis, never epidermis.

questions.text: One of the following is endodermal in origin:
questions.explanation: Most epithelial lining of the gut tube is endodermal, with ectodermal exceptions at the oral and distal anal regions. Gut connective tissue and smooth muscle are largely mesodermal.
questions.keyConcept: Gut epithelium is endodermal; enamel is ectodermal; kidney, muscle and bone are mesodermal.

questions.text: The arteries, veins and lymphatic channels develop from:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is Mesoderm because all blood vessels and lymphatics arise by vasculogenesis and angiogenesis from mesodermal blood islands and from angioblasts of mesodermal origin. Neither the ectoderm nor the endoderm forms vascular tissue, and the villi and amnion are structures rather than germ layers.
questions.keyConcept: The whole cardiovascular and lymphatic system is mesodermal in origin.

questions.text: Amniotic cavity is temporarily connected to yolk sac cavity via:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the Neurenteric canal because it is the transient passage formed when the notochordal canal opens into the yolk sac while still communicating with the amniotic cavity through the primitive pit. The vitello-intestinal duct connects the gut to the yolk sac rather than the amnion, and the allantois is a diverticulum of the hindgut.
questions.keyConcept: The neurenteric canal temporarily joins the amniotic cavity to the yolk sac.

questions.text: All the following are parts of the intraembryonic mesoderm EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the connecting stalk because it is composed of extra-embryonic mesoderm and lies outside the embryonic disc, later becoming part of the umbilical cord. The sclerotome and dermatome are subdivisions of the paraxial mesoderm, and the intermediate cell mass and lateral plate are the other two columns of intraembryonic mesoderm.
questions.keyConcept: Intraembryonic mesoderm = paraxial (somites) + intermediate + lateral plate; the connecting stalk is extra-embryonic.

questions.text: All are true regarding the normal umbilical cord at birth EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is that it contains the ductus venosus, because that vessel is an intra-embryonic shunt lying within the liver which connects the umbilical vein to the inferior vena cava, and it is never a content of the cord. The cord is genuinely covered by amnion, contains one umbilical vein and two umbilical arteries, and measures about 50 cm at term.
questions.keyConcept: The ductus venosus lies in the liver, not in the umbilical cord.

questions.text: At which day in development does the somites start to appear?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the 20th day because the first pair of somites appears in the occipital region on day 20, marking the start of the somite period. Days 10 and 15 precede the formation of the paraxial mesoderm columns, while by days 28 to 35 the full complement of about 4 2 pairs is already established.
questions.keyConcept: Somites begin to appear on day 20 and are added at about three pairs per day.

questions.text: A case of hydramnios would make you suspect the baby may have:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is oesophageal atresia because an obstructed oesophagus prevents the fetus from swallowing amniotic fluid, so the volume rises and hydramnios results. Renal agenesis reduces fetal urine and therefore produces oligohydramnios, the opposite picture, while immature lungs, an absent spleen and cardiac anomalies do not classically alter the fluid volume.
questions.keyConcept: Hydramnios suggests oesophageal atresia; oligohydramnios suggests renal agenesis.

questions.text: Match the syndrome with the correct chromosomal formula.
questions.explanation: Klinefelter's syndrome is an extra X in a male giving 44 + XXY, while Turner's syndrome is monosomy X giving 44 + XO. Down's syndrome is the autosomal trisomy 21, the superfemale carries an extra X as 44 + XXX, and the supermale carries an extra Y as 44 + XYY.
questions.keyConcept: Sex chromosome formulae: Klinefelter 44+XXY, Turner 44+XO, superfemale 44+XXX, supermale 44+XYY; Down = trisomy 21.

questions.text: Match the syndrome in the column "I" with its chromosomal alteration in column "II".
questions.explanation: The supermale has an extra Y chromosome (44 + XYY) and Klinefelter's an extra X in a male (44 + XXY), while Turner's is the monosomy 44 + XO. Among the autosomal trisomies, Patau's syndrome is trisomy 13 and Down's syndrome is trisomy 21.
questions.keyConcept: Autosomal trisomies: 13 Patau, 18 Edward, 21 Down.

questions.text: Mesoderm is absent in:
questions.explanation: The oropharyngeal and cloacal membranes have apposed ectoderm and endoderm without intervening mesoderm. The notochord is itself axial mesoderm and must not be described as a site devoid of mesoderm.
questions.keyConcept: Mesoderm is absent at the oral (oropharyngeal) and cloacal membranes.

questions.text: Skin develops from:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is ectoderm and mesoderm because the skin is a dual-origin organ: the epidermis with its hairs, nails and glands comes from surface ectoderm, while the dermis comes from mesoderm, chiefly the dermatomes of the somites. The endoderm makes no contribution to the skin at all.
questions.keyConcept: Skin is ectoderm (epidermis and appendages) plus mesoderm (dermis).

questions.text: Primitive streak:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is that its formation indicates the beginning of gastrulation, since the appearance of the streak is the event that initiates the migration of epiblast cells to form the three germ layers. It appears at the caudal end of the disc, is formed by epiblast rather than hypoblast cells, appears at the beginning rather than the end of the third week, and its primitive node lies at its cranial end.
questions.keyConcept: The primitive streak appears caudally at the start of week 3 and marks the beginning of gastrulation.
options: Appears at the cranial end of the embryonic disc
Its formation indicates the beginning of gastrulation
Appears at the end of the 3rd week
Forms the primitive node at its caudal end

questions.text: Neurenteric canal is a temporary connection between:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the amniotic cavity and the yolk sac, which the neurenteric canal joins transiently when the floor of the notochordal canal breaks down while the primitive pit still opens into the amnion. It disappears when the notochordal plate folds off to form the definitive notochord, and it never communicates with the coelomic cavities.
questions.keyConcept: Neurenteric canal: a temporary communication between amniotic cavity and yolk sac.

questions.text: Visceral pericardium originates from:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the splanchnic layer of the lateral plate mesoderm because it clothes the developing viscera and therefore forms the visceral layer of every serous membrane, that is the visceral pericardium, the visceral pleura and the visceral peritoneum. The somatic layer lines the body wall and forms the corresponding parietal layers.
questions.keyConcept: Splanchnic layer forms all visceral serous layers; somatic layer forms all parietal layers.
options: Splanchnic layer of lateral plate mesoderm
Somatic layer of lateral plate mesoderm

questions.text: As regards the primitive node, choose the INCORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is that it is formed of ectoderm and endoderm, because the primitive node is in fact a heaping-up of epiblast cells at the cranial end of the streak. The other statements are correct: it appears in the third week, it contains the primitive pit, and the cells migrating through it form the notochordal process.
questions.keyConcept: The primitive node is an epiblast elevation at the cranial end of the streak containing the primitive pit.
options: It appears during the 3rd week after fertilization
It is formed of ectoderm & endoderm
It has a small pit in its middle
It is formed at the cephalic end of the primitive streak

questions.text: At caudal end of the primitive streak, ectoderm & endoderm meet at:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the cloacal membrane because it is the caudal bilaminar area where ectoderm and endoderm are directly apposed without intervening mesoderm. The buccopharyngeal membrane is the equivalent structure at the cranial end of the disc, so it is the wrong end for this question.
questions.keyConcept: Cloacal membrane caudally, buccopharyngeal membrane cranially.

questions.text: The intraembryonic mesoderm develops in:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the 3rd week because the intraembryonic mesoderm is formed during gastrulation, when epiblast cells migrate through the primitive streak between the epiblast and hypoblast. In the second week only the two layers of the bilaminar disc exist, and by the fourth week the mesoderm has already differentiated into paraxial, intermediate and lateral plate columns.
questions.keyConcept: Intraembryonic mesoderm appears in week 3 during gastrulation.

questions.text: The neural crest appears along the prominent margins of:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the neural fold because the neural crest cells arise at the crests of the elevated neural folds and detach as the folds fuse to form the neural tube. The neuropores are merely the temporary openings at each end of the closing tube, and the notochord lies ventral to the tube.
questions.keyConcept: Neural crest cells arise from the margins of the neural folds as the tube closes.

questions.text: Which of the following is derived from endoderm?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the lining epithelium of the alveoli because the whole respiratory epithelium, down to the alveolar lining, develops from the endodermal respiratory diverticulum of the foregut. The spleen, kidneys, blood vessels and lymphatics are all mesodermal derivatives.
questions.keyConcept: Alveolar lining epithelium is endodermal, derived from the foregut diverticulum.

questions.text: All the following are results of folding EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is that the connecting stalk becomes dorsal, because folding in fact carries it to the ventral aspect of the embryo where it contributes to the umbilical cord. The other statements are true results of folding: the forebrain comes to lie most cranially, the head and tail folds enclose the foregut and hindgut respectively, and the oral membrane is rotated to a ventral position.
questions.keyConcept: Folding brings the connecting stalk ventral, not dorsal.
options: Forebrain is at cranial end of embryo
Hindgut is enclosed within the tail fold
Foregut is enclosed within the head fold

questions.text: As regards the somites, all the following statements are true EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is that they develop from lateral plate mesoderm, because somites in fact arise by segmentation of the paraxial mesoderm alongside the neural tube. The remaining statements are true: the ventromedial part becomes the sclerotome which forms the vertebral column, and the dorsolateral part becomes the dermomyotome whose dermatome forms the dermis.
questions.keyConcept: Somites come from paraxial, never lateral plate, mesoderm.
options: They develop from lateral plate mesoderm
Its dermatomes form dermis of skin

questions.text: Somites form by segmentation of which subdivision of intraembryonic mesoderm?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the paraxial mesoderm because it is the only column that breaks up into the repeating blocks called somites, the basis of the segmental plan of the body. The intermediate and lateral plate mesoderm remain unsegmented, the lateral plate splitting instead into somatic and splanchnic layers around the coelom.
questions.keyConcept: Only the paraxial mesoderm segments, forming the somites.

questions.text: Neural plate is derived from:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the ectoderm dorsal to the notochord, because only that midline strip of ectoderm receives the inducing signal from the underlying notochord and thickens into the neural plate. The remaining dorsal ectoderm stays as surface ectoderm and becomes the epidermis, so the answer specifying the whole dorsal aspect is too broad.
questions.keyConcept: The neural plate is the strip of ectoderm induced by the notochord lying directly beneath it.
options: Ectoderm on whole dorsal aspect of embryo

questions.text: At the cranial end of the notochord, ectoderm & endoderm meet at:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the oropharyngeal membrane because this bilaminar area at the cranial end of the notochord, also called the buccopharyngeal membrane, is where ectoderm and endoderm are directly apposed. It later ruptures to open the mouth into the foregut, while the corresponding caudal structure is the cloacal membrane.
questions.keyConcept: Oropharyngeal membrane cranially; cloacal membrane caudally.

questions.text: As regards the notochord, all the following statements are true EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The notochord is an axial mesodermal structure derived from migrating epiblast cells. Its remnant contributes to the nucleus pulposus of intervertebral discs.
questions.keyConcept: The notochord is ectodermal (epiblast) in origin, not endodermal.
options: Shares in formation of intervertebral disc
Forms the axis of the embryo
Is caudal to the prochordal plate

questions.text: The notochord:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is that it forms the nucleus pulposus of the intervertebral disc, its only persisting adult derivative. It is derived from epiblast rather than from the roof of the yolk sac, it lies cranial to the cloacal membrane, and the spinal cord and vertebral bodies are formed by the neural tube and the sclerotomes respectively.
questions.keyConcept: The sole adult remnant of the notochord is the nucleus pulposus.
options: Is derived from roof of yolk sac
Forms the nucleus pulposus of intervertebral disc
Is found caudal to cloacal membrane

questions.text: All the following are derivatives of ectoderm EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the Pancreas because it develops as dorsal and ventral endodermal buds from the foregut. The pituitary is ectodermal from both Rathke's pouch and the neurohypophyseal bud, the nervous system from neuroectoderm, the adrenal medulla from neural crest, and enamel from the ectodermal enamel organ.
questions.keyConcept: The pancreas is an endodermal foregut derivative.

questions.text: All the following are derivatives of ectoderm EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the dermis of the skin because it is mesodermal, formed from the dermatomes of the somites and from lateral plate mesoderm. The epidermis and all its appendages, that is the hairs, nails and sweat glands, are derivatives of the surface ectoderm.
questions.keyConcept: Epidermis and its appendages are ectodermal; the dermis is mesodermal.

questions.text: All the following are derivatives of ectoderm EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Most of the gastrointestinal epithelial lining is endodermal. Oral and distal anal epithelial regions are ectodermal exceptions. The other listed structures are surface ectoderm, neuroectoderm or neural-crest derivatives.
questions.keyConcept: Gut epithelium is the endodermal exception among these ectodermal derivatives.
options: Sensory epithelium of ear, nose & eye

questions.text: All the following are fetal membranes EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the Notochord because it is an intra-embryonic axial structure, not a fetal membrane. The fetal membranes are the extra-embryonic structures that support the embryo, namely the amnion, chorion and placenta, the yolk sac, the allantois and the umbilical cord.
questions.keyConcept: Fetal membranes: amnion, chorion/placenta, yolk sac, allantois and umbilical cord.

questions.text: Secondary yolk sac cavity is lined by:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is Endoderm because the cavity of the secondary yolk sac is lined by extra-embryonic endodermal cells derived from the hypoblast. Extra-embryonic mesoderm covers this endoderm on the outside, but it does not line the cavity itself.
questions.keyConcept: The secondary yolk sac is lined by endoderm and covered by extra-embryonic mesoderm.

questions.text: As regards amnion, all the following are true EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is that it prevents fetal movements, because the amniotic fluid does the opposite and permits free symmetrical movement of the fetus, which is essential for normal musculoskeletal development. Its other functions are correctly stated: it cushions the fetus as a water jacket, receives fetal urine and forms the bag of forewaters that helps dilate the cervix in labour.
questions.keyConcept: Amniotic fluid allows fetal movement; restriction of movement is a feature of oligohydramnios.
options: It acts as a protective water jacket for the body
It is a medium for excretion of urine
It forms the bag of forewater during labor

questions.text: The primitive umbilical cord contains all the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is one umbilical artery because the cord contains two umbilical arteries, and a single artery is an anomaly associated with other congenital defects. The primitive cord correctly contains the vitelline duct, the allantois, the single persisting left umbilical vein and a portion of the extra-embryonic coelom holding the physiological midgut hernia.
questions.keyConcept: The primitive cord has TWO umbilical arteries and one vein.

questions.text: As regards anomalies of umbilical cord, the following are true EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is that a true knot is due to accumulation of Wharton's jelly, because it is a local heaping of Wharton's jelly that produces a harmless FALSE knot. A true knot results from the fetus actually passing through a loop of a long cord and can obstruct the circulation, while the other statements are correct.
questions.keyConcept: False knot = local Wharton's jelly and harmless; true knot = a real knot and dangerous.
options: A long cord may coil around the neck of the fetus
A short cord may cause early placental separation
A true knot is due to local accumulation of Wharton's jelly
A false knot does not affect the fetus
In battledore placenta, the umbilical cord is attached to margin of placenta

questions.text: Drugs will produce the greater teratogenic effect during the following period of pregnancy:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is during the first 10 to 1 2 weeks because organogenesis takes place in the embryonic period, making this the phase of maximum susceptibility to teratogens. Exposure at conception tends to follow an all-or-none pattern, and later exposure in the fetal period usually causes growth or functional disturbance rather than gross structural malformation.
questions.keyConcept: The teratogenic critical period is the first trimester, roughly weeks 3 to 12.
options: During the first 10-1 2 weeks of pregnancy
At the terminal stage of pregnancy

questions.text: Down syndrome is due to:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is trisomy of autosomes because Down syndrome is caused by three copies of chromosome 21, an autosome, usually from meiotic non-disjunction. Monosomy of a sex chromosome describes Turner's syndrome and trisomy of the sex chromosomes describes Klinefelter's and the super sex syndromes.
questions.keyConcept: Down syndrome = trisomy 21 = an autosomal trisomy.

questions.text: As regards the allantois, choose the correct statement:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is that it is a diverticulum of the hindgut, an endodermal outpouching that extends into the connecting stalk. It does not disappear completely, since its intra-embryonic part persists as the urachus, later the median umbilical ligament, and it is indeed present within the umbilical cord.
questions.keyConcept: The allantois is an endodermal hindgut diverticulum that persists as the urachus.
options: Is a diverticulum of the hindgut
Is an outpouching of the coelom into the connecting stalk
Is not found in the umbilical cord at any time

questions.text: All the following are mesodermal derivatives EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Enamel is ectodermal because it is produced by ameloblasts derived from the enamel organ. Bone, kidney, skeletal muscle, and dermis are mesodermal, whereas dentine, pulp, and cementum arise from neural crest-derived ectomesenchyme rather than mesoderm proper.
questions.keyConcept: Enamel is ectodermal; dentine, pulp, and cementum are neural crest-derived ectomesenchyme.

questions.text: All the following are derivatives of ectoderm EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the cortex of the suprarenal gland because it develops from the coelomic mesothelium and is therefore mesodermal, whereas the medulla is neural crest. The spinal cord and retina come from the neural tube, the spinal sensory ganglia from the neural crest, and the anterior pituitary from Rathke's pouch of the stomodeal ectoderm.
questions.keyConcept: Suprarenal cortex = mesoderm; suprarenal medulla = neural crest ectoderm.

questions.text: All the following are derivatives of mesoderm EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the suprarenal medulla because its chromaffin cells are modified postganglionic sympathetic neurons derived from the neural crest, and so are ectodermal. Skeletal, smooth vascular and cardiac muscle are all mesodermal, as is the suprarenal cortex which arises from coelomic epithelium.
questions.keyConcept: The suprarenal medulla is the ectodermal (neural crest) exception in a mesodermal gland.

questions.text: As regards the somites, choose the correct statement:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is all of the above because every statement describes the somites accurately. They arise by segmentation of the paraxial mesoderm and each one differentiates into a myotome forming trunk muscle, a sclerotome forming the vertebrae, and a dermatome forming the dermis of the skin.
questions.keyConcept: Somites: segmented paraxial mesoderm giving myotome, sclerotome and dermatome.
options: Differentiate into myotomes which give rise to muscles of trunk
Differentiate into sclerotomes which give rise to vertebrae
Arise by segmentation of paraxial mesoderm
Differentiate into dermatomes which give rise to dermis of skin

questions.text: The placental barrier does not include:
questions.explanation: Maternal blood enters the intervillous space directly and is not separated from the chorionic villi by maternal vascular endothelium. The early placental barrier includes syncytiotrophoblast, cytotrophoblast, villous connective tissue (extraembryonic mesoderm), and fetal capillary endothelium.
questions.keyConcept: The maternal vascular endothelium is not part of the placental barrier; maternal blood directly bathes the chorionic villi.
options: The endothelium of maternal blood vessels
The endothelium of fetal blood vessels

questions.text: The fetal part of the placenta is derived from:
questions.explanation: The chorion frondosum is the villous, fetal component of the placenta. The decidua basalis forms the maternal component, while the chorion laeve is the smooth, non-villous chorion.
questions.keyConcept: Fetal placenta = chorion frondosum; maternal placenta = decidua basalis.

questions.text: The wall of the chorionic vesicle is made of:
questions.explanation: The chorion is formed by trophoblast—cytotrophoblast plus syncytiotrophoblast—together with the extraembryonic somatic mesoderm lining it. Extraembryonic splanchnic mesoderm instead covers the yolk sac.
questions.keyConcept: Chorion = trophoblast + extraembryonic somatic mesoderm.

questions.text: The placenta is derived from:
questions.explanation: The placenta has a fetal component, the chorion frondosum, and a maternal component, the decidua basalis. The capsularis covers the conceptus and the parietalis lines the remainder of the uterus.
questions.keyConcept: Placenta = chorion frondosum + decidua basalis.

questions.text: A secondary chorionic villus is made of:
questions.explanation: A secondary villus forms when extraembryonic mesoderm grows into the trophoblastic core of a primary villus. Fetal capillaries appear later, converting it into a tertiary villus.
questions.keyConcept: Primary villus = trophoblast; secondary villus = trophoblast + mesoderm; tertiary villus adds fetal capillaries.
options: Trophoblast, primary mesoderm, and fetal capillaries

questions.text: Attachment of the umbilical cord to the margin of the placenta is called:
questions.explanation: A battledore placenta has marginal insertion of the umbilical cord. In velamentous insertion, the vessels enter the membranes before reaching the placental disc.
questions.keyConcept: Marginal cord insertion is called a battledore placenta.

questions.text: When a chorionic villus becomes invaded by mesoderm, it is called:
questions.explanation: Mesodermal invasion converts a primary chorionic villus into a secondary villus. It becomes tertiary only after fetal capillaries differentiate within the mesodermal core.
questions.keyConcept: Mesoderm creates a secondary villus; fetal vessels create a tertiary villus.

questions.text: Pygopagus means:
questions.explanation: Pygopagus twins are conjoined monozygotic twins joined posteriorly at the sacral or buttock region. Thoracic fusion is thoracopagus, and fusion at the head is craniopagus.
questions.keyConcept: Pygopagus twins are monozygotic twins fused at the sacral region.
options: Monozygotic twins fused at the thoracic region
Dizygotic twins fused at the thoracic region
Monozygotic twins fused at the sacral region
Dizygotic twins fused at the sacral region
Monozygotic twins fused at the head region

questions.text: Which listed layers are markedly reduced as the placental barrier thins during the second half of pregnancy?
questions.explanation: During pregnancy the placental barrier becomes much thinner: the cytotrophoblastic layer becomes discontinuous and largely disappears, and the villous connective tissue between trophoblast and fetal capillaries is markedly reduced. Syncytiotrophoblast and fetal capillary endothelium persist.
questions.keyConcept: The late placental barrier is thinned mainly by loss of cytotrophoblast and reduction of villous mesoderm.

questions.text: Which of the following hormones is secreted by the placenta?
questions.explanation: The syncytiotrophoblast secretes human chorionic gonadotrophin (hCG), which maintains the corpus luteum in early pregnancy. LH and FSH are pituitary hormones.
questions.keyConcept: Placental syncytiotrophoblast secretes hCG.

questions.text: On what day after fertilization does the morula reach the uterine cavity?
questions.explanation: The conceptus undergoes cleavage while moving through the uterine tube and enters the uterine cavity as a morula at about day 4. It then becomes a blastocyst before implantation begins around day 6.
questions.keyConcept: The morula reaches the uterine cavity at about day 4.

questions.text: As regards the extraembryonic mesoderm, all the following are true EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: In the terminology used by this course, extraembryonic mesoderm is the primary mesoderm, not secondary mesoderm. It contributes to the connecting stalk and chorion, surrounds the yolk sac, and splits to create the extraembryonic coelom.
questions.keyConcept: Extraembryonic mesoderm forms the connecting stalk and part of the chorion and surrounds the yolk sac.
options: It shares in formation of the chorion

questions.text: The intervillous spaces contain:
questions.explanation: Maternal blood from the spiral arteries fills the intervillous spaces and bathes the chorionic villi. Fetal blood remains within capillaries inside the villi, so the two circulations normally do not mix.
questions.keyConcept: Intervillous spaces contain maternal blood; fetal blood remains inside villous capillaries.
options: A mixture of fetal and maternal blood
Blood with high carbon dioxide content

questions.text: Which one of the following hormones is not secreted by the placenta?
questions.explanation: The placenta secretes progesterone, estrogens, human placental lactogen, and hCG. Luteinizing hormone is secreted by the anterior pituitary, not by the placenta.
questions.keyConcept: LH is pituitary; hCG, hPL, progesterone, and estrogens are placental hormones.

questions.text: Which of the following abnormalities of the placenta is due to an abnormality in implantation?
questions.explanation: Placenta praevia results from implantation in the lower uterine segment, where the placenta approaches or covers the internal cervical os. The other choices describe abnormalities of placental shape, lobulation, or cord insertion.
questions.keyConcept: Low implantation causes placenta praevia.
